General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

Has Congress Learned How To Conduct Effective Oversight?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that democratic leaders have promised that their newly introduced congressional majorities will focus on affordability and accountability.
  • It has been revealed that listening to some talk about their intends, such as in this Ezra Klein interview with incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia, I wonder whether House Democrats have learned that Congress's oversight and investigation authority is not as all-encompassing as some might think.
  • It has been revealed that I discuss the legal contours of Congressional oversight and investigatory authority in my latest Civitas Outlook column.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that democratic leaders have promised that their newly introduced congressional majorities will focus on affordability and accountability. They have also pledged to engage in extensive oversight and investigation of the Trump Administration, and firms and individuals that have operated within the White House's orbit.

It has been revealed that listening to some talk about their intends, such as in this Ezra Klein interview with incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia, I wonder whether House Democrats have learned that Congress's oversight and investigation authority is not as all-encompassing as some might think. The authority to conduct inquiries for legislative purposes is broad, but it has limits. And during the first Trump Administration, the failure of House Democrats to contend with those limits hampered oversight efforts.

It has been revealed that I discuss the legal contours of Congressional oversight and investigatory authority in my latest Civitas Outlook column. In this piece, I explain why Trump v. Mazars is the greater constraint on free-wheeling fishing expeditions than is the Trump immunity decision.

Nothing in the Constitution expressly grants Congress the power to investigate executive branch agencies, let alone the President (or anyone else, for that matter). The authority to conduct oversight is an adjunct to Congress's legislative powers. In the simplest terms, it is often necessary and proper for Congress to secure information and conduct inquiries as it considers legislation and makes appropriation decisions. Or, as the Court explained in Mazars, this "power of inquiry—with process to enforce it—is an essential and appropriate auxiliary to the legislative function." , , ,.

According to recent reports, no justice in Mazars endorsed the then-common view that Congress could demand all information it sought, subject only to the constraints imposed by Executive Privilege. Rather, the justices were unanimous that Congress lacks the power to investigate for investigation's sake, or to conduct oversight for the purpose of public disclosure or inducing prosecution. Congress has no authority to try private citizens in a committee hearing. As the Chief Justice explained in his opinion for the Court, congressional subpoenas are valid only insofar as they are "related to, and in furtherance of, a legitimate task of the Congress." More generally, congressional subpoenas must serve "a valid legislative purpose," and Congress bears the burden of demonstrating this standard is met. Document demands that appear designed more to harass or punish the political opposition than to inform legitimate legislative activity will not be enforced.

Insofar as Congress wishes to investigate the White House or high-ranking officials, its greatest investigatory authority is not the power to inquire for legislative purposes. Rather, it is the power to impeach. In practice, this means some of the greater restraints on Congressional oversight are political, rather than legal.

Industry observers note that while the Court's decision in Mazars focused on the connection between document demands and the legislative process, this is not the only path Congress may take. The Constitution grants Congress the power to enact legislation for various purposes. It also delegates the power to impeach, and these powers are distinct. As Judge Neomi Rao explained when the Mazars case was before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, "investigations of impeachable offenses simply are not, and never have been, within Congress's legislative power." They stand on their own bottom.

Sources indicate that this distinction matters, because if Congress wishes to investigate potentially impeachable offenses, it must be clear that is what it is doing so voters can evaluate its actions accordingly. "Allowing Congress to investigate impeachable officials for suspicions of criminality pursuant to the legislative power has serious consequences for the separation of powers because it allows Congress to escape the responsibility and accountability inherent in impeachment proceedings," Judge Rao warned. This wolf must come as a wolf.

In a recent development, and on Trump v. U.S., I take a different view than some other legal commentators:.

Some commentators fear that the Supreme Court's presidential immunity decision in Trump v. United States will hamper otherwise legitimate congressional inquiries. "Congress cannot act on, and courts cannot examine, the President's actions on subjects within his 'conclusive and preclusive' constitutional authority," the Court declared. While this insulates the President from criminal prosecution for actions within the core of executive authority and would accordingly limit the Congress' ability to subpoena related information for legislative oversight purposes, it is no shield in matters of impeachment.

Aggressive Congressional oversight of the executive branch is not upcoming. Nor is the politicization of oversight. Once political parties emerged, it was inevitable that party loyalty would rival (if not overcome) each branch's institutional imperatives. Oversight fights were once more political than legal, but Congress could also defend its prerogatives without invoking the courts. A Congress that legislates and appropriates through regular order has more weapons to deploy and a greater ability to force executive branch acquiescence. Insofar as the next round of oversight fights are resolved in court, it will be yet another sign of Congress's decline.

For a deeper dive, my Cato Supreme Court Review article on the Mazars and Vance decisions is here.

He notes, “The most popular thermostat features include Wi-Fi–enabled remote temperature and humidity control, custom programmable schedules, responsive touch screen with color display, fresh air ventilation control, HVAC system maintenance reminders/alerts, energy savings mode, and over-the-air upgradable software.”.

How much a fresh home thermostat costs typically depends on whether it’s a manual, a programmable, or a smart thermostat. Manual thermostats are the most basic and least expensive models—as low as $20. They usually have an LED screen, a few room temperature buttons, a fan setting, and an AC switch that allows you to set the unit to cool in the summer and heat in the winter.

According to recent reports, choosing a programmable thermostat lets customers set heating and cooling schedules based on activity, like having the heat automatically turn on at 6 a.m. on winter weekdays before everyone wakes up.

Smart thermostats allow you to adjust a home’s temperature via an app and include a wide range of features and functions, like occupancy sensing, geofencing, and smart-home integration. These thermostats can cost around $300 or more.

Industry observers note that “Programmable thermostats often provide a very basic scheduling functionality, where a smart thermostat provides wider flexibility in scheduling, as well as the ability to make changes on the go,” explains Morey. “Some use geofencing to adjust the temperature when it senses that all a home’s occupants have left and readjust when the occupants are heading back home.”.

Sources indicate that the best home thermostats must be well made, dependable, and accurate. Any extra features may benefit some customers but not others. While these home thermostats vary in features and functions, each one is a quality instrument that will help to reduce heating and cooling costs and is sure to be an asset to any home.

The Google Nest Learning Thermostat notes repetitive tasks—like when the room temperature is usually turned up or down—and adjusts the temperature automatically. Most of the time, this is relatively simple with a basic knowledge of routers and networks.

Recent findings suggest that thermostats were always meant to be functional, not decorative. While many basic models that lean more toward functionality are still available today, a lot has changed over the years in terms of aesthetics. These days, many thermostats have sleek digital display screens that look more appealing than their older counterparts. Some allow people to download a chosen background image onto the display. Most are low profile, so they don’t stick out far from the wall. A few newer models are even designed for recessing in a wall stud space, making the front of the screen nearly flush with the wall’s surface for a sleek, clean look.

Before upgrading to a new thermostat, many shoppers often have questions about which option they should choose. While some would rather stick to a functional, manual thermostat, others interested in creating cooling and heating schedules want to know more about programmable and smart options. In a recent development, dual coffee makers, also known as two-in-one or two-way coffee makers, typically produce full carafes of coffee along with single servings of drip coffee, instant coffee, espresso, and tea. They’re the ideal appliances for households with a variety of coffee preferences.

While choosing the best dual coffee maker might seem like a simple decision, there are actually a number of considerations to weigh. We’ve tested some of the top dual coffee makers on the market and reviewed them here so you can choose the ideal machine to fulfill your daily coffee fix. Our top choice was the Cuisinart Coffee Center 4-in-1 Barista Bar, but there are plenty of options to suit your coffee brewing needs.Read on for reviews of the best coffee makers available today.

Bottom line: Explore the best dual coffee makers of 2026, offering options for every budget and preference, from versatile all-in-one models to specialized espresso machines.

Recent findings suggest that these top picks take into account key shopping considerations for the best dual coffee maker in addition to overall quality and value. Read on to discover some of the top-rated options on the market in a variety of categories for delicious coffee every time.

Sources indicate that the versatility of this multifunctional barista bar helped it earn our top spot. Cuisinart’s Coffee Center is a great option for those who enjoy a variety of brews, from morning coffee to a pick-me-up cappuccino or espresso in the afternoon. It comes equipped with a standard 12-cup coffee maker on one side and a single-service brewer on the other. There’s also a steam wand that froths milk for cappuccinos, lattes, and the like.

Not only does it boast two separate reservoirs, one for the standard coffee maker and one for barista-style beverages, it has the ability to steam milk for a latte while simultaneously brewing a full pot of coffee. The single-service side works with 6-ounce, 8-ounce, and 10-ounce capsules, which means it can take both Nespresso capsules and Keurig K-cups.

In testing, we found that the control knob design makes it easy to toggle through and select from different brewing options. But we did have one gripe: The steam wand extended a little low for our usage; we had to search for a glass small enough to fit underneath it so we could froth our milk.

Cleaning the Cuisinart is similar to other dual coffee makers. We liked that most of the removable parts are dishwasher-safe, eliminating the need to hand-wash. While we appreciated the clean feature on the control panel, we’re not sure it’s much different from pressing the “Brew” button. The Cuisinart is one of the larger dual-function coffee makers we tested. While it certainly offers space savings over a Nespresso or Keurig machine and coffee maker, it does take up a fair amount of real estate on the countertop. Still, that larger size is worth it given the versatility it offers.

Read our full review: Cuisinart Coffee Center 4-in-1 Barista Bar.

In a recent development, what our tester states: “As for taste, the coffee-maker side produces robust flavors, especially when engaging the “Bold” option on the control panel. We tried both types of capsules in the single-serve side and found them to be comparable in flavor to the Nespresso and Keurig machines we tested.”—Tony Carrick, Product Reviews tester and writer.

Get the Cuisinart Coffee Center 4-in-1 dual coffee maker at Amazon or Wayfair.

It has been revealed that ninja’s specialty coffee maker is one of the most versatile products on the market, capable of brewing a full glass carafe of drip coffee as well as iced coffee and concentrated espresso-style drinks. The built-in milk frother allows you to heat milk and create silky foam for lattes, cappuccinos, and more.

Sources indicate that flavor and serving size options abound with this machine. Use the brew strength control feature to choose between three settings (classic brew, rich brew, super-rich brew) and then select from six brew sizes—single cup, XL single cup, travel mug, XL travel mug, half carafe, and full 10-cup carafe.

Industry observers note that all these options could make setting up the Ninja confusing, especially when your brain is still trying to wake up. Luckily, Ninja makes the process easy thanks to a handy double-ended scoop that clearly labels the amount of grounds to add to the filter and a water reservoir with clear markings for each serving size option. The measuring spoon attaches to the side of the machine so it won’t get lost. The reservoir on the Ninja is also a bit shorter than on other dual coffee makers we tested, which makes it easier to fit under the fridge water dispenser to fill with filtered water.

Sources indicate that the labeled control knob on the front of the unit makes it easy to dial in the desired size. There are also separate buttons for normal brewing, rich brew, iced coffee, and specialty 4-ounce espresso-style drinks. A built-in steaming wand folds out from the side of the machine for frothing milk.

We found that the Ninja makes a strong, good-tasting brew, especially when using the “Rich” setting. The frother is a nice addition but, unlike with some models we tested, milk must be frothed manually by holding a cup of milk under the wand. This requires a bit more effort to create a cappuccino, latte, or some other specialty drink.

Overall, the Ninja is an excellent and surprisingly affordable choice for anyone who wants to brew coffee as well as a variety of other types of coffee drinks.

Get the Ninja CM401 dual coffee maker at Amazon.

Dual coffee makers tend to be pricier than standard drip coffee makers. However, this Hamilton Beach model boasts both a 12-cup carafe of coffee and single servings at an affordable price. The single-serve function brews up to 14 ounces of coffee, but it uses grounds rather than pods.

According to recent reports, the two brewing options are separate (each with their own reservoirs), a setup that lets you brew a single serving while the carafe stays in place. This is useful in households with both coffee drinkers who are on the go and those who work from home. A switch on the control panel makes it easy to toggle between single serving and carafe.

Sources indicate that this Hamilton Beach machine isn’t as flashy as some higher-priced models that take K-cups or Nespresso cups, and it doesn’t make cappuccinos or lattes. It does, however, boast some useful additional features, including a 24-hour timer, auto shutoff, and brew pausing. There’s also a brew strength selector that allows coffee drinkers to choose between regular and bold flavors.Though it may lack the bells and whistles of other machines, the budget-friendly Hamilton Beach dual coffee maker is a great choice for those who want the option to brew full pots and single servings.

Get the Hamilton Beach dual coffee maker at Amazon or Best Buy.

Recent findings suggest that when a plain cup of Joe just won’t cut it, Nespresso’s Lattissima One is a premium option to brew espresso, cappuccinos, and other specialty coffee drinks. While a number of machines perform these functions for far less money, the Lattissima makes brewing these barista-style beverages much easier. Simply fill the small milk container to suit the size of cappuccino or latte desired and press the frothing button. About a minute or two later, the specialty coffee drink, complete with a good head of milk froth on the top, is ready to enjoy. There’s no need to hold milk under a frother or even spoon the froth on the drink. The Lattissima does it all automatically.

With loads of Nespresso flavors to choose from (the Lattissima comes with a large sample pack), coffee fans have plenty of options when it comes to the strength and flavor of specialty drinks. Yet while we love how the Lattissima takes the effort out of brewing, the machine cannot brew more than one drink at a time, and it doesn’t make regular coffee. That stated, given that the Lattissima is compact at just about 6 inches wide by 13 inches deep, it’s certainly possible to pair it with a traditional coffee machine on a kitchen counter.

Get the Nespresso dual coffee maker at Amazon.

Industry observers note that this dual coffee maker brews a full 12-cup glass carafe on one side and single-serving pods on the other. Various aspects of this Cuisinart’s design impressed us in testing. We liked that each side has its own reservoir, so people needn’t empty and refill the reservoir when switching from one brewing mode to the other. From Judge Justin Olson (S.D. Ind.) Friday in Robinson-Cooper v. Ivy Tech South Bend-Elkhart:.

According to recent reports, plaintiff's response brief was initially due October 2, 2026. Dkt. 99. She received two extensions, pushing back her response deadline to November 16. Dkts. 91, 100. Plaintiff argues she has met the standard of excusable neglect because presenting all the evidence in her response, including evidence of five comparators in this employment-law case, "took more time than counsel had anticipated." Dkt. 105 at 2. The Court finds Plaintiff has shown excusable neglect, including because her filing was less than an hour late and because Defendants do not claim to be prejudiced by it, dkt. 107, and so GRANTS the motion at docket entry [105] and accepts docket entry 103 as timely filed.

A court will often cut you slack for filing a day late (especially if it's just an hour late), unless the requirement is jurisdictional and thus not waivable. But no slack here as to the page limit, and because of the denial of leave to file a longer brief, "The Court will not consider any arguments Plaintiff makes after page 30 of her briefing." This means that plaintiff's arguments related to her Family Medical Leave Act claims are basically being forfeited, though her race and sex discrimination arguments are preserved. The court's reasoning:.

The Court's practices and procedures state:.

In a recent development, if a party files a motion to extend the page limit at the same time the party's brief is due, the extension request will be denied absent a compelling and unanticipated reason for violating this rule. The Court will also not consider any arguments made in pages which exceed the Local Rules' requirements.

Plaintiff acknowledges this requirement. She states her oversized filing, "results from counsel's underestimate of the space and time needed to present the comparator evidence, and the space needed to reference each cite pursuant to the docket number." As Defendants point out, Plaintiff has not provided a "compelling and unanticipated" reason for her oversized brief. The Court accordingly DENIES her motion to file an oversize response.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

If, like me, you think multi-tools are gimmicky gadgets, you might change your mind once you discover how handy they are when your toolbox isn’t within reach.

Industry observers note that our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

I admit I scoffed when my partner first started raving about his Leatherman Wave+ multi-tool. I thought it looked like an expensive, over-elaborate gadget that was destined to gather dust in a junk drawer.

However, as a keen hiker and camper, I’ve discovered how useful it is to have pliers, knives, a saw, scissors, files and other tools packed into one compact, quality piece of kit. I’ve also watched my tech-obsessed partner regularly reach for its precision tools when tinkering with his electrical equipment.

Ahead, I’ll share how a tool I once dismissed as a gimmick earned a permanent spot in my pack, and what two experts think makes a Leatherman worth the price tag.

Gemma Johnstone For Family Handyman.

I had to realize that our Leatherman Wave+ isn’t meant to replace a well-stocked toolbox to understand its value. Instead, it fills the gap when dedicated tools aren’t conveniently available or really needed.

Sources indicate that at home, I regularly use the tool’s tiny scissors to carefully prune dead leaves from our many houseplants, the knife to open packages and the small screwdriver to tighten the legs on my glasses. My partner is an IT professional who also has an impressive collection of synthesizers, and he regularly reaches for the tool to make small technical repairs and splice wires.

I’ve found the Wave+ even more useful when we’re borrowing my parents’ campervan, hiking, or camping. The bottle opener is handy for those after-adventure beers, the serrated knife slices baguettes for trailside sandwiches, the saw cuts small, dry branches for kindling, and the screwdriver has adjusted our portable stove and tightened folding chairs.

Sources indicate that the pocket-sized multi-tool packs 18 functions into a stainless-steel form that measures just four inches when closed and weighs 8.5 ounces. Alongside the tools I’ve mentioned, it has pliers, bit drivers, a wire stripper and crimper, a ruler, an extra knife blade and file, and an admittedly slightly-tricky-to-use can opener.

While I don’t regularly use all 18 tools, and I might never use some, having the selection provides peace of mind, especially in remote places.

According to recent reports, daniel Kilburn, founder of Emergency Action Planning and a preparedness expert, has carried his Leatherman Surge since his military service in 2006. “It’s an expedient tool to have on hand when you know you’re going to be someplace where you won’t have access to any others,” he states.

Scott Emanuel of knives, multi-tools, and outdoor equipment retailer Heinnie Haynes is also a multi-tool convert. He appreciated having one for quick fixes while renovating his cottage, and particularly rates the needle-nose pliers, which rival standard models rather than acting as an emergency substitute.

Kilburn suggests multi-tools can be a useful starting point for someone who doesn’t own a toolbox, and at the other end of the spectrum are the tinkerers and prepared problem-solvers Emanuel sees as natural fits.

“The person who will value a Leatherman is the one who spends their after-hours in the garage building stuff that they probably never need, it’s the kind of self-reliant and prepared person who you rely on to solve a problem,” Emanuel says.

The Leatherman Wave+ currently costs $129.95, meaning it should be a well-considered purchase rather than an impulse buy.

According to recent reports, it’s reassuring to know that you’ll be investing in a refined product designed because of a genuine practical need. Founder Tim Leatherman conceived a pliers-based multi-tool after encountering car and plumbing problems while traveling through Europe in the 1970s, and after careful development, he launched the original Pocket Survival Tool in 1983.

Today you’re paying for that established reputation and durable construction, and Leatherman backs its products with a 25-year warranty.

Recent findings suggest that “They’re ridiculously well built, really well regarded, and their choice of tools is good,” Emanuel claims. He describes sought-after Leathermans as the “collectible top end of the multi-tool market.”.

Kilburn recalls seeing lower-priced multi-tools failing his comrades during their military career. “Some disintegrate over time because they were just cheaply made with poor-quality material [and] poor-quality steel,” he indicates. His Leatherman Surge, meanwhile, has lasted over 20 years. If replacing it again, he says he would choose Leatherman over his backup Gerber multi-tool because he prefers its feel and durability.

Gemma Johnstone For Family Handyman.

According to recent reports, leatherman makes a wide range of multi-tools, so it pays to consider which functions you’ll genuinely use. The Signal model adds outdoor-focused features suited to camping, including a ferrocerium rod, emergency whistle and sharpener, but omits scissors. I use scissors enough for plant pruning, first aid and gear repairs that the Wave+ remains the better fit for me.

If you’re unlikely to use most of its functions, a smaller, cheaper multi-tool could make more sense. The Wave+ is also heavier than minimalist models, and there’s a learning curve when figuring out where everything lives.

Don’t forget that a premium multi-tool only represents good value if you look after it. We remove dirt after outdoor adventures and dry and lubricate it before storing. We also avoid forcing it to tackle jobs better suited to full-size tools. I wouldn’t, for example, choose its compact saw over a dedicated full-size version for pruning substantial tree branches in my yard.

It has been revealed that if you’re using a Wave+ in the UK, like me, be aware of the country’s knife laws. You need a “good reason” to carry it in public because its blades lock. However, Emanuel explains that the legal language is ambiguous, so you shouldn’t assume you can carry one wherever you go just because it’s part of a multi-tool.

It has been revealed that the Wave+ has convinced me that a good multi-tool is more than merely an expensive gimmick. It may not replace dedicated tools, but having so many functions at my fingertips in a form that is so compact, portable and easy to use makes it a practical, worthwhile investment.

The Wave Plus is a multi-tool workhorse. It packs 18 tools in one, including sharp blades, spring scissors, wire cutters, and more.

Still, it comes at a great price for a WQA Gold Seal-certified unit with filters that last 6 months to 1 year, making it a good water filter for homes with high-volume needs.

Get the Brondell countertop water filter at Amazon or Brondell.

According to recent reports, there’s no denying the popularity of the Substantial Berkey: its stainless steel construction and massive 8.5-liter capacity have made it a staple for large households and off-grid enthusiasts. Because it relies strictly on gravity and its proprietary Black Berkey filters, it functions entirely without electricity, plumbing, or tap pressure—you simply pour water into the top chamber and let it drip down. It also has an extremely long filter lifespan of up to 6,000 gallons per pair, meaning you won’t be constantly buying replacements.

However, its popularity comes with a couple of drawbacks. Despite the hefty price tag, Berkey lacks any official certifications, relying instead on independent lab testing. And like all gravity systems, it’s also quite bulky, standing almost 20 inches tall with no option for fridge storage. Also, because it relies on gravity, the filtration rate is quite slow—we got into the habit of filling the top reservoir a couple of times a day so it had several hours to make its way to the bottom. Still, with no gauge of any sort, we never really had any idea how much water was even in the bottom chamber. All that aside, Berkey has an almost cult-like following, and the durable stainless steel water filter body and straightforward operation are likely why.

Get the Massive Berkey countertop water filter at Amazon.

To find a selection of the best countertop water filters for home use, we began by evaluating dozens of popular models, focusing on ease of installation and use, filtration claims, capacity, and price.

After selecting seven units for testing, we performed the same set of steps with each, starting with installation. Next, we performed water quality tests before and after filtration to measure contaminant reduction, followed by blind taste tests to rate flavor and odor. We measured flow rate by timing how long each unit took to process or dispense a quart of water, assessed how easy each unit was to clean and change filters on, and rated general convenience of extra features like filter life indicators and removable pitchers.

We used each model for a minimum of 2 days to get a feel for how much we liked them overall, and for the faucet-connected models, to see whether they got in the way during regular tasks like washing hands or dishes.

The best countertop water filtration system for your home will depend on the quality concerns you want to address, how much filtered water your household uses, and how much daily upkeep you’re willing to take on. It’s smart to request a copy of your local utility’s Consumer Confidence Report or use a home water test kit, then compare potential systems’ filtration claims, capacity, footprint, and replacement-filter cost.

In a recent development, countertop water filters generally fall into two broad categories: reservoir-based systems and faucet-connected systems. Reservoir models don’t connect to your plumbing at all, while faucet-connected models attach to a standard faucet or use a diverter valve under your sink.

It has been revealed that reservoir systems hold untreated water in one tank or chamber and deliver clean water into another after it passes through the system’s filter(s). The simplest versions are water pitchers like the Epic Water Filters Pure XP Water Filter Pitcher or gravity systems like the Massive Berkey Gravity-Fed Water Filter. Since they don’t connect to your faucet, they’re great for apartments, dorms, RVs, and kitchens with incompatible faucets.

Sources indicate that countertop reverse osmosis systems also use a refillable reservoir, but rather than relying on gravity, they have an internal pump that forces the water through their filters before delivering it to a pitcher or your glass. RO systems have the added benefit of reducing dissolved solids in untreated water, but that includes beneficial minerals like calcium and magnesium and also creates wastewater that must be dumped (or used for things like cleaning or watering plants).

Faucet-connected filters either attach directly to your faucet or connect via a hose and diverter valve. When the diverter is switched to the filtration setting, tap water filters through the unit on demand and into your glass, bottle, or pot. When the diverter is off, water flows straight out of the tap as normal.

According to recent reports, two major things to consider regarding faucet-connected systems are faucet compatibility and installation. Most aren’t compatible with pull-down, pull-out, spray, sensor-operated, or nonstandard faucets, and many also have small hoses that connect the faucet to the machine, which takes up a bit of space and can look cluttered. Some allow you to run the hoses from the machine to the plumbing under your sink, but that will require an adapter and a hole in the counter for the cords to route through.

While it can be tempting to choose the purification system for water that has the longest list of contaminants removed, it’s ultimately more important to pair the system you choose with what you’re actually trying to filter out of your water.

Industry observers note that most of the best water filters have activated-carbon filters that remove unpleasant tastes and odors and may reduce other chemicals or particulates. Some systems add sediment filtration or specialty media to target things like lead, fluoride, or PFAS compounds. Since performance varies by model, always check the manufacturer’s claims rather than assuming they all work the same.

It has been revealed that reverse-osmosis systems use a membrane designed to reduce dissolved solids, which means they generally remove more contaminants than basic filtration systems. However, they can also reduce beneficial minerals, which is why some manufacturers are now adding a remineralization stage to return the filtered water to a more alkaline state.

Many of the units on this list carry third-party certification to verify tested performance beyond manufacturer claims. NSF International’s drinking-water treatment standards are the most commonly used, although you may also see mentions of accredited organizations like IAPMO R&T or WQA. While our tests using the Varify Complete Drinking Water Test Kit for this guide backed up the manufacturers’ claims, it’s still a good idea to prioritize products that carry filter certifications and look up which contaminants the product is certified to remove.

Sources indicate that then, match the certification to your specific concern. For example, if lead reduction is your main goal, you’ll want a model with NSF 53 and 58 listings.

According to recent reports, capacity has two meanings: how much water a filter can treat before replacement and how much filtered water the unit can provide at once. For our purposes, we’re defining it as how much it can filter at once, as we discuss filter life in the next section.

Since reservoir models’ ready-to-drink supply is based on the size of their clean-water chambers, larger households or those with greater needs will want to prioritize a model that holds multiple liters or gallons. Faucet-connected models can also be a good choice in those situations, as they can deliver clean water continuously as long as the tap is on.

In a recent development, flow rate—how quickly the filter provides clean drinking water—is another vital consideration. However, many manufacturers don’t list this information, and it can also vary depending on water pressure, source-water quality, temperature, and cartridge age. If this is a major concern, you may want to reach out to manufacturers directly or read online reviews for mentions of filtration speed.

It has been revealed that every countertop drinking water filter system requires filter replacement on a set schedule, which means the true cost of ownership ends up being more than what you paid for it. When choosing between systems, compare the number of filters, their individual projected filter capacity, and each one’s replacement cost.

It has been revealed that A basic pitcher may use a single cartridge that’s easy to change but needs more frequent replacement, while a multistage RO unit may have multiple filters that each have different change intervals and prices. While systems with filter-life indicators can make it much easier to know when it’s time to swap them, if your unit is noticeably slower or isn’t providing the same quality, you may still need to change filters even if it isn’t technically time.

Countertop water filters are generally pretty straightforward, but the following answers to commonly asked questions can answer any lingering queries you may have.

Recent findings suggest that water filters work by using a filtration mechanism to capture organisms and chemicals that lead to unsafe or cloudy water. A fabricated surface traps the larger contaminants, while a compound like activated carbon works as a magnet to trap smaller contaminants.

Installation depends on the type: A faucet-connected filtration system typically attaches to a compatible faucet aerator or diverter valve, while dispenser, pitcher, gravity-fed, and countertop RO models generally only require rinsing the parts, installing the filters, and filling the reservoir. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions, especially for RO units that may also require an initial flush cycle.

No, countertop water purification filters do not work with every type of kitchen faucet. Specifically, more modern designs and detachable faucets with spray nozzles may be incompatible with faucet-connected countertop water filters.

Recent findings suggest that most filters can remove chlorine, fluoride, bacteria, and parasites. To know exactly which contaminants a specific filter can remove or reduce, consult the manufacturer’s information regarding filter certification.

Yes, bacteria can grow in a countertop filter, so it’s a good idea to flush the faucet for about 20 seconds after turning on the water and then for an additional 5 to 10 seconds to filter and flush out any bacteria that may be lingering in the faucet.

Industry observers note that yes, countertop reverse osmosis systems are worth it for households seeking to remove dissolved contaminants like lead and fluoride and who prefer a plumbing-free setup. However, they generally cost more and require more maintenance than pitchers or carbon-filter-only units, so they’re best when your water test or local report identifies concerns simpler filters can’t address.

Industry observers note that filter replacement timing varies by system and filter type, so it’s best to follow the manufacturer’s schedule for your specific system. Generally speaking, pitcher and faucet units may need newly introduced filters every few months, while countertop RO filters and membranes may last anywhere from 6 months to 2 years. You may need to replace filters sooner if the flow slows noticeably or your water develops an unusual taste or odor.

In a recent development, white and Sarah (a pseudonym) met as children and, after reconnecting in their 20s, dated for more than 10 years. Sarah knew that the relationship was "toxic" and recognized the "abuse that went on throughout the years" but believed she was "trauma bonded" to White and still had feelings for him….

In a recent development, on one occasion in June 2021, White emailed Sarah with an attached video of the two of them engaging in sexual activity. Near that same time, White texted photographs to Sarah of the two of them having sex…. [T]he State charged White with two counts of breach of privacy for White unlawfully disseminating the illicit video and photographs to Sarah ….

The breach of privacy statute provides:.

"(a) Breach of privacy is knowingly and without lawful authority: …. (8) disseminating any videotape, photograph, film or image of another identifiable person 18 years of age or older who is nude or engaged in sexual activity and under circumstances in which such identifiable person had a reasonable expectation of privacy, with the intent to harass, threaten or intimidate such identifiable person, and such identifiable person did not consent to such dissemination." ….

The court held White didn't violate the statute:.

It has been revealed that here Sarah consented to the photos being taken and the video being made. White later emailed and texted the sexually explicit material only to Sarah. How did that conduct breach Sarah's privacy? ….

In a recent development, sarah had an expectation of privacy as to the photos and the video to the extent that she could reasonably expect that no one other than she and White would ever see the sexually explicit images. White did not violate that expectation of privacy.

In a recent development, the evidence indicated that White transmitted the sexually explicit material to Sarah with the intent to harass her. But for there to be a breach of privacy under [the statute], the term "disseminating" requires that the illicit material be sent to someone other than the person depicted in the material and who consented to the illicit material being made. White's conduct here more than likely constituted harassment by telecommunication device in violation of K.S.A. 21-6206, but we find it did not constitute breach of privacy….

Tech Report: "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press": "Ambiguous Evidence: Enjoining Repetition of Libels"

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I'm serializing my new Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the third and last Part:.
  • Throughout much of American history, the dominant view has been that courts can't enjoin libels.
  • Industry observers note that yet since then, many state courts have allowed permanent injunctions against libels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I'm serializing my new Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the third and last Part:.

Throughout much of American history, the dominant view has been that courts can't enjoin libels. The first precedent on this was Brandreth v. Lance (1839), an 1839 Upcoming York trial court decision. This was followed by State ex rel. Liversey v. Judge (1882), an 1882 Louisiana Supreme Court decision. Subsequent decisions helped establish this as a firm rule, seemingly culminating in Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson.

Industry observers note that yet since then, many state courts have allowed permanent injunctions against libels. By my count the court systems of thirty-four states have either so held or have in practice been so acting, with only six states plus D.C. continuing to categorically bar such injunctions. {See Eugene Volokh, Anti-Libel Injunctions, 168 U. Pa. L. Rev. 73 (2019).}.

This trend seems to have accelerated with the rise of the internet. Historically, a libel has been a short, sharp shock—typically, a one-time article in a newspaper that is printed and can't be removed—with the only possible remedy being damages or criminal prosecution. But the internet can turn libel into a steady drip, drip, drip of damage, with more readers seeing a libelous web page every day. Injunctions thus seem a more useful remedy.

Industry observers note that the internet also makes it easier for judgment-proof defendants to cause real damage; an injunction can thus be useful in a way that a damages remedy might not be. Criminal libel is theoretically available in about ten states, and there are indeed likely a couple of dozen criminal libel prosecutions in the United States each year. But in most states the only way to deploy criminal remedies in service of protecting reputation is through getting an injunction that can be enforced through the threat of criminal contempt.

Industry observers note that are these injunctions contrary to the original meaning of the First Amendment? The answer turns out to be complicated, especially if we focus on permanent injunctions, entered to forbid the repetition of material found to be libelous in a final judgment (with the defendant having had an opportunity to call for a jury trial).

It's true that early sources often view the freedom of the press as precluding prior restraints: To quote William Blackstone, "The liberty of the press is indeed essential to the nature of a free state: but this consists in laying no previous restraints upon publications, and not in freedom from censure for criminal matter when published." Yet this doesn't quite speak to the modern question whether the law may restrain repetition of material for matter found to be criminal (or tortious).

Nor does it speak to whether the law may require removal of such matter after a trial: Removal just wasn't practically an option in the print era. In such situations of injunctions against repetition of an already published libel or ordering its removal, "[e]very freeman" would retain the "undoubted right to lay what sentiments he pleases before the public" (again quoting Blackstone) at least in the first instance.

Nor is there a "restrictive power of a licenser" or "control of an inspector" in the sense that the Framers likely understood licensers, which is to say officials administering a licensing system. (To quote St. George Tucker, under that system "all books printed were previously licensed by some of the great offices of state, or the two universities, and all foreign books were exposed to a similar scrutiny before they were vended.") The injunction is imposed by a judge, often following a jury verdict, administering justice between two parties, not running a traditional licensing system that "subject[s] all freedom of sentiment to the prejudices of one man, and make[s] him the arbitrary and infallible judge of all controverted points in learning, religion, and government.".

Sources indicate that likewise, early sources stressed the importance of allowing a jury to resolve what is true and false in libel cases. But, as I noted, the modern permanent injunction in libel cases is entered after a final judgment on the merits, which at least in principle allows a defendant to demand a jury trial. If the defendant has so demanded, then any injunction would be based on the jury verdict.

This stems in part from the twentieth-century merger of law and equity, since equitable remedies, such as injunctions, can now be issued following the use of the legal procedure of a jury trial. (Historically, one argument against injunctions in libel cases has been that "equity will not enjoin a libel," a statement about the limits of the equity courts more than about constitutional protections for free expression.) Indeed, the Delaware Court of Chancery, which operates in a state system where law and equity remain largely separate, has continued to hold that it generally can't enjoin libel. But it expressly left open the possibility that, once the Delaware Superior Court (the law court) concludes—after a jury trial, if the parties don't choose a bench trial—that a statement is libelous, an injunction can then be issued.

According to recent reports, in practice, anti-libel injunctions are often parts of default judgments, or follow bench trials, and thus don't involve factual findings by juries. In both those situations, though, the defendant can be noted to have waived his right to a jury trial. To be sure, temporary restraining orders and preliminary injunctions are entered before any opportunity for a jury trial—but for that reason many courts continue to reject them on First Amendment grounds.

Industry observers note that and, as the California Supreme Court held in allowing such post-final-judgment permanent injunctions, the reasoning of Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson expressly sets aside injunctions in traditional civil libel disputes:.

Industry observers note that the high court was careful to point out … that the statute being considered was "not aimed at the redress of individual or private wrongs. Remedies for libel remain available and unaffected." … But most significant is that the court … clarified that it was not addressing "questions as to the extent of authority to prevent publications in order to protect private rights according to the principles governing the exercise of the jurisdiction of courts of equity." In a footnote, the court cited [an] … article by Roscoe Pound that observed that English courts permit "an injunction in case the libel was repeated or publication was continued after a jury had found the matter libelous." Therefore, Near expressly did not address the issue posed in the present case.

The Supreme Court hasn't confronted such permanent injunctions against repetition of proven libel since Near, but it has authorized injunctions against obscenity (which Near had anticipated) and against commercial speech that proposes illegal transactions. The one case in which it granted certiorari as to anti-libel injunctions, Tory v. Cochran (2005), largely disappeared when the plaintiff, famed lawyer Johnnie Cochran, died while the case was pending. None of these cases discussed the original meaning of the First Amendment, and the lower court cases dealing with the matter have largely not discussed it, either.

So here we have a fairly rich body of originalist evidence related to libel law generally. We have a considerable body of evidence from before and shortly after the Framing that talks about "previous restraints." And we have some nineteenth-century sources that seem to take the view that all injunctions in libel cases are unconstitutional. But how exactly do the Framing-era sources apply to a permanent anti-libel injunction issued by a court following the resolution of a libel case? Hard to know for sure.

I’ve tested a lot of air purifiers, and most look like appliances I’d rather tuck out of sight in a corner. The Dupray Bloom Air Purifier is different. It combines a HEPA air purifier with a removable planter, turning something purely functional into a decorative accent. I planted a small fiddle-leaf fig in mine, and I love how it looks in the room. But I also wanted to know whether the Bloom’s unusual design would interfere with its primary job of filtering the air.

According to recent reports, absolutely, and that’s what makes the Bloom so appealing. The top features a removable planting pot with a root tray that helps keep roots above excess water. I chose a small fiddle-leaf fig, and once it was planted, the Bloom looked more like a decorative planter than an air-cleaning appliance.

Sources indicate that there is one thing I’d caution buyers about: The planter doesn’t have drainage holes. The root tray provides some separation from standing water, but it isn’t a substitute for proper watering. I’d recommend using an olla, a small porous automatic watering vessel that slowly releases moisture into the soil. It’s a good option for keeping the plant watered without repeatedly pouring water into a pot that can’t drain.

I also appreciated that the planter lifts completely out. That means I can move the plant for maintenance or repotting without having to move the entire purifier. And when it’s time to replace the round HEPA filter, I can remove the planter, turn the unit over, and access the filter from the bottom.

According to recent reports, behind its decorative design, the Bloom is a serious air purifier. It uses an H13 HEPA filter with activated carbon to capture airborne particles, including dust, pollen, and pet dander, while helping reduce odors. Dupray rates it as capable of capturing 99.97 percent of particles as small as 0.1 micron.

Sources indicate that one feature I particularly liked was the stretchy fabric prefilter. It slips snugly over the purifier’s base, creating a smooth, modern appearance while catching larger airborne particles before they reach the HEPA filter. It’s washable, too, and Dupray offers replacement prefilters in different colors.

The Bloom also has an AutoDetect mode that monitors air quality and adjusts the fan speed. There are three manual fan settings, along with a sleep mode for quieter operation. Dupray rates its lowest noise level at just 24 decibels, making it suitable for bedrooms and other living spaces where a loud fan would be distracting.

In a recent development, it’s remarkably simple. The removable planter makes the HEPA filter accessible, and the fabric prefilter stretches on and off without clips or complicated fasteners.

Another smart touch is the universal power adapter. It comes with interchangeable plug configurations for the U.S., U.K., and Europe. That’s not something I typically see included with an air purifier.

My only complaint—and it’s minor—is the digital control display. The symbols for Auto, Sleep, and the fan-speed bars looked slightly blurry to me. I could still identify them and operate the purifier, but a sharper display would have been easier to read. Or I might need a newly introduced prescription for glasses.

In a recent development, at $249.99, the Bloom isn’t the cheapest way to get HEPA filtration, but its design sets it apart from the usual boxy models. It’s particularly appealing for living rooms, bedrooms, and home offices where an ordinary air purifier might detract from the decor.

According to recent reports, dupray advertises coverage up to 1,517 square feet, but that’s based on just one air change per hour. For more frequent air cleaning, it’s rated to cover 316 square feet at 4.8 air changes per hour. I’d use that smaller figure when choosing where to place it.

The Bloom also offers an optional wood tabletop model for anyone who prefers an accent table instead of a planter.

I love having a living plant incorporated into an appliance I’d otherwise try to hide. The Bloom is one of the few air purifiers I’ve tested that I’d happily put on display.

Kapnick, Kelly O'Neill Levy, and Matthew Parker-Raso); the respondent, Marc Fernich, is a prominent New York criminal defense lawyer, who represented, among others, Jeffrey Epstein, John Gotti, and Joaquin Guzman (drug cartel leader El Chapo):.

In a recent development, the motion arises from an altercation between respondent and participants in a demonstration outside of the federal courthouse for the Southern District of Newly introduced York on September 29, 2025. On May 27, 2026, the AGC served respondent with a notice and petition of charges alleging one charge of professional misconduct under Rules of Professional Misconduct (22 NYCRR 1200.0) rule 8.4(h), which prohibits conduct that adversely reflects on the lawyer's fitness as a lawyer. The parties have submitted a stipulation of facts, respondent's affidavit, and materials addressing aggravation and mitigation. Respondent admits to the stipulated misconduct, acknowledges the consequences of consenting to discipline, and agrees to a public censure.

On September 29, 2025, respondent, then 61 years old, was leaving a meeting at the Newly introduced York County District Attorney's Office and was walking toward the Brooklyn Bridge. On Centre Street, he came upon a group of demonstrators in support of Palestine outside of the federal courthouse. Some demonstrators were singing and chanting, one played a guitar, and others held a banner reading "Jewish Artists for Palestine.".

Respondent attempted to make his way through a circle of demonstrators, and admits that physical contact occurred as he attempted to proceed. Respondent grabbed a demonstrator's arm, pushed and grabbed others while moving through the circle, and engaged in heated verbal confrontation. The cellphone recordings of the incident also show respondent holding a demonstrator from behind with his arms around the person's waist, with the demonstrator shouting at him to remove his arms, respondent pushing and grabbing others, and respondent holding another demonstrator from behind with his arms around the individual's neck.

Among other things, respondent's threatening and antisemitic remarks included "Back off me, Kapo, Kike, Jew Boy!," "You fucking animal, you're worse than a fucking Muslim!," "You should have been aborted," and "You should have been thrown into an oven, I'd throw you in if I could!" He also said that the demonstrators' grandparents should have died in the Holocaust, as well as other inflammatory remarks invoking violence. Respondent remained at the demonstration for approximately one hour, until it ended.

According to recent reports, at his deposition, respondent maintained that the video depiction of the incident was a compilation of cellphone recordings made by several individuals and that they were out of sequence and out of context. He asserted that the confrontation had not been one-sided; demonstrators had been linking arms, blocking his way, pushing back, and squeezing his genitals.

He also maintained that the recordings had purposefully omitted much of the physical contact and extreme anti-Israel and anti-Zionist rhetoric directed at him. Nonetheless, he recognized that the demonstrators had been exercising their constitutional rights to assemble and engage in free speech, and that his words and actions could not be justified. He was deeply ashamed of his conduct and expressed remorse.

The parties have stipulated that respondent's misconduct is aggravated by his substantial experience in the practice of law. They have also stipulated to considerable mitigation. Respondent has no prior disciplinary history. The incident was unrelated to his representation of a client or the practice of law, and did not disrupt a court proceeding. Respondent self-reported his misconduct to the AGC through counsel, cooperated with the AGC investigation, voluntarily appeared for examination, accepted responsibility, and expressed remorse and embarrassment for his actions. Fifteen character references described respondent as being well-regarded in the community and having character traits of honesty, integrity, and trustworthiness.

According to recent reports, the record further reflects that respondent was experiencing significant medical issues at the time of the incident. He was recovering from a recent back surgery and experiencing significant pain, and had undergone emergency surgery for retinal tears shortly beforehand. He was also undergoing psychiatric treatment and taking medication for depression, anxiety, and ADHD. A report submitted by respondent's treating psychiatrist explains how the pain, emotional distress, and psychiatric symptoms respondent was experiencing may have contributed to his impaired judgment and agitation and, while respondent had been under his care for 13 years, he would never have expected him to engage in the kind of "angry and out-of-control conduct that he engaged in outside the Courthouse." Respondent, who has family in Israel, also maintains that the October 7, 2023 attacks in Israel affected him deeply and that his memory of those attacks caused his anger to boil over.

Under 22 NYCRR 1240.8(a)(5), the Court may resolve a disciplinary matter by consent where the submissions establish an admitted violation and an appropriate agreed-upon sanction. In support of the proposal for a public censure, the parties cite decisions imposing a censure for similarly offensive, abusive, and discriminatory remarks and other isolated misconduct (see e.g. Matter of Melogy, 233 AD3d 135 [1st Dept 2024]; Matter of Mukambetova, 204 AD3d 158 [1st Dept 2022]; Matter of Schlossberg, 192 AD3d 8 [1st Dept 2020]).

Industry observers note that respondent's use of antisemitic and threatening language, together with his physical aggression towards demonstrators, warrants public discipline. At the same time, the absence of a disciplinary history, the isolated nature of the incident, the medical and psychological circumstances, his cooperation, and his acceptance of responsibility supports the sanction jointly proposed. Public censure appropriately expresses the profession's condemnation of the relevant conduct while also recognizing the substantial mitigation.

Accordingly, the parties' joint motion for discipline by consent pursuant to 22 NYCRR 1240.8(a)(5) should be granted, … and respondent publicly censured….

Jorge Dopico and Raymond Vallejo represent the Committee.

At $2,395 for the king size I tested, the Perfectly Snug Smart Topper is absolutely a luxury purchase. After sleeping on it for 2 months during a Florida summer, however, I can say that its temperature-control technology delivers. This 2-inch topper uses fans, airflow, heating elements, and temperature sensors to regulate each side of the bed independently, creating a surprisingly effective way to stay comfortable throughout the night. While some aspects of the design could use a little more refinement, the actual cooling performance left me impressed.

It has been revealed that installation was straightforward. I unpacked the vacuum-sealed topper, laid it over my king mattress, added my usual fitted sheet, and plugged it in. The power supply is fairly big, but I had no trouble tucking it down behind my headboard. The cables emerge from the head of the topper, which is worth keeping in mind if you tend to stretch your arms overhead while sleeping. As for comfort, the topper has an unusual feel at first—slightly firm but with enough give to stay comfortable. Its internal mesh structure allows air to circulate beneath you, and the effect is immediately noticeable, even on lower settings.

The cooling performance is easily my favorite feature. Even at level 3, I could feel a gentle, pleasant stream of cool air underneath me, which was especially welcome during warm Florida nights. The one trade-off is fan noise, which becomes quite noticeable at higher settings. Anything above level 5 was too loud for my sleeping preferences, but I found an easy workaround using the app’s scheduling feature. I’d run the cooling at a higher setting for about an hour before bedtime, then lower it to level 3 when I climbed into bed. This gave me the best of both worlds: a wonderfully cool mattress at bedtime and gentle, nearly silent cooling throughout the night.

There are a few areas where I’d love to see Perfectly Snug make improvements, especially considering the premium price. The power supply and small side-mounted control panel are functional but have a fairly basic appearance. I also occasionally brushed against the fans positioned at the foot of the topper, which could briefly interrupt their operation (making a noticeable “you’ve just stopped a fan from moving” type of buzzing sound). The companion app was another underwhelming aspect of the experience. While it offers useful features like scheduling and temperature adjustments, its interface feels super dated and could benefit from a much more polished, intuitive design. None of these complications prevented me from enjoying the topper, but they’re details I’d expect to see addressed at this price point.

In a recent development, ultimately, the Perfectly Snug Smart Topper gets the most notable thing right: keeping your bed at a comfortable temperature. I enjoyed slipping into a perfectly cooled bed each night, and the subtle airflow on lower settings noticeably improved my sleep comfort. It’s an innovative product with plenty to offer, particularly for hot sleepers or couples with different temperature preferences. Although the fan noise and a few less-refined design elements keep it from feeling like a truly premium experience, the core technology is admirable. With some thoughtful improvements, this could be an outstanding luxury sleep upgrade.

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Police sirens can sound very different, from a slow wail to a rapid yelp. Here’s why officers switch tones and what drivers should do.

Everyone recognizes an emergency siren. Or do they?

According to recent reports, officers can choose different tones to make their vehicles easier to notice on busy streets or open roads. Some departments also use certain sounds for special warnings. With electronic siren systems offering several options, drivers might hear multiple tones during a single emergency response.

Learn what the common sounds mean, why officers switch between them, whether different tones signal different emergencies, and how drivers should react.

Different police siren sounds serve different purposes, but they don’t necessarily indicate specific emergencies. Officers often switch tones based on traffic conditions or to get drivers’ attention. A faster siren doesn’t always mean a more serious emergency.

The most common police siren sounds include:.

Modern police vehicles typically use electronic sirens that allow officers to switch between these sounds. Older mechanical sirens use a spinning mechanism to produce a traditional wail.

It has been revealed that officers also adjust their sirens based on traffic conditions. Faster tones can help get drivers’ attention in heavy traffic, while a slower wail may work on quieter roads. Departments set their own policies for siren use, so there isn’t one standard sound for daytime or nighttime driving.

Recent findings suggest that regardless of the siren sound, drivers should respond the same way when an emergency vehicle approaches. Drivers should check their mirrors, signal, and safely pull toward the right side of the road to let the police vehicle pass. They should avoid sudden braking or stopping in an intersection.

Anyone already in an intersection should continue through before pulling over. Drivers waiting at a red light shouldn’t enter the intersection unless an officer directs them to do so. After the police vehicle passes, drivers should check for other emergency vehicles before returning to traffic. Specific rules may vary by state.

Sources indicate that leaf vacuums come in various types and with different-size collection bags. There are also three power source types—gas, electric, and cordless/battery—with each option affecting runtime and suction. Take a look below at some important factors to help determine the motor type, power, and design that will work best for you.

Leaf vacuums are made in a few types, and some kinds work better in certain situations and setups than others.

Like lawn mowers, leaf vacuums are available in electric- and gas-powered versions.

To figure out the power of a leaf vacuum, check the product description for two numbers: mph and CFM. The mph stands for miles per hour—in this case, referring to how promptly air is suctioned into the unit and through the tube. Most units run between 110 and 180 mph, although some may reach extremes of 250 mph or so.

Recent findings suggest that somewhat more notable than airspeed, however, is CFM. This describes how much air moves through the vacuum in the span of 60 seconds, indicating how powerful the unit is. While mph provides an idea of how promptly leaves can go through the tube, CFM indicates how much can go through all at once.

The CFM rankings for leaf vacuums range between 150 to 600. A unit with a CFM under 200 may be all that’s needed to clean up an apartment balcony or a small yard, but for larger areas, it may be desirable to invest in a unit with higher CFM.

Saunders recommends a leaf vacuum with a strong motor “that can really get the job done.” He adds, “Something like a 12-amp electric motor, which you’ll find in some top models, will give you the suction power you need to handle a good amount of leaves without getting bogged down.”.

Sources indicate that the runtime of a battery-powered leaf vacuum can limit the amount of work that can be done. Most models offer at least 20 to 30 minutes of runtime on the highest power levels. At lower levels, the battery may run for 45 minutes or more.

According to recent reports, battery-powered models that include two or more interchangeable batteries can increase the available work time. While one battery is in use, the other battery charges. Charge times vary from 1.5 to 3 hours and sometimes longer depending on the battery size. The amount of work may still be limited with interchangeable batteries, but it will provide more work time than a single battery.

Some manufacturers provide batteries that are interchangeable with the brand’s other power tools. In these cases, buying power tools of the same brand can add to the number of batteries available. Ultimately, that can extend possible work time even more.

Some leaf vacuums offer bells and whistles beyond simple suction. In fact, most vacuums these days are actually leaf blowers with a vacuum function. That provides extra use options with a single tool.

Leaf vacuums are best suited for smaller outdoor spaces, like those surrounding garden apartments and duplexes. Some models also offer a mulching option, which is great for repurposing leaves into healthy plant beds.

Industry observers note that A leaf vacuum’s mix of features and design can make it easier or harder to use. Bag size, for example, determines how often it will need to be emptied. Larger bags mean less frequent emptying, but they can be awkward and heavy to carry.

In a recent development, weight also affects ease of use. Gas-powered leaf vacuums weigh the most, though some battery-powered models are almost as heavy. For those with a large yard, gas power makes sense because it can keep a consistent high power throughout the whole yard.

However, for those with smaller yards, the lightweight nature of a handheld or a battery-powered model can be more comfortable. Models with a backpack bag combine the lighter weight of a handheld leaf vacuum with the convenience of a backpack.

Ergonomics is also something to take into consideration. “You’re going to be using this tool for a while, so it needs to be comfortable,” Saunders notes. “Lightweight models are easier on the arms and back, especially if you’re working in a large yard. Features like an ergonomically designed tube can also make a big difference by reducing strain.”.

Finally, there are controls to consider. Trigger switches and on/off buttons directly on the handle are easier to use. This allows you to turn the machine on or off with one hand. Toolless conversion for hybrid models can also add to ease of use.

Sources indicate that leaf vacuums aren’t complicated once you understand how they work and what features are needed for specific jobs. However, since they aren’t as common as leaf blowers, you might still find yourself scratching your head as you look at the specs. Here, we answer some of the most common questions about leaf vacuums to help you make the right choice.

It has been revealed that A leaf vacuum is the best machine for picking up leaves. Choose one that matches your yard size and typical leaf volume. Battery-powered handheld models work best for small yards with a moderate amount of leaves. Electric and gas models offer longer running times and a larger collection bag capacity for larger areas and heavier leaf cover.

According to recent reports, A leaf vacuum needs a minimum rating of 340 CFM and 150 mph to pick up dry material effectively. Leaf removal equipment rated above 500 CFM and 180 mph is best for large areas and wet leaves and debris.

Yes, a lawn vacuum will effectively pick up dry and clumped grass clippings.

Sources indicate that no, leaf vacuums are not designed to clean gutters. They don’t offer the required suction or reach to do the job.

To switch a dual-purpose leaf blower/vac from blower to vacuum mode, remove the blower tube and intake guard; then attach the vacuum tube (to the air intake) and the collection bag (where the blower tube came off). Check the owner’s manual for specific instructions.

Yes, leaf vacuums can be noisy, especially those with gas engines. Some models can reach 90 decibels. However, those powered by rechargeable batteries are much quieter, in the 60 to 80 decibel range.

To clean an outdoor vacuum for leaves, first turn it off and disconnect the power cord or battery. Empty the collection bag, including anything that may not easily dump out. Remove and unclog the suction nozzle, and clear any debris from the impeller.

Leaf vacuums will last 8 to 10 years or longer with routine maintenance.

Leaf vacuum prices range from about $100 to more than $1000, depending on the design and size.
