    This is followed by an ambiguous comment that might be interpreted as bringing this gratitude to “our forefathers” in line with the orthodox view of the primary agency of God: “Let us therefore proclaim our gratitude to Providence for manifold blessings—let us be humbly thankful for inherited ideals—and let us resolve to share those blessings and those ideals with our fellow human beings throughout the world.”[REF] By speaking of gratitude for the nation’s forefathers, Kennedy is still able to express gratitude to God.

    According to recent reports, lyndon B. Johnson’s proclamations were largely traditional. Thanksgiving is “a special day dedicated to giving thanks to God” (1964); “let us, therefore, in this splendid American tradition, thank Him who created us and all that we have” (1966); “thanking Him for His goodness, we thank Him as well for the promise and the achievement of America” (1967).[REF] Although “Americans, looking back on the tumultuous events of 1968, may be more inclined to ask God’s mercy and guidance than to offer Him thanks for His blessings,” he wrote in 1968, that would be a mistake; many events “deserve our remembrance, and give us cause for thanksgiving.”[REF].

    In a recent development, also traditional were the proclamations of Richard Nixon: “Lincoln…knew that it is precisely at those times of hardship when men most need to recognize that the Source of all good constantly bestows His blessings of on mankind,” and “we know we can rely on a strength greater than ourselves” (1969).[REF] According to Nixon, “Lincoln wisely knew that a man’s declaration of his gratitude to God is, in itself, an act which strengthens the thanksgiver because it renews his own realization of his relationship to his God,” and “we give thanks for God’s strength and guidance upon which we confidently rely today and every day” (1970).[REF] “Our country can look back with special gratitude…and we can look forward with trust in Divine Providence” (1972); “in the first Thanksgiving, man affirmed his determination to live in God’s grace and to act in God’s will…. Time has not dimmed, nor circumstance diminished the need for God’s hand in all that America may justly endeavor” (1973).[REF].

    In a recent development, the principle of secondary causality was a strikingly consistent feature of Thanksgiving proclamations through Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s presidency, bridging partisan divides between Republicans and Democrats and philosophical divides between small-government conservatives and the early architects of the administrative state. The past half-century has seen a widening chasm between progressive, secular, and horizontal proclamations that depart from the traditional purpose of the holiday and reassertions of the traditional, religious, and vertical orientation of Thanksgiving. Secondary causality, and with it the distinctive nature of Thanksgiving, is increasingly a partisan belief. During this period, every Democratic Administration (Carter, Clinton, Obama, and Biden) has slid further from the Thanksgiving tradition, while Republican Presidents have either conformed to the postwar inconsistency discussed in the previous section (Ford, George H. W. Bush, and George W. Bush) or, in the case of Ronald Reagan and Donald Trump, vigorously reasserted the traditional theology of Thanksgiving.

    Gerald Ford’s 1975 proclamation is striking because it is the first to make no clear reference to God. Instead, Ford calls on Americans to “reaffirm our belief in a dynamic spirit that will continue to nurture and guide us as we prepare to meet the challenge of our third century.” Unsurprisingly, then, Ford also fails in his 1975 proclamation to affirm the traditional teaching of secondary causality. Instead, direct and unqualified gratitude to our fellow men and to other strictly human aspects of national life takes its place:.

    Our nation draws its strength from people of every creed, of every color, of every race—native Americans and people from every nation in the world who for two centuries have come to share in the rewards and responsibilities of our American Republic. On the eve of our 200th year, Thanksgiving Day should be a day of special reflection upon the qualities of heart, mind and character of the men and women who founded and built our great Nation. Let us join in giving thanks for our cultural pluralism. Let us celebrate our diversity and the great strengths that have come from sharing our traditions, our ideas, our resources, our hopes and our dreams. Let us be grateful that for 200 years our people have been dedicated to fulfilling the democratic ideal—dedicated to securing “liberty and justice for all.”[REF].

    It is no mere coincidence that in the same statement, Ford fails to affirm God’s ultimate Providence—or even to refer to God by a recognizable name or description—and recasts American history in progressive terms. The progressive vision is one of men “fulfilling the democratic ideal” through their own efforts—or, if they are aided by something beyond themselves, it is by “belief in a dynamic spirit” rather than the real Divine Person encountered, prayed to, and discussed in the biblical tradition. It would be unfair to reduce Ford himself to this single statement; his other Thanksgiving proclamations refer to God, the Almighty, or Divine Providence and attribute to God the “blessings” of this life.[REF] The fact that his 1975 proclamation, anticipating the bicentennial of the Declaration of Independence, veered so far from the tradition anticipates the increasingly progressive, atheistic, and horizontal character of later presidential statements.

    Jimmy Carter initially attempts in 1977 to hold the traditional, vertical dimension of Thanksgiving together with the progressive, horizontal dimension. He claims that “our forebears never lost faith in the Creator, in their cause, or in themselves,” and “we have never lost sight of the principles upon which our Nation was founded. For that reason we can look to the future with hope and confidence.” Our “hope and confidence” come not from faith in God, or even from the strength of our principles, but from our dedication to our “principles,” which Carter does not explicitly connect to God. Yet Carter reaffirms the purpose of Thanksgiving when he asks Americans to gather “to give thanks for the blessings Almighty God has bestowed upon us”[REF].

    In 1978, Carter continues to blend the traditional with the progressive: On the one hand, “Providence has provided Americans with fertile land and bountiful harvests.” On the other, “On this Thanksgiving Day, we affirm our faith in our heritage of freedom, and our spirit of sharing,” so “let us observe Thanksgiving in the spirit of peace and sharing, by declaring it a day of Thankful Giving, a day upon which the American people share their plenty with the hungry of other lands.”[REF] God is still present, still acknowledged, but thanking Him for His blessings and Providence has become secondary to faith in American qualities and to American efforts to alleviate human suffering.

    Sources indicate that by the end of his presidency, Carter has almost entirely abandoned the traditional religious focus of Thanksgiving; he speaks of gratitude to men instead of gratitude to God and diminishes the originally religious character of Thanksgiving by recasting it as an exercise in human solidarity: “The greatest bounty of our Nation is the bounty of our heritage—our diversity as immigrants and descendants of immigrants, our common identity as Americans.” It is not to God, but to national diversity that Americans are most indebted. Carter’s brief allusion to the first Thanksgiving makes the natives, not the Pilgrims, the protagonists:.

    Thanksgiving…is a commemoration—of the day America’s earliest inhabitants sat down to table with European colonists. That occasion was historic not only because it established a national holiday, but because it marked the start of a national tradition of cooperation, unity and tolerance.[REF].

    It has been revealed that for Carter, the most notable feature of the first Thanksgiving is a strictly horizontal phenomenon of some men’s relationships with other men. When Carter does note the importance of the divine, he immediately adds the equal, if not greater, importance of the human: “As we pause on Thanksgiving to offer thanks to God, we should not forget that we also owe thanks to this country’s forefathers who had the vision to join together in Thanksgiving, and who gave us so much of the vision of brotherhood that is ours today.”[REF] Americans are indebted to their “forefathers” for a vision of “brotherhood”; for what, exactly, Americans are indebted to God is apparently not worth mentioning.

    Ronald Reagan’s proclamations reassert the traditional, vertical understanding of Thanksgiving:.

    According to recent reports, in 1985, like Nixon in 1972, Reagan traced the American Thanksgiving tradition to “our Judeo-Christian heritage,” a phrase he repeated in 1986 and that George H. W. Bush echoed in 1992. Having recounted the history of the Thanksgiving tradition in greater detail than most other Presidents, Reagan attributes a host of human accomplishments to God by framing his litany of “honest toil” by human hands in calls to give thanks to God:.

    It has been revealed that we manifest our gratitude to God for the many blessings he has showered upon our land and upon its people. In this season of Thanksgiving we are grateful for our abundant harvests and the productivity of our industries; for the discoveries of our laboratories; for the researches of our scientists and scholars; for the achievements of our artists, musicians, writers, clergy, teachers, physicians, businessmen, engineers, public servants, farmers, mechanics, artisans, and workers of every sort whose honest toil of mind and body in a free land rewards them and their families and enriches our entire Nation. Let us thank God for our families, friends, and neighbors, and for the joy of this very festival we celebrate in His name. Let every house of worship in the land and every home and every heart be filled with the spirit of gratitude and praise and love of this Thanksgiving Day.[REF].

    Reagan suggests that Thanksgiving “reveals our character as Nation” more clearly than any other custom: “[R]ooted deeply in our Judeo-Christian heritage, the practice of offering thanksgiving underscores our unshakeable belief in God as the foundation of our Nation and our firm reliance upon Him from Whom all blessings flow.”[REF] For the Bicentennial of the U.S. Constitution, Reagan noted that all that is good in the law of the land itself ought to be attributed to God rather than to its human Framers—not a boastful claim of the Constitution’s infallibility, but an acknowledgement of God as the ultimate source of all blessings:.

    In 1789 the government established by that great charter of freedom, and ‘the civil and religious liberty with which we are blessed,’ were cited by George Washington in the first Presidential Thanksgiving Proclamation as among ‘the great and various favors’ conferred upon us by the Lord and Ruler of Nations. […] Let us, in this unbroken chain of observance, dedicate ourselves to honor anew the Author of Liberty and to publicly acknowledge our debt to all those who have sacrificed so much in our behalf. May our gratitude always be coupled with petitions for divine guidance and protection for our Nation and with ready help for our neighbors in times of need.[REF].

    Reagan calls upon Americans to thank God and their fellow men, but always to acknowledge the priority of God. In his final proclamation, Reagan restates the traditional position: “Thanksgiving Day summons every American to pause in the midst of activity, however necessary and valuable, to give simple and humble thanks to God.… The blessings that are ours must be understood as the gift of a loving God Whose greatest gift is healing.”[REF] He concludes by quoting the opening verses of Psalm 105: “O give thanks to the Lord, call on His name, / Make known his deeds among the people!” Thanksgiving directs us to proclaim God’s deeds, manifest through the secondary causality of genuinely free human agents who nevertheless work His providential purpose.

    In a recent development, george H. W. Bush mostly reaffirms the traditional purpose of the Thanksgiving proclamation—to be “reminded of our dependence upon our Heavenly Father and of the debt of gratitude we owe to Him”—and declares that “we continue to offer thanks and praise to our Creator.”[REF] Bush’s subsequent proclamations quote from William Bradford’s account of “a day of thanksgiving at Plymouth in 1621” and John Winthrop’s 1630 interpretation of the Puritan “quest for freedom as an enterprise no less historic than the ancient Israelite’s exodus from Egypt.”[REF] Though he generally affirms the priority of expressing “our gratitude for the goodness and generosity of our Creator,” there are some passages in which Bush’s focus is strictly horizontal, as when he asks Americans “to be thankful for” the Peace Corps volunteers, diplomats, and members of the military serving overseas (1990).[REF].

    William J. Clinton’s proclamations reflect a more horizontal conception of Thanksgiving. He opens in 1993 with traditional statements of the American custom of “recogniz[ing] the providence and mercy of God” and identifying “the true spirit of Thanksgiving: acknowledging God’s graciousness, and in response, reaching out in service to others.” But his emphasis then shifts: The “spirit of Thanksgiving” “inspires” our actions; our gratitude extends even to “the relief efforts that our Nation and others have undertaken where natural disasters have struck unmercifully”—in other words, being “thankful” for our own efforts. Clinton’s proclamation becomes more and more progressive: “As we gather together during this sacred and cherished time, let us pledge to build a new America,” “to place the strength and benevolence of this great Nation at the service of all its people, indeed of all the peoples of the earth. Then, in these richer years, we will reap a true and fruitful harvest.” Clinton’s first proclamation concludes with another innovation: the places where Americans ought to “gather” has been expanded from “homes” and “places of worship” to include “wherever they may choose.”[REF] Clinton’s proclamations contain traditional statements of gratitude to God followed by an increasingly progressive focus on human efforts without reference to God’s ultimate agency.

    Industry observers note that clinton makes reference to the Pilgrims’ First Thanksgiving in six of eight proclamations, but frequently in a distorted way. For example, in 1995, Clinton describes the 1621 gathering of Pilgrims and Wampanoags as a “3 day festival” that “brought people together to delight in the richness of the earth and to give praise for their new friendships and progress.” The Pilgrims praise “new friendships and progress,” not Providence. Later, Clinton notes that this gathering inspired a “holiday” that “unites citizens from every culture, race, and background in common thanks for the gifts we receive from God.”[REF].

    Clinton’s proclamations blend the merely descriptive with the traditionally hortatory. On the one hand, “millions of us will gather with family and friends to give thanks to God for the many blessings that He has bestowed upon us,”[REF] and “Americans join with family and friends to give thanks to a provident God.”[REF] On the other, “I encourage”[REF] or “urge the citizens”[REF] or “encourage all the people”[REF] or “all Americans”[REF] “to assemble in their homes, places of worship, or community center to share the spirit of goodwill and prayer; to express heartfelt thanks to God for the many blessings He has bestowed upon us….”[REF].

    George W. Bush’s first Thanksgiving proclamation, issued mere months after the September 11 attacks, noted that “we find particular assurance from our Thanksgiving tradition, which reminds us that we, as a people and individually, always have reason to hope and trust in God, despite great adversity.” “In thankfulness and humility, we acknowledge, especially now, our dependence on One greater than ourselves.” Bush maintained the traditional principle of secondary causality and the correspondingly “vertical” emphasis of the proclamation: “Americans of every belief and heritage give thanks to God for the many blessings we enjoy…. Let us particularly give thanks for the selfless sacrifices of those who responded in service to others after the terrorist attacks….”[REF].

    Recent findings suggest that bush maintained this vertical emphasis when he gave thanks “for the resolve and generosity of so many of our people who are touching countless hearts and souls through thoughtful acts of kindness,” “for the Americans in our Armed Forces,” “for the men and women who work to keep America safe and secure,” and “for the freedoms guaranteed by our Constitution.”[REF] Yet his proclamations sometimes took on a more horizontal tone. In 2002, Bush declared that “we also honor and salute the selfless sacrifice of the brave men and women of our Armed Forces,” a statement more appropriate to Veterans Day or Memorial Day than to Thanksgiving. The same proclamation attributed American greatness to human virtues and effort without reference to God: “This Thanksgiving, we recognize the ties of friendship and respect that bind us together. And we renew our pledge to uphold the timeless principles of freedom, equality, and opportunity that have made our country into a great Nation.”[REF].

    In 2003, Bush began by noting that “on Thanksgiving, we gather with family and friends to thank God” and concluded by exhorting Americans to “live by that same trust” in God that animated the Founders, but in the center of his proclamation, he attributed Americans’ “abundance, prosperity, and hope” to strictly human causes: “a firm foundation of freedom, justice, and equality; a belief in democracy and the rule of law; and our fundamental rights to gather, speak, and worship freely.”[REF] However, Bush’s final proclamation reasserted the traditional principle of secondary causality: “We recognize that all of these blessings, and life itself, come not from the hand of man but from Almighty God” (2008).

    It has been revealed that strikingly for a President whose fervent evangelical faith formed such a prominent part of his public image and whose father incorporated extensive and explicit quotations from the Bible (Psalm 100:2–5 in 1989; Luke 12:48 in 1990 and 1991; Psalm 107:40–41 in 1991; Proverbs 19:17 in 1992), Bush never once quoted from Scripture in his eight proclamations. Nor does he make any specific claim of the Christian or Judeo–Christian character of America in general or Thanksgiving in particular as did Reagan, the elder Bush, and numerous preceding Presidents. That said, his first proclamation’s invocation of “Almighty God, who is our refuge and our strength in this time of trouble” borrows language from Psalm 46, and two of his later proclamations refer to “the universal call to love a neighbor,”[REF] an allusion to the commandment found in Leviticus 19:18 and identified by Christ as the second great commandment of the Law (Matthew 22:39; Mark 12:31).

    Barack Obama’s proclamations contain significantly fewer references to God than is typical.[REF] Two of Obama’s proclamations refer to God only by quoting previous proclamations: 2009’s “Almighty God” (quoting Washington, 1789) and 2015’s “the providence of Almighty God” and “commend to [God’s] tender care” (quoting Washington, 1789, and Lincoln, 1863).[REF] Obama studiously avoids using masculine pronouns for God or speaking of God as “Father,” even modifying a quote from Lincoln’s 1863 proclamation (“commend to His tender care”) to “[God’s] tender care.”[REF] Obama directly refers to God in his 2010–2014 proclamations[REF] but never once refers to God in the concluding formal exhortation, preferring to “encourage” Americans to “give thanks for all we have received in the past year, express appreciation to those whose lives enrich our own, and share our bounty with others.”[REF] To whom Americans ought to give thanks is left ambiguous.

    Obama’s final proclamation is only the second in history, after Ford’s 1975 proclamation, to make no reference to God at all. Ford referred vaguely to “a dynamic spirit.” As one scholar has noted, “Obama’s Thanksgiving proclamations may have been the most ‘God’-less in U.S. history, but they were the most ‘spirit’-filled”[REF]—except for the 2016 proclamation, which is transparently written as a rebuke to the incoming President Trump for running on a platform of immigration restrictionism. Obama’s 2016 proclamation describes the Pilgrims as “refugees” who were met by “the friendly embrace of an indigenous people, the Wampanoag; the Pilgrims were “grateful they could rely on the generosity of the Wampanoag people,” and thus began “the tradition of an annual day of giving thanks.”[REF] Obama recast the first Thanksgiving as a festival of Pilgrim refugees giving thanks to the Wampanoags—not to God. Accordingly, the entire proclamation has a horizontal emphasis on the “American instinct…to find strength in our common creed and forge unity from our great diversity.”.

    Concomitant with a more secular and anthropocentric conception of Thanksgiving is a posture toward future progress rather than gratitude for what we have inherited and currently enjoy.

    According to recent reports, joseph R. Biden’s proclamations are significantly more horizontal, secular, and progressive than those of any preceding President. Each of Biden’s four proclamations concludes by encouraging Americans, in identical language, to “join together and give thanks for the friends, neighbors, family members, and strangers who have supported each other over the past year in a reflection of goodwill and unity.”[REF] This language is horizontal rather than vertical in the sense that Americans are to be grateful to one another—to other persons—rather than to God. When he “encourages” Americans to join together, Biden—unlike previous Presidents, who spoke of particular places (churches and other places of worship)—is completely silent on where Americans ought to gather. Biden’s 2021 proclamation is structured as a litany of thanks to different kinds of Americans working to benefit the nation: “farm workers and frontline workers, many of whom are immigrants,” “educators,” “parents,” “health care professionals,” “researchers and scientists.”[REF] These are expressions of gratitude, to be sure, but more appropriate for Labor Day than for Thanksgiving.

    God is mentioned in only two of Biden’s four proclamations, making his proclamations even more “God”-less than Obama’s. The 2021 opening sentence, “Thanksgiving provides us with a time to reflect on our many blessings—from God, this Nation, and each other,” describes an opportunity to reflect on God as one of several sources of our blessings rather than exhorting Americans not merely to reflect, but actually to give thanks to God. This is a sharp break from the Thanksgiving tradition. In his 2022 proclamation, Biden refers to God only by paraphrasing Lincoln’s proclamation of a national Thanksgiving, which “ask[ed] God to bring us together to care for one another and heal our Nation.” He also quotes Scripture—“Let us rejoice always, pray continually, and give thanks in all circumstances”—but does not complete the quotation: “for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus” (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18, NIV). Biden’s comment on this passage is emphatically horizontal and future-oriented: “This is a special time in the greatest country on Earth, so let us be grateful. America is a great Nation because we are a good people. This holiday, we celebrate all that brings us together, grounded in history and our shared hopes for the future.”[REF].

    As with Obama’s proclamation in 2016, there are no references to God in Biden’s 2023 and 2024 proclamations. Instead, Biden refers to the nation’s “limitless possibilities,”[REF] claiming that “there is nothing beyond our capacity if we do it together.”[REF] In all four proclamations, Biden (again like Obama in 2016) recasts the Pilgrim Thanksgiving as a celebration of gratitude “to the generosity and support of the Wampanoag”[REF] “who made [the harvest] possible”[REF] through their “generosity and kindness.”[REF] Biden’s progressive reformulation of Thanksgiving almost entirely sidelines God and tradition, substituting human communities and human solidarity for dependence upon the Almighty: “[W]e are grateful for our Nation and the incredible soul of America,”[REF] and Americans should “celebrate all that unites us,” finding hope “in our Nation’s families, who sacrifice so much to achieve the American Dream and build a future worthy of our highest aspirations.”[REF].

    Amid these progressive reformulations, it is refreshing to turn to Donald Trump’s proclamations, which, like Reagan’s, reassert the traditional and religious character of the holiday and in particular reestablish the recognition that all thanks are ultimately due to God even as they manifest through human efforts.

    Trump’s first proclamation declares unequivocally that “[o]n Thanksgiving Day, as we have for nearly four centuries, Americans give thanks to Almighty God for our abundant blessings.” Most of this proclamation is dedicated to describing the endurance of the Pilgrims and of Americans during the Civil War and their insistence on giving thanks to God amidst their trials. Trump’s purpose is to highlight “in the courageous Pilgrims who stood on Plymouth Rock in new land, the intrepidness that lies at the core of the American spirit.” Trump acknowledges human efforts (“with the help of the Wampanoag tribe, and a bountiful harvest, they were regaining their health and strength”) but treats them as secondary causes: “In thanks to God for these blessings, the new governor of the Plymouth Colony, William Bradford, proclaimed a day of thanksgiving….” Trump concludes by “encourag[ing] all Americans to gather, in homes and places of worship, to offer a prayer of thanks to God for our many blessings.”[REF].

    Trump’s other first-term proclamations begin in similar fashion by “recall[ing] the courageous and inspiring journey of the Pilgrims,”[REF] by “remember[ing] with reverence and gratitude the bountiful blessings afforded to us by our Creator,”[REF] and reminding us succinctly that “[o]n Thanksgiving Day, we thank God for the abundant blessings in our lives.”[REF].

    Trump’s 2020 proclamation doubled as an official commemoration of the quadricentennial of the Mayflower’s journey, an anniversary that was largely forgotten amid the panicked reaction to the coronavirus that began in the spring, the wave of riots throughout the summer, and the unprecedented post-election disputes and delays in resolving the election results in the fall.[REF] In all that they did, “these first Americans… trusted in God to provide for them.” It also anticipates the 400th anniversary of 1621: “[T]he following year, they celebrated a successful harvest alongside their Native American neighbors—the first Thanksgiving. This seminal event in the history of our Nation is a continual reminder of the power of faith, love, perseverance, prayer, and fellowship.”[REF] By contrast, Biden confined his commemoration of 1621 to a subordinate adverbial clause of a single sentence: “Just as 400 years ago when the Pilgrims were able to celebrate a successful first harvest thanks to the generosity and support of the Wampanoag, today we too express our gratitude for those who have helped us get through this difficult past year.”[REF].

    In 2025, Trump began by recalling Washington’s 1789 proclamation and quoting its opening sentence that asserts “the duty of all Nations to acknowledge the providence of Almighty God.” Trump quotes from Lincoln’s 1863 proclamation with its acknowledgment of “our beneficent Father who dwelleth in the Heavens” and adds that “[i]n every generation since, this spirit of reverence, trust, and gratitude has preserved our way of life and made America the strongest, greatest, and most resilient Nation the world has ever known.” He goes on to attribute to the Pilgrims, patriots, pioneers, and warriors of American history “a spirit of gratitude and grit embodied by those who celebrated the first Thanksgiving more than 400 years ago,” a spirit that stands “at the very heart of what it means to be an American.” And because “this year, God has bestowed abundant blessings all across our land and indeed the entire world,” the President “encourage[s] all Americans to gather in homes and places of worship, to offer a prayer of thanks to God for our many blessings.”[REF].

    Industry observers note that “Gratitude and grit” sums up how President Trump has combined his distinctive rhetorical emphasis on American daring, exploration, and endurance with Thanksgiving’s traditional acknowledgment of God’s primacy. It stands in sharp contrast to President Biden’s language of “limitless possibilities” and abandonment of any reference to God. Both seek to emphasize the nation’s ability to overcome obstacles, but in Biden’s case, such emphasis comes at the price of piety.

    Ceremonial rhetoric is significant because it shapes citizens’ moral evaluations: their sense of what is noble and thus worthy of admiration; their code of justice; and the proper objects of their affection or love. Unlike the rhetoric used in a deliberative body or courtroom, ceremonial rhetoric does not produce an immediate decision. Its power is more fundamental and long-lasting, shaping the moral imagination of the citizens who vote in elections, serve on juries, and actually compose “We the People.” Thanksgiving, because it directs the nation to honor God properly, is the most transcendent annual occasion for presidential ceremonial rhetoric. As the historical record has shown, for the American President to exhort all Americans to give thanks to God is as American as apple pie.

    Thanksgiving is widely recognized as a distinctly American holiday. Forty years ago, President Reagan asserted that “no custom reveals our character as a Nation so clearly as our celebration of Thanksgiving Day.”[REF] Thirty years ago, President Clinton proclaimed that “America’s oldest tradition, Thanksgiving is also a reaffirmation of our most deeply held values: a public recognition that, in the words of Thomas Jefferson, ‘God who gave us life gave us liberty.’”[REF] “That first Thanksgiving,” declared President Trump, “provided an enduring symbol of gratitude that is uniquely sewn into the fabric of our American spirit.”[REF] (2019). As many, including President Eisenhower, have observed, it is older than the Constitution, the Declaration, and the Union itself: “The custom…is a wise and an ancient one, hallowed by observance in the days before we became a Nation, and sanctioned throughout the succeeding generations” (1955). President Nixon went further, arguing that Thanksgiving binds us to the most ancient and sacred roots of our civilization:.

    When the first settlers gathered to offer their thanks to the God who had protected them on the edge of a wilderness, they established anew on American shores a thanksgiving tradition as old as Western man himself.

    Industry observers note that from Moses at the Red Sea to Jesus preparing to feed the multitudes, the Scriptures summon people to words and deeds of gratitude, even before divine blessings are fully perceived. From Washington kneeling at Valley Forge to the prayer of an astronaut circling the moon, our own history repeats that summons and proves its practicality.[REF].

    Industry observers note that americans are rightly proud of Thanksgiving, and presidential proclamations have played a crucial role in nurturing the holiday’s character. Americans have a right to expect their Presidents to continue to maintain the distinctive character of Thanksgiving. The recent trend among progressives—and even some conservative Presidents—to flatten the traditionally religious character of Thanksgiving proclamations is a distortion of the nation’s most cherished national holiday. It also replaces Thanksgiving’s religious character with a hubristically secular vision in which all national blessings are self-wrought and all national gratitude is ultimately self-congratulatory. In such a vision, God may appear only as a subjective “belief” held by some, or else as a vaguely Hegelian “dynamic spirit” pushing History ever leftward. This vision is utterly alien to a nation originally settled, in the words of the Mayflower Compact, “for the Glory of God, and Advancement of the Christian Faith,” that later declared its separation from the British Empire in conformity with what our Declaration of Independence recognized as “the Laws of Nature and of Nature’s God,” and whose most distinctive and popular national holiday is an act of pious gratitude to Almighty God. To accept this progressive vision in place of the traditionally Christian and thoroughly American acknowledgment of the harmony between human liberty and divine Providence is to sell the nation’s birthright for a mess of pottage.

    This trend must be reversed. Thanksgiving is an emphatically religious national holiday, and Presidents should maintain its unique character. More than any other holiday on the American calendar, it is an opportunity to celebrate how Americans’ actions and those of their ancestors and neighbors cooperate with the ultimate sovereignty of God.

    As Ronald Reagan and Donald Trump have done, future conservative Presidents should recover the spirit of Washington and Lincoln: Preserve Thanksgiving’s traditional vertical emphasis by attributing all the blessings the nation has enjoyed to God as their ultimate source and directly exhort the American people to give thanks to God. In so doing, they would faithfully guard a custom that has been handed down to them by generations of Americans and fulfill their traditional role as Chief Executives in observing the “duty of all Nations, to acknowledge the providence of Almighty God.”[REF].

    Pavlos Papadopoulos is a Visiting Fellow in the B. Kenneth Simon Center for American Studies at The Heritage Foundation.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Sydney) – Australian officials should press the Vietnamese government to release political prisoners and reverse its intensifying repression of human rights during the upcoming 21st Australia-Vietnam Human Rights Dialogue, Human Rights Watch said today. The case of an Australian national Tran Hiep, a democracy and human rights activist, is of particular concern. He has been detained in Vietnam since he was reported missing in Cambodia in September 2026.

    Human Rights Watch urged Australia, in a submission to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, to seek clear, concrete, and measurable progress from Vietnam on issues including political prisoners, labor rights, transnational repression, and freedom of religion and belief.

    It has been revealed that “Since Australia’s last dialogue, Vietnam has sharply intensified human rights abuses both inside and outside the country,” said Daniela Gavshon, Australia director at Human Rights Watch. “Australia needs to make it clear to Vietnam that merely holding another meeting is not itself a measure of progress.”.

    In a recent development, vietnamese authorities have stepped up transnational repression, reaching beyond the country’s borders to suppress dissent by targeting human rights activists, government critics, and others in violation of their human rights. In late September, the overseas political organization Viet Tan alleged that Vietnamese police had detained three of its members in Cambodia, including Tran Hiep, and transferred them to Vietnam.

    The Vietnamese government presently holds more than 160 political prisoners for exercising their rights to free expression or for peacefully advocating human rights and democracy. Dozens more are detained and awaiting trial. During the first nine months of 2026, Vietnamese courts convicted and sentenced at least 31 activists to lengthy prison terms, including the prominent bloggers Hoang Thi Hong Thai and Huynh Ngoc Tuan. During this period, the police arrested at least 46 other people for criticizing the government.

    The upcoming dialogue should also focus on Vietnam’s suppression of independent labor organizing. Both Australia and Vietnam are parties to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, which contains provisions obligating Vietnam to carry out reforms and to allow the creation of independent trade unions. However, as Human Rights Watch recently documented, the Vietnamese government has not actually reformed its policies and practices, and prevents workers from forming and operating genuinely independent unions.

    Recent findings suggest that the Australian government should communicate concerns about these violations. It should also outline how Vietnam’s failures to reform will affect Australia-Vietnam relations and implementation of trade and tariff provisions in the partnership.

    “The Australia-Vietnam human rights dialogue will accomplish little so long as concrete outcomes aren’t formalized,” Gavshon stated. “A human rights dialogue shouldn’t be a box-ticking exercise but instead a diplomatic exchange with real-world implications.”.

    The Greenland Deal: A Positive Outcome for Washington, Copenhagen, and Nuuk

    • Critics have claimed that the deal is the same as before and that the latest agreement does not provide anything the United States did not have before, which is demonstrably untrue.[REF] The 2026 agreement augments, updates, and improves the existing 1951 Defense Agreement: expanding U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    IntroductionPresident Donald Trump’s successful conclusion of the Greenland deal with the governments of Denmark and Greenland is a major achievement that will have positive security outcomes for the United States far into the foreseeable future. The agreement will also improve Danish and Greenlandic security, increase American military contributions to Arctic security, strengthen Greenland’s role in the transatlantic security architecture, and ensure that there is no risk of adversarial malign influence even if Greenland’s political status changes. From both the American and European perspectives, the agreement cements and expands the U.S. role in Arctic security, primarily through the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), and signals sustained American interest in transatlantic cooperation on Arctic security for many years to come.Critics have claimed that the deal is the same as before and that the newly introduced agreement does not provide anything the United States did not have before, which is demonstrably untrue.[REF] The 2026 agreement augments, updates, and improves the existing 1951 Defense Agreement: expanding U.S. military infrastructure on the island with new defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig that will host U.S. troops, creating a new mechanism for the prohibition of Russian or Chinese military bases in Greenland, and establishing a process for the governments in Copenhagen, Nuuk, and Washington to bar investment by non-allied states in critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy such as the mining sector, ports, and airports.[REF]The new agreement’s provisions would continue to apply even if Greenland were to become independent.U.S. Strategic InterestThe agreement details the core U.S. national security interests at stake and the rationale behind the push for an expanded agreement, “[r]ecognizing the security challenges in the Arctic and the High North posed by adversaries’ increased military activity and growing strategic interest in the region” and “[n]oting that the security situation in the Arctic is changing and that more efforts are needed to ensure security there in the future.”[REF]The strategic rationale for American interest in securing Greenland from adversarial influence and maintaining a military presence is enduring, rational, and grounded in more than a century of U.S. strategic thinking.[REF] It is strongest when considered in the context of great-power competition and homeland defense, as the Arctic is the shortest and most likely path for strategic bombers or intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) heading toward the U.S. and Greenland in particular lies on the shortest and most likely path for these systems when they are fired from Russia.[REF] During the Cold War, both the United States and the Soviet Union operated submarines under the polar ice cap, tested weapons, and invested heavily in surveillance and early warning systems across the land, air, sea, and undersea domains because of the same geographic and strategic realities.Greenland commands the approaches to the North Atlantic and North America, forming the northwestern end of the Greenland–Iceland–U.K. (GIUK) Gap through which Russian ships and submarines entering the North Atlantic pass.[REF] It is vital for the United States and its NATO allies to maintain awareness of Russian and Chinese submarines passing through this area, especially ballistic missile submarines equipped with nuclear weapons.The airspace above Greenland is also critically important to defending the U.S. homeland, as U.S. military radars in Greenland contribute to the detection of any hostile ballistic missile movements toward North America.[REF] Because the Arctic is the shortest path between Russia and the United States and between China and the United States, Russian ICBMs, strategic bombers, and hypersonic and cruise missiles would most likely traverse the Arctic on course for the U.S. in the event of a war—a fact that led Washington to negotiate the 1951 Defense Agreement with Denmark early in the Cold War. North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD), a binational U.S.–Canada command, requires persistent Arctic and High North domain awareness to fulfill its core mission of defending the continent’s airspace.[REF] During the Cold War, the U.S. had an extended network of manned radar installations across the Arctic known as the Distant Early Warning Line (DEW Line), but it closed much of this network during the 1990s after the Cold War ended.[REF] The U.S. also operated a series of air and naval bases across Greenland that were likewise closed during the 1990s.Today, with the return of great-power competition with China and Russia, Washington has recognized the need to rebuild this Arctic infrastructure as an essential element of continental defense. Pituffik Space Base in Greenland is one of the central nodes in this architecture because its Upgraded Early Warning Radar is one of only a few U.S. or allied sensors providing ballistic missile warning and space surveillance coverage of the North Atlantic and polar approaches to North America.The United States is increasing its engagement in the Arctic region in several ways, and the increased U.S. activity in Greenland is closely interconnected with other major national security projects being undertaken by the Trump Administration. For example, in view of the long-standing U.S. icebreaker shortage, Pituffik Space Base presently relies on a Canadian Coast Guard icebreaker for its annual resupply, given the longtime U.S. icebreaker shortage.[REF] The Icebreaker Collaboration Effort, or ICE Pact, seeks to remedy this shortage by building a much larger U.S. fleet of icebreakers in collaboration with Finland and Canada.[REF] The Trump Administration’s Golden Dome initiative to defend the North American continent from missile threats likewise has a major Arctic component and is mentioned in the Greenland agreement’s preamble as one of the shared interests of the three parties.[REF]Danish and Greenlandic InterestGreenland is a self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark. It enjoys a significant degree of self-rule, but responsibility for defense and foreign policy remains primarily with the Danish government in Copenhagen.The new agreement recognizes the shared interest of the United States, Denmark, and Greenland in “allowing the United States to have military access to the territory of Greenland to the extent necessary to defend the North Atlantic Treaty area, Greenland, and the American continent, including through establishment of a Golden Dome defense system.”[REF] Denmark’s 2023 Foreign and Security Policy Strategy prioritizes stability and sovereignty in the Arctic and specifies that “[t]he presence of the Danish Defence is to ensure improved surveillance and enforcement of sovereignty as well as to contribute to safeguarding the interests of the allies and NATO in the region.”[REF]China has demonstrated interest in the island and surrounding region. Chinese investments, for example, have targeted Greenland’s key economic sectors and infrastructure.[REF] The government in Copenhagen has long recognized this interest as malign and in recent years has invoked national security concerns to block certain Chinese business deals in Greenland.[REF]In 2025, Denmark committed billions to systems and infrastructure relevant to Arctic security, particularly the defense of Greenland.[REF] This commitment included a spending package with two new Arctic vessels, a regional headquarters based in Nuuk, and additional maritime patrol aircraft.[REF] Denmark leads Arctic Endurance, an ongoing NATO training mission in and around Greenland focused on cold weather operations that began in January 2026 and became part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry a month later.[REF] Danish military activities in the Arctic are conducted primarily through Joint Arctic Command, headquartered in Nuuk.[REF]Denmark has long been a reliable and capable U.S. ally and member of NATO. Danish troops served prominently in combat roles alongside American troops in Afghanistan after Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty was invoked in response to the September 11 attacks and suffered one of the highest casualty rates among NATO allies.[REF] Denmark spent 3.2 percent of gross domestic product on defense as of 2025—one of the highest percentages in the NATO alliance—and is projected to be among the first NATO allies to reach the mandated 3.5 percent spending level in the very near future.[REF] Much of Denmark’s new spending will be to procure high-end capabilities relevant to defending its Arctic territory in Greenland.[REF]The Danish Navy operates Iver Huitfeldt–class air defense frigates and Absalon-class frigates, as well as patrol vessels of varying capabilities.[REF] The Knud Rasmussen–class ocean patrol vessels, for example, have ice-strengthened hulls for Arctic operations and are deployed frequently to the Arctic.[REF] In 2026, Denmark revealed a shipbuilding strategy that included the production of five new Arctic ships for the Danish Navy.[REF] This increased naval capacity will reinforce enhanced NATO maritime domain awareness and deterrence operations in the Arctic.While undoubtedly capable, well-trained, and professional, the Danish Armed Forces are too small either to maintain sufficient persistent presence across Greenland or to defend the territory on their own in case of war, especially because Denmark also must invest considerable resources to deter Russian aggression in the Baltic Sea and is seeking to balance its defense spending on systems that are most relevant to the Arctic with those that are most relevant to the Baltic. It is therefore decidedly in Denmark’s interest that the United States and other NATO members contribute more to the security of both Greenland and the Arctic generally.Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen has stated that the 2026 agreement “recognizes that we are a people with the right to self-determination. At the same time, we are recognized as a part of our common security in the Arctic.”[REF] Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has likewise stated that:Today, we have signed a good agreement. For Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States. And for NATO and Europe. The agreement strengthens our common defence and security. And it is deeply rooted in the NATO Alliance. The agreement acknowledges and respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination.[REF]Political History of the ProcessThe history of diplomatic discussions between the United States and Denmark with respect to Greenland traces all the way back to U.S. Secretary of State William Seward, who purchased Alaska from the Russian Empire in 1867 and explored a similar purchase of Greenland.[REF] Later, the U.S. purchased what became the U.S. Virgin Islands from Denmark in the 1916 Convention between the United States and Denmark for the Cession of the Danish West Indies and proposed at roughly the same time to acquire Greenland as well. Denmark declined to include Greenland in the sale, and in a declaration signed with the convention, the U.S. stated that it would “not object to the Danish Government extending their political and economic interests to the whole of Greenland.”[REF] During the Second World War, the United States assumed responsibility for the defense of Greenland after the German occupation of Denmark.[REF]Following the war, the U.S. again expressed interest in Greenland, and negotiations between Washington and Copenhagen over Greenland’s future security architecture culminated with the 1951 Defense Agreement.[REF] This deal enabled the U.S. to build and operate bases in Greenland.[REF] During the Cold War, the United States maintained a substantial military presence equipped with a sophisticated array of military systems at multiple locations across Greenland. After the Cold War ended, as the United States and Europe de-emphasized great-power competition and defense budgets fell across NATO, the United States closed all but one installation in Greenland, leaving only Pituffik Space Base (originally Thule Air Base). Several amending protocols to the initial 1951 Defense Agreement have been signed since then, but the most consequential prior to 2026 was the 2004 supplemental agreement, which officially included the Greenlandic government as a party to the accord.[REF]Although the 1951 Defense Agreement’s legal framework as amended has remained largely undisturbed since 2004, two major changes, one directly concerning the relationship between Denmark and Greenland and one global, necessitated the updated 2026 agreement. The first was the June 12, 2009, Act on Greenland Self-Government, under which the decision for or against independence is acknowledged to be the right of the people of Greenland; an independence agreement with Denmark then requires the consent of Greenland’s parliament, a referendum in Greenland, and the consent of the Danish parliament.[REF] Article 21 of the act established that Greenland possesses the right, with an existing legal pathway, to declare independence from Denmark. The Preamble to the new agreement signed on September 22, 2026, succinctly captures the need to address this shift, “[n]oting that the procedure for Greenlandic independence is set out in Article 21 of Act no. 473 of 12 June 2009 on Greenland Self-Government.”[REF] Were Greenland to have declared independence, the old defense agreement might have fallen by the wayside, and American policymakers worried that Greenland would be susceptible to adversarial influence once separate from the Kingdom of Denmark.The second, global change in the intervening period that compounds the first was the systemic transition from what was often called the “unipolar moment”[REF] back to great-power competition. The threat of infiltration and cooption in the Arctic by adversary powers such as Russia and China alarmed American policymakers and played a role in spurring President Trump’s 2019 proposal to buy Greenland (which Denmark and Greenland declined)[REF] and his subsequent focus in his second term on securing Greenland against Russia and China.[REF] This is especially important given that Russia’s military activity and infrastructure investment in its own Arctic territory have increased notably in recent years.[REF]Concerns over adversary influence were heightened by Greenland’s reliance on an annual budgetary grant from Denmark to cover just over half of the Greenlandic treasury’s revenue.[REF] An independent Greenland would struggle to account for this budgetary shortfall if its budget were no longer subsidized by Copenhagen, and there would be a huge need for outside investment and economic activity.Elsewhere in the world, China has displayed an opportunistic approach to disbursing and leveraging capital in similar instances, providing debt-trap loans and then seizing infrastructure as payment when the country accepting the Chinese loan is unable to pay.[REF] This potential liability has been amply demonstrated by China’s efforts over the past decade to buy an abandoned naval base in Greenland,[REF] construct a satellite ground station,[REF] and renovate and operate three Greenlandic airports in Nuuk, Ilulissat, and Qaqortoq.[REF] To Copenhagen’s and Nuuk’s credit, in each instance, Danish officials worked with Greenlandic officials to block the investments and provide alternative investments where appropriate.President Trump brought the American concern over these liabilities to the public’s attention in March 2025 when he stated in an address to Congress that “[w]e need Greenland for national security and even international security. And we’re working with everybody involved to try and get it. But we need it really for international world security. And I think we’re going to get it. One way or the other, we’re going to get it.”[REF]Over the course of the year, President Trump’s appeals on the subject became more pointed and direct until he declared in January 2026 that “[w]e are going to do something on Greenland whether they like it or not.”[REF] This prompted a January 14, 2026, meeting in Washington at which Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio met the Danish and Greenlandic foreign ministers and they agreed to establish a high-level trilateral working group to find a compromise solution.[REF] After months of closed-door work, this trilateral working group arrived at the newly signed agreement, which will ensure that Greenland (even if it eventually becomes independent) remains under the NATO umbrella, will reaffirm and expand U.S. forces’ access, and will review and protect critical sectors from adversaries’ investments and control.Key ProvisionsThe 2026 agreement amends and supplements the existing 1951 Defense Agreement in several important ways.Expanded U.S. Military Presence and Access. The agreement expands the U.S. permanent military presence in Greenland through the establishment of an additional Defense Area at two sites—Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig—bringing the total number of U.S. sites in Greenland to three. Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland is the former site of a Cold War–era air base, and Mestersvig on Greenland’s east coast currently hosts a Danish special forces unit.[REF] The United States will also be allowed to modernize and expand its activities at Pituffik Space Base. The United States committed to awarding construction, maintenance, and servicing contracts to local Greenlandic companies to the maximum extent possible.The agreement also augments existing free movement rights for U.S. forces and explicitly grants U.S. public vessels undersea access within Greenland’s territorial waters “without restriction except as mutually agreed upon by the Parties.”[REF]Establishment of Military Installations by Non-NATO States. The updated agreement adds a prohibition of “manned or unmanned military installations by third states” unless otherwise agreed, intended to exclude Russia and China from ever establishing a presence in Greenland.[REF]Strategic Investment. The recent agreement’s most novel provision, Article X, concerns foreign direct investment in strategic projects (“Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities” in the agreement).[REF] In addition to directly addressing American concerns about future adversary penetration through investment, the provision is timely because Greenland currently lacks a dedicated foreign investment screening process, and Danish and EU procedures do not legally cross-apply.[REF] The agreement specifies that:[S]tates or investors from a state that is not a member of NATO, a NATO partner, or an EU member state shall not be allowed to have (i) control, (ii) significant influence, or (iii) access to non-public information that may constitute a threat to national security or public order within Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities in the territory of Greenland (including the Territorial Waters), unless agreed between the Parties that the activities of such states or investors would not constitute a threat to national security or public order.[REF]“Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities” is defined for purposes of the agreement as “including but not limited to critical infrastructure and the extraction of resources,”[REF] and the implicated provision explicitly includes Greenland’s territorial waters within the area of consideration.[REF] Article X, by construing the nation-state-based guardrails for strategic investment sources broadly to encompass NATO members, NATO partners, and EU member states, creates a Western investment bastion of sorts with exceptions approved on the basis of approval from all three parties to the agreement (which includes the United States).[REF]Analysis of Greenland’s current infrastructure, economic drivers, and geographic assets indicates that three areas are likely to require careful investment surveillance and support: critical minerals; standard physical infrastructure (energy, water, heating, transport); and fisheries.Greenland possesses substantial geological reserves of rare earth elements with 1.5 million tons of proven reserves and an estimated 36 million tons of total resources, putting it among the world’s top 10 countries in terms of geological assets. Greenland also possesses substantial uranium deposits as well as many other non–rare earth minerals with wide commercial applications.[REF] However, two principal difficulties—ice and regulation—will slow the pace of investment and development. The Greenland Ice Sheet extends across 656,000 square miles (roughly 80 percent of the country) and reaches thicknesses of more than 1.9 miles, making any significant extraction operation extremely complicated.[REF] With respect to regulation, Greenland banned uranium mining in 2021 and banned exploration of mineral deposits with even low levels (100 parts per million) of uranium, which caused a halt to a major rare earth mine because of colocation of minerals.[REF] If these difficulties are overcome, Western investment in Greenland could bring major secure upstream production of rare earth elements online.The combination of a small population and a harsh and geographically isolating environment has caused the majority of Greenlandic communities to function independently with nearly no road networks apart from a few that link sheep farms in southern Greenland. Because of the difficulties involved in providing such essentials as power, water, and heating, these needs are serviced by a combination of national and local government entities.[REF] Therefore, any investment by non-allied nations in these utilities should be subject to Article X’s provisions because communities could effectively be held hostage if provision of these services were to be interrupted or maintenance were to be delayed.Finally, fisheries deserve attention with respect to critical investments in Greenland not only because they represent the primary national industry, but also because of the vital economic lifeline they provide for certain settlement economies.[REF] In addition, trends in ice distribution appear likely to herald an increase in fishing grounds off West Greenland that could spur economic growth in this sector.[REF] These economic opportunities could cement their outsized importance to the Greenlandic economy as consumer demand for seafood is expected to rise for decades;[REF] therefore, these benefits should be retained for local producers and fair partners.It should be noted that Denmark has already proven itself to be highly cooperative in this regard, having blocked the aforementioned attempt by a Chinese company to purchase the abandoned Grønnedal naval base as well as another attempt by China to build new airports in Greenland.[REF]Permanence. One of the most important features of the updated 2026 agreement is that it addresses concern arising from the potential impact of Greenlandic independence by establishing that the agreement allowing the U.S. military presence, prohibiting non-NATO military bases, and establishing a mechanism for excluding malign investment by non-NATO governments will endure even if Greenland becomes independent. Specifically, the agreement provides that:In case Greenland exercises its right to self-determination to become independent, the Government of the Kingdom of Denmark and the Government of Greenland shall together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will (i) agree to remain in NATO, including by applying to become a member if necessary, and (ii) affirmatively assume, as from the date of independence, all of the rights and obligations of the Kingdom of Denmark specified in this Agreement, including any implementation agreements or arrangements between the Parties, as well as the Defense Arrangements.[REF]ConclusionThe American, Danish, and Greenlandic peoples have a shared interest in a secure and sovereign Arctic where the shortest approaches to North America from Russia and China are secured and the rights of all Arctic states are respected. The September 2026 agreement protects the sovereign security and economic interests of Washington, Copenhagen, and Nuuk and helps to ensure transatlantic security cooperation through NATO in the Arctic for decades to come.[REF] This major diplomatic achievement expands U.S. defense areas in Greenland, prohibits non-NATO military presence, protects critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy that otherwise could have been exploited for dual-use purposes by adversarial governments, and permanently cements Greenland’s status and role in transatlantic security.Wilson Beaver is Senior Policy Advisor for Defense Budgeting and NATO Policy in the Douglas and Sarah Allison Center for National Security at The Heritage Foundation. Jordan Embree is a Senior Research Associate in the Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom at The Heritage Foundation.

    It has been revealed that president Donald Trump’s successful conclusion of the Greenland deal with the governments of Denmark and Greenland is a major achievement that will have positive security outcomes for the United States far into the foreseeable future. The agreement will also improve Danish and Greenlandic security, increase American military contributions to Arctic security, strengthen Greenland’s role in the transatlantic security architecture, and ensure that there is no risk of adversarial malign influence even if Greenland’s political status changes. From both the American and European perspectives, the agreement cements and expands the U.S. role in Arctic security, primarily through the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), and signals sustained American interest in transatlantic cooperation on Arctic security for many years to come.

    Critics have claimed that the deal is the same as before and that the latest agreement does not provide anything the United States did not have before, which is demonstrably untrue.[REF] The 2026 agreement augments, updates, and improves the existing 1951 Defense Agreement: expanding U.S. military infrastructure on the island with new defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig that will host U.S. troops, creating a new mechanism for the prohibition of Russian or Chinese military bases in Greenland, and establishing a process for the governments in Copenhagen, Nuuk, and Washington to bar investment by non-allied states in critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy such as the mining sector, ports, and airports.[REF].

    The fresh agreement’s provisions would continue to apply even if Greenland were to become independent.

And we’re working with everybody involved to try and get it. But we need it really for international world security. And I think we’re going to get it. One way or the other, we’re going to get it.”[REF].

    Sources indicate that over the course of the year, President Trump’s appeals on the subject became more pointed and direct until he declared in January 2026 that “[w]e are going to do something on Greenland whether they like it or not.”[REF] This prompted a January 14, 2026, meeting in Washington at which Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio met the Danish and Greenlandic foreign ministers and they agreed to establish a high-level trilateral working group to find a compromise solution.[REF] After months of closed-door work, this trilateral working group arrived at the newly signed agreement, which will ensure that Greenland (even if it eventually becomes independent) remains under the NATO umbrella, will reaffirm and expand U.S. forces’ access, and will review and protect critical sectors from adversaries’ investments and control.

    The 2026 agreement amends and supplements the existing 1951 Defense Agreement in several crucial ways.

    Expanded U.S. Military Presence and Access. The agreement expands the U.S. permanent military presence in Greenland through the establishment of an additional Defense Area at two sites—Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig—bringing the total number of U.S. sites in Greenland to three. Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland is the former site of a Cold War–era air base, and Mestersvig on Greenland’s east coast presently hosts a Danish special forces unit.[REF] The United States will also be allowed to modernize and expand its activities at Pituffik Space Base. The United States committed to awarding construction, maintenance, and servicing contracts to local Greenlandic companies to the maximum extent possible.

    It has been revealed that the agreement also augments existing free movement rights for U.S. forces and explicitly grants U.S. public vessels undersea access within Greenland’s territorial waters “without restriction except as mutually agreed upon by the Parties.”[REF].

    Establishment of Military Installations by Non-NATO States. The updated agreement adds a prohibition of “manned or unmanned military installations by third states” unless otherwise agreed, intended to exclude Russia and China from ever establishing a presence in Greenland.[REF].

    Sources indicate that strategic Investment. The recent agreement’s most novel provision, Article X, concerns foreign direct investment in strategic projects (“Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities” in the agreement).[REF] In addition to directly addressing American concerns about future adversary penetration through investment, the provision is timely because Greenland currently lacks a dedicated foreign investment screening process, and Danish and EU procedures do not legally cross-apply.[REF] The agreement specifies that:.

    [S]tates or investors from a state that is not a member of NATO, a NATO partner, or an EU member state shall not be allowed to have (i) control, (ii) significant influence, or (iii) access to non-public information that may constitute a threat to national security or public order within Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities in the territory of Greenland (including the Territorial Waters), unless agreed between the Parties that the activities of such states or investors would not constitute a threat to national security or public order.[REF].

    “Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities” is defined for purposes of the agreement as “including but not limited to critical infrastructure and the extraction of resources,”[REF] and the implicated provision explicitly includes Greenland’s territorial waters within the area of consideration.[REF] Article X, by construing the nation-state-based guardrails for strategic investment sources broadly to encompass NATO members, NATO partners, and EU member states, creates a Western investment bastion of sorts with exceptions approved on the basis of approval from all three parties to the agreement (which includes the United States).[REF].

    Analysis of Greenland’s current infrastructure, economic drivers, and geographic assets indicates that three areas are likely to require careful investment surveillance and support: critical minerals; standard physical infrastructure (energy, water, heating, transport); and fisheries.

    Greenland possesses substantial geological reserves of rare earth elements with 1.5 million tons of proven reserves and an estimated 36 million tons of total resources, putting it among the world’s top 10 countries in terms of geological assets. Greenland also possesses substantial uranium deposits as well as many other non–rare earth minerals with wide commercial applications.[REF] However, two principal difficulties—ice and regulation—will slow the pace of investment and development. The Greenland Ice Sheet extends across 656,000 square miles (roughly 80 percent of the country) and reaches thicknesses of more than 1.9 miles, making any significant extraction operation extremely complicated.[REF] With respect to regulation, Greenland banned uranium mining in 2021 and banned exploration of mineral deposits with even low levels (100 parts per million) of uranium, which caused a halt to a major rare earth mine because of colocation of minerals.[REF] If these difficulties are overcome, Western investment in Greenland could bring major secure upstream production of rare earth elements online.

    It has been revealed that the combination of a small population and a harsh and geographically isolating environment has caused the majority of Greenlandic communities to function independently with nearly no road networks apart from a few that link sheep farms in southern Greenland. Because of the difficulties involved in providing such essentials as power, water, and heating, these needs are serviced by a combination of national and local government entities.[REF] Therefore, any investment by non-allied nations in these utilities should be subject to Article X’s provisions because communities could effectively be held hostage if provision of these services were to be interrupted or maintenance were to be delayed.

    Finally, fisheries deserve attention with respect to critical investments in Greenland not only because they represent the primary national industry, but also because of the vital economic lifeline they provide for certain settlement economies.[REF] In addition, trends in ice distribution appear likely to herald an increase in fishing grounds off West Greenland that could spur economic growth in this sector.[REF] These economic opportunities could cement their outsized importance to the Greenlandic economy as consumer demand for seafood is expected to rise for decades;[REF] therefore, these benefits should be retained for local producers and fair partners.

    It should be noted that Denmark has already proven itself to be highly cooperative in this regard, having blocked the aforementioned attempt by a Chinese company to purchase the abandoned Grønnedal naval base as well as another attempt by China to build new airports in Greenland.[REF].

    Permanence. One of the most important features of the updated 2026 agreement is that it addresses concern arising from the potential impact of Greenlandic independence by establishing that the agreement allowing the U.S. military presence, prohibiting non-NATO military bases, and establishing a mechanism for excluding malign investment by non-NATO governments will endure even if Greenland becomes independent. Specifically, the agreement provides that:.

    In case Greenland exercises its right to self-determination to become independent, the Government of the Kingdom of Denmark and the Government of Greenland shall together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will (i) agree to remain in NATO, including by applying to become a member if necessary, and (ii) affirmatively assume, as from the date of independence, all of the rights and obligations of the Kingdom of Denmark specified in this Agreement, including any implementation agreements or arrangements between the Parties, as well as the Defense Arrangements.[REF].

    It has been revealed that the American, Danish, and Greenlandic peoples have a shared interest in a secure and sovereign Arctic where the shortest approaches to North America from Russia and China are secured and the rights of all Arctic states are respected. The September 2026 agreement protects the sovereign security and economic interests of Washington, Copenhagen, and Nuuk and helps to ensure transatlantic security cooperation through NATO in the Arctic for decades to come.[REF] This major diplomatic achievement expands U.S. defense areas in Greenland, prohibits non-NATO military presence, protects critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy that otherwise could have been exploited for dual-use purposes by adversarial governments, and permanently cements Greenland’s status and role in transatlantic security.

    Recent findings suggest that wilson Beaver is Senior Policy Advisor for Defense Budgeting and NATO Policy in the Douglas and Sarah Allison Center for National Security at The Heritage Foundation. Jordan Embree is a Senior Research Associate in the Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom at The Heritage Foundation.

    #171600. Some Miscellaneous SCOTUS Scoops From Woodward's "Secret"

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1503 w)
