    Some Miscellaneous SCOTUS Scoops From Woodward's "Secret"

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1503 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, bob Woodward's new book is a bit unusual.
    • According to recent reports, beyond any particulars about the Justices, I found most insightful his craft in getting people to speak.
    • Sources indicate that scott and I were intensely pursuing interviews with clerks all over the country.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, bob Woodward's new book is a bit unusual. There is no coherent narrative or flow. Each chapter simply tells the story of another one of his sources. Chapters 36 through 43 walk through his interviews with Supreme Court Justices, law clerks, and others for The Brethren. The book is a collection of his recollections, mostly from recorded memos, and what all of his source noted.

    According to recent reports, beyond any particulars about the Justices, I found most insightful his craft in getting people to speak. He invariably starts by finding someone low on the totem pole, building trust, and working his way up.

    Sources indicate that scott and I were intensely pursuing interviews with clerks all over the country. The names of all the law clerks, past and present, was readily available public information. I cannot underscore enough how important it is in journalism to focus on the low end of the totem pole. Presidents, justices, cabinet officials are all important interviews.

    What began as a somewhat random "catch-as-catch-can" for Scott and me helped us get inside, as we used what we collected to dig deeper. Quoting information or documents we already possessed helped give confidence to other clerks who would then sometimes reach into their own archives to add details and documents. . . .

    Most of the information in our book, The Brethren, is based on interviews with more than 200 people, including five justices who talked, 170 former and current law clerks, and several dozen former employees of the court. Virtually all the interviews were conducted on deep background, meaning that the identity of the sources would be kept confidential for their lifetimes but all the information could be used in the book. Since all of the justices are now deceased, I am lifting the lid on our interviews with them.

    This sort of journalism takes time and time and more time. But eventually, he has enough information that principals feel comfortable talking to him. And even if he learned what happened from multiple sources, asking yet another source opens up the possibility for even more insights to be gleaned.

    It has been revealed that chapter 36 recounts Woodward's interactions with Justice Stewart, who invited the reporter to his home for an interview. Stewart spoke very critically of Chief Justice Burger. That interview convinced Woodward there was enough to write a book. The publisher gave him and Scott Armstrong a $300,000 advance. That is more than $1.5 million in present-day value.

    Chapter 37 recounts Woodward's interview with Justice Powell. Powell invited him to the Court—right away. Woodward arrived at 4:30 p.m. that day. Powell stated, "Intellectually there is no Brandeis or Frankfurter or Cardozo on the court now." I've made similar comments since Justice Scalia's passing. I wonder if any members of the current Court think they are at the intellectual level of Holmes or Story? I appreciate Powell's humility.

    It has been revealed that woodward would interview Powell two more times. I found these comments about Roe striking:.

    I asked him about the Supreme Court's landmark 1973 abortion decisions in Roe v. Wade and Doe v. Bolton, which legalized abortion nationwide. "It was hard for me and I was frankly strongly result oriented," Powell said of the decision. "I would support abortion funding by the states if I was in the legislature," he added. This caught me off-guard and seemed contrary to the opinions he had written saying there was no right to a state-funded abortion.

    Recent findings suggest that "I thought the abortion laws were atrocious," Powell continued, referring to the state abortion laws prohibiting abortion. "If you wanted to pay for an abortion you could get one." I noted his selection of the word "wanted" instead of "could afford" which was a major part of the glitch as I saw it.

    Sources indicate that there should be no doubt that Roe was an outcome-driven decision. There was no law—just policy.

    Industry observers note that chapter 38 focuses on how he interviewed more than 170 law clerks. Powell authorized his law clerks to speak to Woodward. Burger's former clerks were "at times the most helpful," especially since Woodward never bothered asking Burger to speak. I already recounted the story in which he "borrowed" Justice Brennan's history of the Watergate tape case.

    Chapter 39 explains how Justice Powell thought the Justices should talk to reporters to minimize the bad press. Powell wrote in a draft letter to Burger that he never sent: "I had rather someone on the Court discussed this with him accurately than leave him to reach his own conclusions with the right to say that he was stonewalled by the Justices.".

    Chapter 40 discusses Armstrong's interview with Justice Blackmun, and the resulting "19-page single-spaced memo." There were a few useful nuggets. Blackmun appreciated how he wasn't Nixon's first or even second choice for the seat.

    According to recent reports, "I am humbled by the fact that I was number three, not the number one choice," Blackmun noted of his appointment to the Supreme Court. Nixon's first choice, Clement Haynsworth, a federal judge from South Carolina, and second choice, G. Harrold Carswell, a federal judge from Florida, were rejected narrowly in brutal public fights, largely over concerns that Nixon was attempting to shift the court's ideology, which of course he was. Blackmun had been confirmed unanimously in May 1970 in a 94-to-0 vote. "A scarecrow could get nominated after what had happened," Blackmun continued. "It was a difficult period for the Senate. A number of [senators] told me that they wanted to get it over with. They had a real sense of relief that an average guy had come along with whom they couldn't find much wrong.".

    I wonder if Justice Kennedy ever had similar marks of humility, as a fellow third-choice?

    Blackmun was also assigned the Roe opinion because Chief didn't want to take the heat:.

    Blackmun mentioned he was well aware that no matter what he wrote, the opinion would be controversial and he would be hated and vilified. The chief could not afford to take on such a controversial case himself, particularly from the minority. "That's why I was assigned the abortion memo. We were scattered on it," Blackmun said. Douglas was the court's mischievous liberal, the rebel, and couldn't be the author. Any abortion opinion Douglas wrote would be widely questioned outside the court. Brennan was a firm vote for striking down the state abortion laws, but he was the court's only sitting Catholic. As such, Brennan could not be expected to take the heat from the Catholic anti-abortion groups. Marshall could not author for similar reasons: An opinion by the court's only Black man could be perceived as specifically designed for Black people or incite race-fueled blame for the decision. Stewart would have trouble going very far… That left one option: Blackmun.

    Recent findings suggest that by Chapter 41, the first draft of the book was complete. Now, Powell declined to talk further with Woodward.

    Chapter 42 recounts a fairly gruff interview with Justice White, who gave up virtually nothing.

    According to recent reports, chapter 43 relays how Justice Powell wrote to Chief Justice Burger about the new book. Powell, of course, did not disclose how he spoke with Woodward, and how he authorized his clerks to do the same. I can get Burger's frustration.

    Recent findings suggest that chief Justice Warren Burger erupted in a letter back to Powell, squarely blaming the clerks and noting "there are hazards in talking with certain 'categories' in this life"—meaning me and Scott, or reporters in general. He criticized the clerks for seeming to have succumbed to the "glamour" of rubbing shoulders with "print names!" . . .

    I wondered if Burger knew that five of the seven justices in his ranks had talked to us and several had given their clerks permission to assist us.

    It has been revealed that if only Burger knew that Powell and others blabbed. I suspect Chief Justice Roberts can relate.

    It also turns out that Woodward asked a young Stephen Breyer to fact-check the book.

    Recent findings suggest that another secret that has a certain historic value today was that one weekend before The Brethren went to the printers, a young man named Stephen Breyer came over to my home. He sat in the living room and read the book cover to cover. At that time he was chief counsel to the Senate Judiciary Committee chaired by Senator Ted Kennedy. Scott had insisted we have the book's use of legal terms checked for obvious errors. After reading, Breyer told us it was "a hell of a book.".

    It has been revealed that I would note there is no discussion of interviewing Justice Rehnquist, even though Rehnquist is named as a source. Something is off.

    That's it. Nothing earth-shattering. But it is a shame Woodward decided to relay non-public communications with Breyer and Kagan, who are both alive and well.

    Tech Report: Australia’s Sanctions on West Bank Settlers Increase Pressure

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Australia declared on November 18 further targeted sanctions on three individuals and four entities involved in illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank.
    • It has been revealed that the situation in the West Bank is dire.
    • On the same day as Australia’s announcement, the United Kingdom revealed sanctions against eight construction companies and property development firms that have not, until now, been sanctioned by any government.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Australia declared on November 18 further targeted sanctions on three individuals and four entities involved in illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank. Although these sanctions are a welcome step, they are long overdue and don’t go far enough.

    It has been revealed that the situation in the West Bank is dire. State-backed settler violence has risen to all-time highs. Tens of thousands of Palestinians have been displaced and 1,394 killed by settlers or soldiers in the West Bank since the start of 2023. The number of illegal Israeli settlements has nearly doubled, including the E1 settlement project, which even Israel’s allies have called a “red line,” and which Israeli ministers openly boast is intended to erase any possibility of a future Palestinian state.

    On the same day as Australia’s announcement, the United Kingdom revealed sanctions against eight construction companies and property development firms that have not, until now, been sanctioned by any government. The individuals and companies sanctioned by Australia, however, have previously been sanctioned by the United Kingdom and other states.

    When the United Kingdom, France, and Canada revealed a ban on Israel’s illegal settlements in September, Australia did not join. Instead, at the time, Foreign Minister Wong promised further sanctions to deter illegal settlement, which are the ones just announced.

    Industry observers note that israel’s settlements are illegal. In its 2024 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice found that all states have an obligation to “take steps to prevent trade or investment relations that assist in the maintenance of the illegal situation created by Israel in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.” Banning trade with illegal settlements isn’t optional. It’s required by international law.

    Australia indicates it is genuinely committed to upholding international law while continuing to trade with unlawful settlements that rob Palestinians of their land and livelihoods. Recent reporting suggested that the majority of agricultural shipments coming to Australia marked as “products of Israel” are from illegal settlements.

    It’s past time for Australia to do everything in its power to stop the expansion of settlements, both through a trade ban and targeted sanctions on construction companies engaged in illegal settlement expansion.

    Sources indicate that the midterm postmortem will continue for some time. Conservatives need careful data analysis from people who can interpret the numbers and understand politics, and politicians who can respond to public opinion with prudence and guiding rhetoric.

    Recent findings suggest that but as The Daily Wire hosts noted, there is an even deeper problem that needs attention: no one has made a “robust argument for Americanism as an argument, a fully fleshed out argument.” What are the values that make America, America? What is the positive vision?

    According to recent reports, america as a nation is defined by the organic intertwining of people, place, and principles. Each contributes something unique, and they reinforce one another to form a whole even greater than the sum of its parts.

    James Madison’s theory of separation of powers and checks and balances provides a helpful analogy. Each branch of government has particular responsibilities, but they are not strictly divided from one another. Instead, each branch holds pieces of the others. The president, for example, has the power to veto legislation, giving the executive branch a legislative function. With this dynamic, the three branches check each other to ensure that all act with fidelity and cohere as a single entity.

    >>> How To Win Back the Disillusioned American Dream.

    The same is true of the American nation of people, place, and principles.

    People.

    America is a people sustained over generations by what Americans hold in common: language, history, traditions, and religion, to name a few. As John Jay wrote in Federalist 2:.

    Providence has been pleased to give this one connected country to one united people—a people descended from the same ancestors, speaking the same language, professing the same religion, attached to the same principles of government, very similar in their manners and customs, and who, by their joint counsels, arms, and efforts, fighting side by side throughout a long and bloody war, have nobly established general liberty and independence.

    A shared culture binds Americans together and supports American principles. For example, speaking the same language allows neighbors to interact, thereby building goodwill and friendship. Communication also enables civic participation and deliberation, which are necessary for self-government.

    According to recent reports, religious institutions have historically played a major role in that deliberation. Churches are gathering places and seedbeds for community activity; they are the most important civic associations. At the time of the Founding, 70–80% of American colonists attended services regularly, and the ideas of the Revolution, consistent with biblical principles, spread through sermons, pamphlets, and newspapers.

    Religion is not the only way a people sustain itself. As George Washington wrote in his Farewell Address, an individual can develop a moral framework independently, but “reason and experience both forbid us to expect that National morality can prevail in exclusion of religious principle.” The Founders and ancient philosophers alike argued that a republic cannot survive without a virtuous people, and religious belief and practice are indispensable for morality.

    Place.

    Human embodiment comes with an instinctive love of home. America’s physical wonders and gifts inspire awe and gratitude. A sense of reverence reigns over the places where many of our ancestors gave the last full measure of their devotion. And fondness builds in the communities where Americans practice civic rituals and raise posterity. These attachments are good and serious.

    Yet America as a place is even more: it has fostered American principles and formed the national character.

    In a recent development, from the outset, James Madison argued that America’s extended territory mitigates the problem of faction: groups adverse to the common good. America has numerous factions, which makes it harder for any single faction to gain a majority. Instead, people and representatives must work with one another and communicate to achieve their goals. That deliberative process slows things down and makes it more likely that justice will prevail.

    John Jay further observed that America was composed not of “detached and distant territories” but of “one connected, fertile, wide-spreading country” with a “succession of navigable waters” almost made “to bind it together.” The Founders’ response to America as a place was consistent with democratic principles and reinforced the sovereignty of the people.

    It has been revealed that through the Potomac River Project, which connected regions by roads and waterways, George Washington sought to bind the nation and the character of the American people. Thomas Jefferson led the repeal of primogeniture and entail laws in Virginia. The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 extended that vision to the frontier, and the taming of America’s heartland was given over to those who would steward the land, rather than left to be worked by the many and owned by a few aristocrats.

    The frontier spirit is part of the American heritage as a result. Americans are adventurous, informal, resilient, industrious, and somewhat gritty. Both the yeoman farmer and the entrepreneur animate the American moral imagination, as America’s physical resources, free institutions, and the human capacity for creativity unleashed profound prosperity.

    Principles.

    America is the experiment in self-government, and self-government has a multi-layered meaning.

    Self-government at the institutional level means republican government, in which the people have a real say in the nation’s laws through mechanisms such as popular elections. As James Madison wrote, “no other form” of government “would be reconcilable with the genius of the people of America; with the fundamental principles of the Revolution; or with that honorable determination which animates every votary of freedom, to rest all our political experiments on the capacity of mankind for self-government.”.

    It has been revealed that as Madison suggests, self-government at the individual level underlies republican government. Because human beings have reason and conscience, they are responsible for their actions and can order reason above their passions and impulses.

    The maxim “all men are created equal” expressed in the Declaration of Independence recognizes the nature of human beings and situates mankind in an ordered universe. As John Adams wrote:.

    It has been revealed that [Equality] really means little more than that We are all of the same Species: made by the same God: possessed of Minds and Bodies alike in Essence: having all the same Reason, Passions, Affections and appetites. All Men are Men and not Beasts…. The blind are Men, and not Insects, the deaf are Men and not reptiles, the dumb are Men and not Trees. All these are Men and not Angells….

    America as a nation is dedicated to these principles, which define the American national character.

    It has been revealed that as distinguished Washington and Founding scholar Dr. William B. Allen has written, Lincoln and others believed that regimes are guided by “a shared view of justice that makes a people a people. This was a very old idea, one expressed by Plato, and Aristotle, and Cicero, and Aquinas, and even Jefferson.”.

    Shared understanding imposes limits on behavior and introduces the possibility of friendship, love, and goodwill. As a people, Americans have declared that “life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness” are inalienable rights, and that rights and duties are non-negotiable. Citizens can reasonably take for granted that neighbors will not use force or steal one another’s property, and those boundaries allow interaction and harmony.

    Conclusion.

    Articulating a positive vision of the American nation helps identify policy solutions and cultural difficulties.

    Challenges to self-government include the growth of the administrative state and the erosion of deliberation by instant communication.

    >>> Freedom Isn’t Automatic—Each Generation Must Fight To Keep It.

    In a recent development, this customizable and disembodied world erodes shared memories and experiences. Americans are less likely to gather for small-town parades and fireworks, as spending a solitary evening of Netflix and Uber Eats is more comfortable than eating a hot dog with a neighbor. For such reasons, preserving and defending the physical historic sites that transmit the American story and bring citizens together is even more urgent.

    Political and legal decisions have driven religion out of the public square, and churches have lost parishioners as they have diluted doctrine and required less of the human person.

    Industry observers note that immigration remains a concern as insular communities fail to assimilate into the American way of life. Explaining why others should assimilate requires educating the native-born population in the nation’s Founding principles, so its members can articulate why America is exceptional and worthy of loyalty.

    The nation’s Founding story teaches Americans who they are: a people committed to the principles of self-government, rights and duties, human equality, and the dictates of the natural order.

    In a recent development, these are just a few solutions that would reinforce people, place, and principles. Clarity about what constitutes the American nation guides policy prescriptions. Establishing that clarity is a necessary step in responding to the midterms.

    #171595. Breaking: Quorums in Times of Crisis

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1543 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Quorums in Times of Crisis

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1543 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Last week the Fifth Circuit ruled that the House's proxy-quorum policy violated the Quorum Clause.
    • It has been revealed that much of the doomsaying is out of proportion to reality.
    • Perhaps the only major outlier is the Electoral Count Reform Act.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Last week the Fifth Circuit ruled that the House's proxy-quorum policy violated the Quorum Clause. I've yet to read any actual substantive disagreements with the merits. Rather, there have been a smattering of warnings about the potential consequences of the decision, attacks on the Fifth Circuit's track record in past cases, and predictive judgments about what the Supreme Court will do. I assure you. If you actually read the Fifth Circuit's decision and the dissent, there is not even a close call. Unless consequentialism matters more than originalism.

    It has been revealed that much of the doomsaying is out of proportion to reality. In order for anyone to challenge a federal statute passed during this period, they would need to have both a reason and standing. Litigation is expensive and time-consuming. Parties do not simply file lawsuits for principle. Again, any remedy would be targeted to a particular law, so it is not possible to wipe out all legislation from this period. The courts do not have a magic eraser for the U.S. Code. Moreover, spending bills and related laws generally do not inflict injuries, so there is no obvious way to challenge many of the bills. Remember that Judge Hendrix found that Texas lacked standing to challenge the DHS Pilot Program, another proxy-passed-statute.

    Perhaps the only major outlier is the Electoral Count Reform Act. The validity of this statute would only arise in the case of a contested election. There is good reason to have the validity of this law settled. But there is an easy path forward. This was a bipartisan statute that could be re-enacted to eliminate any doubts.

    You might say it is unfair to make Congress re-enact a bill it already passed. I have zero sympathy for the House, which passed a landmark piece of legislation in the face of serious constitutional doubts. There was no actual health emergency that required the rule. The House could have easily followed social distancing protocols to allow members to spread out. The gallery upstairs would serve that purpose well.

    The House also could have opened a Zoom link for those who are unable to attend. Had these members been able to watch and participate in the proceedings and cast their vote at the time of the roll call, the legal matter would have been much closer. In February 2021, I participated as a virtual witness for Merrick Garland's confirmation hearing. It could be done. Senators who were in the chamber posed questions that I was able to answer.

    It has been revealed that the purpose of a deliberative body is to allow members to vote after open deliberation. Designating a vote in advance of the proceeding eliminates any chance for deliberation. Even in my own world, I often walk into a faculty meeting thinking I'll vote one way on a matter, but after hearing other views, I change my position.

    I suspect others can relate. The Supreme Court satisfied its statutory quorum requirement through remote oral argument. No one would have thought that Chief Justice Roberts could have sat alone in the Chamber, posing the questions that his colleagues sent in advance. Absent Justices could not submit signed proxy votes in advance of the oral argument that would be read aloud at conference. The same rules ought to apply to Congress.

    According to recent reports, the truth is the proxy rule was more about Speaker Pelosi's power than actual pandemic relief. As I remarked, I have no sympathy when Congress takes shortcuts. Courts with jurisdiction have an unflagging duty to exercise it. And all of the usual presumptions in favor of democracy do not apply when the legislative body ignores the bright-line procedural rules in the constitution. If INS v. Chadha was right--even though the heavens fell--then the quorum case is even righter.

    What matters to me are originalist principles. And the good judges of the Fifth Circuit followed the law where it leads. They were not cowed by potential consequences in other cases and the predictable hackles from commentators.

    Recent findings suggest that I've started to give the issue a bit more thought, and researched past instances in American history where Congress somehow managed to legislate during times of actual crisis. Here are four highlights.

    In August 1793, a yellow fever epidemic began to spread through Philadelphia—then the capital of the United States. At the time, Congress was in recess, and it was believed that holding meetings in the capital, including meetings of the legislature, would be unsafe. For that reason, President George Washington asked both James Madison and Thomas Jefferson whether he could summon—in effect, order—Congress to meet in a different location. They both advised that the President lacked the power to change the location of the meeting, but they proposed alternatives. Madison advised that Washington could suggest that the members meet him in nearby Lancaster or Reading, Pennsylvania. Jefferson insisted that Congress "must meet in Philadelphia, "even if it be in the open fields, to adjourn themselves to some other place." I am not aware of any evidence that either Jefferson or Madison or any of their peers ever considered the possibility that the Constitution's quorum rule could be relaxed in order to allow members to establish their presence or otherwise participate by proxy.

    It has been revealed that on August 8, 1814, about two weeks before the British would invade Washington, the national capital, and then burn the Capitol, President James Madison called on Congress to convene on September 19. Congress, unwilling to be defeated, found temporary accommodations in the Patent and Post Office Building (now the site of the National Portrait Gallery). Despite the risks of public safety, nearly 90% of the representatives were present. Again, there were no efforts to relax the Constitution's quorum rule, and there were no attempts to facilitate proxies as a means of carrying on legislative business.

    In a recent development, during the American Civil War, debates about the quorum proved particularly vexing by 1864. Should Representatives and Senators from States that took action to join the (purported) Confederate States of America be counted for purposes of a quorum? Ultimately, Senators from the Union States adopted a rule such that quorum was defined as "a majority of the Senators duly chosen." Because the southern state legislatures had not chosen new Senators for the United States Congress, vacancies for authorized senate seats were not filled, and so no one was "duly chosen." Thus, such authorized seats did not count for purposes of the quorum. I do not believe that this rule was an innovation, much less a relaxation of the quorum rule. Rather, the Senate's rule merely clarified the constitutional text and was entirely consistent with prior practice going back to 1790, when the Second Session of the Senate of the First Congress met. Moreover, the Civil War era congresses did not introduce any form of proxy voting.

    According to recent reports, in 1918, the Spanish influenza raged through the United States. It is understood that more than one-half million people in the United States would die from this epidemic. The Senate had passed a resolution to authorize the President to appoint certain medical professionals to the Public Health Service. The House, however, lacked a quorum to act, and the Speaker adjourned that day's meeting. The following day, the members worked out a one-time "gentleman's agreement" where no one would object to the lack of a quorum; absent a timely objection by a member in attendance the chair would presume the presence of a quorum. The bill passed under these somewhat unusual parliamentary circumstances, which the House would not repeat during the remainder of the epidemic. There was no attempt to allow absent members to designate a proxy to vote for them. Moreover, the constitutionality of this practice was never tested in court. I agree with Judge Hendrix's take on the Spanish Influenza incident:.

    This occurrence does not support an argument that the Quorum Clause does not require physical presence. Quite the opposite, the House was aware it lacked a quorum at the time, with members urging those who considered raising points of no quorum to withdraw their points because they knew a quorum call would reveal the obvious—the House lacked the physical presence of a quorum and therefore could not proceed to business. And the members sought to pass the bill by unanimous consent because a roll-call vote would reveal the absence of a quorum. The House's decision to proceed in knowing violation of a constitutional requirement does not alter the proper interpretation of that Clause—"[p]ast practice does not, by itself, create power." See Medellín v. Texas, 552 U.S. 491, 532 (2008) (alteration in original) (quoting Dames & Moore v. Regan, 453 U.S. 654, 686 (1981)). Instead, it may merely represent action beyond constitutional authority. But given the House's own acknowledgement at the time and the history previously discussed, the historical practice of the House—even when acting without a quorum—demonstrates an understanding that members must be physically present in order to count towards the quorum.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that four years ago, the Supreme Court corrected a grave legal error and overturned Roe v. Wade. With abortion no longer enshrined as a “right” in the Constitution, policymakers at all levels of government have stepped up to promote life in law, policy, and culture. For the first session of each upcoming Congress, The Heritage Foundation provides pro-life policy recommendations to Members and the presidential Administration. The following year, a progress report takes stock of what has been accomplished and what remains on the to-do list. Last year, President Donald Trump and a Republican majority in Congress took the reins. Heritage provided a pro-life policy road map of ways to reverse four years of President Joe Biden’s pro-abortion radicalism.[REF] Now, this Backgrounder analyzes legislative and administrative accomplishments and highlights additional ways the Administration and Congress can protect life.In CongressFrom appropriations to the reconciliation process, the 119th Congress protected taxpayers from supporting abortion and abortion businesses.LegislationCongress advanced important legislation to promote a culture of life.Defunding Big Abortion. Congress’s signature pro-life victory in 2025 was the One Big Beautiful Bill (OBBB) budget reconciliation measure. It included a provision preventing abortion providers like Planned Parenthood from receiving Medicaid reimbursements for one year.[REF] Medicaid makes up most of Planned Parenthood’s annual federal funding sources. In 2025, more than 50 clinics closed their doors, and across the country Planned Parenthood clinics are feeling the financial strain.[REF] Some blue states have stepped in to try to supplement funding but this is not sustainable in the long run.[REF] Both Planned Parenthood and blue state Attorneys General went to court to try to block the defund provision from taking effect, but were ultimately unsuccessful.[REF] Congress holds the power of the purse, and nothing in the Constitution entitles the abortion industry to Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars. As discussed below under “More to Accomplish,” another reconciliation bill could allow the defunding provision to extend beyond the OBBB’s one-year time frame, which has already passed. Planned Parenthood and other large abortion providers became eligible to receive Medicaid funds again on July 4, 2026.[REF]Supporting Pregnant and Parenting Students. In January 2026, the House of Representatives passed the Pregnant Students’ Rights Act (H.R. 6359),[REF] which requires universities to provide pregnant women and girls with information about their rights, resources, and available accommodations.Pregnancy Resource Center Support. Also in January 2026, the House also passed the Supporting Pregnant and Parenting Women and Families Act (H.R. 6945),[REF] which provides statutory clarity that states can direct Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) funding to pregnancy resource centers that support mothers, families, and unborn children through services like counseling, material support, and education.Addressing Weaponization and Selective Enforcement. The House Judiciary Committee approved the FACE Act Repeal Act (H.R. 589)[REF] in June 2025. The bill is needed in light of intense weaponization by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) under President Biden, which is also discussed below. The Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances (FACE) Act[REF] was enacted in 1994 and prohibits physically obstructing, injuring, intimidating, or interfering with anyone “obtaining or providing reproductive health services.” Under President Biden, the DOJ deliberately targeted peaceful pro-life Americans while failing to vigorously enforce FACE Act protections that apply to churches and pregnancy centers, which faced increasing attacks following the Dobbs decision overturning Roe v. Wade. Sufficient laws already exist at the state level to address criminal activity, so Congress should repeal the FACE Act once and for all.AppropriationsCongress stood firm to protect life via spending legislation.Maintaining Status Quo of Pro-Life Policies. House-passed appropriations legislation has incorporated numerous pro-life policy riders, such as the Hyde family of amendments that prohibit taxpayer funding for abortions in foreign and domestic programs. However, new pro-life policy riders are routinely stripped during negotiations between the House and Senate.[REF]Addressing Problematic Earmarks. In FY 2024, two hospitals that perform late-term abortion procedures received almost $2.5 million in federal funds via earmarks in that year’s Labor-HHS [U.S. Department of Health and Human Services] funding.[REF] Those were Senate earmarks; the House Labor–HHS subcommittee accepted no earmark requests for FY 2024 through FY 2026.[REF] For FY 2027, the House Appropriations Committee’s Labor–HHS subcommittee provided guidance for earmark requests.[REF] Among requirements going forward, entities that perform or promote abortions are not eligible. Entities that conduct research using embryonic stem cells obtained from an induced abortion, or human germline gene modification, are not eligible. And entities that facilitate sex-rejecting interventions are not eligible.In the Trump AdministrationThe Trump Administration played a significant role in advancing pro-life policies.Previous Executive Orders and PoliciesIn 2025, the Administration quickly acted on a host of policies, which are discussed in the 2025 Backgrounder.[REF] They include:An executive order to disentangle taxpayers from abortion funding.[REF]Reinstatement of the Protecting Life in Global Health Assistance policy, which disentangles foreign aid dollars from international nongovernmental organizations that perform or promote abortions.[REF] As discussed in the following section, the policy has since been expanded.Defunding of the United Nations Population Fund over its complicity with China’s coercive and inhumane population-control practices.[REF]Renewal of membership in the Geneva Consensus Declaration, a partnership of more than 40 countries committed to improving women’s health, protecting innocent life, and strengthening the family.[REF]Partial restoration of Title X family planning program funding to Oklahoma[REF] and Tennessee.[REF] These pro-life states were denied funding by the Biden Administration over their refusal to provide abortion counseling and referrals.Recission of a Department of Defense abortion travel policy that made travel and transportation allowances available to service members and their dependents for abortions.[REF]Rescission of Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA) guidance that wrongly claimed that EMTALA requires doctors to perform elective abortions.[REF]Pro-Life Regulations, Executive Orders, and Other PoliciesOver the past year and a half, the Trump Administration has taken additional steps to promote life-affirming policies. These steps include:Taxpayer Funding for Abortions. In July 2025, the Department of Justice issued an opinion[REF] that the Hyde Amendment, which prohibits taxpayer dollars from paying for elective abortions, means that the HHS cannot spend taxpayer dollars to provide “ancillary services necessary to receive an abortion”—such as the Office of Refugee Resettlement providing transportation for women seeking an abortion. The HHS has said it is reviewing the relevant regulations and guidance.[REF]Abortion in Obamacare Plans. On December 9, 2025, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) issued guidance[REF] about Section 1303 of the Affordable Care Act’s abortion coverage accounting gimmick. Section 1303 requires insurers to collect a separate payment for certain abortion coverage in qualified health plans approved to be sold on the exchanges. Maryland and other pro-abortion states attempted to commandeer excess funds remaining in abortion surcharge accounts to establish grant programs to pay for additional abortion travel and elective abortions.[REF] The CMS clarified that the leftover funds belong to insurers—not states seeking to subsidize additional abortions.As discussed below under “More to Accomplish,” the CMS should re-issue the Section 1303 regulation from President Trump’s first term. In December 2019, the CMS adopted a rule[REF] interpreting that separate payments be just that—separate—and that issuers needed to comply with the letter and spirit of Obamacare requirements. The same has not been true under Presidents Barack Obama and Biden. The CMS should rescind the Biden rule and return to the rule in place during President Trump’s first term.Abortion at the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). On December 18, 2025, the DOJ issued an opinion[REF] that the Biden Administration overstepped its authority by issuing a regulation requiring abortion procedures, referrals, and counseling to veterans at VA medical facilities. The VA quickly issued a memorandum returning to pre-2022 policies that excluded abortion and abortion counseling.[REF] On December 31, the VA issued a final rule formally rescinding the 2022 Biden Administration rule that returned to the pre-2022 abortion exclusions.[REF]International Abortion Funding. In January 2026, the Trump Administration revealed that it is further expanding life-affirming foreign aid policies. Since the 1980s the Mexico City Policy has required (under Republican Administrations) foreign nongovernmental organizations to certify that they will not perform or promote abortion as a condition of receiving U.S. family planning assistance. During President Trump’s first Administration, that policy was expanded to apply to more funding streams and called the Protecting Life in Global Health Assistance Policy. Now, under a new name. the Promoting Human Flourishing in Foreign Assistance (PHFFA) Policy has expanded to encompass abortion,[REF] radical gender ideology,[REF] and diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI)[REF] policies as well.Fetal Tissue Research. In January 2026, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) reinstated a policy from President Trump’s first term ending support for unethical and obsolete research using fetal tissue obtained from elective abortion. The prohibition applies to internal and external projects (such as grants to outside entities). [REF] The NIH can prioritize ethical alternatives instead.Planned Parenthood COVID-19 “Relief” Funding. In January 2026, the Small Business Administration (SBA) announced that it is reviewing whether Planned Parenthood affiliates improperly received more than $88 million in loans during the COVID-19 pandemic. The SBA is demanding that Planned Parenthood clinics either prove that they were eligible to receive Paycheck Protection Program loans or return the funding.[REF] During President Trump’s first term, the SBA preliminarily concluded that Planned Parenthood affiliates were not eligible to receive these loans that were meant to help small businesses, but the Biden Administration later forgave many of those loans.[REF]Department of Justice Weaponization. In April 2026, the DOJ issued an extensive report detailing how the DOJ under President Biden weaponized the FACE Act against pro-life Americans.[REF] The report concluded: (1) The DOJ violated Americans’ rights through biased enforcement; (2) the DOJ collaborated with pro-abortion organizations to track pro-life activists’ activity; (3) prosecutors repeatedly engaged in inappropriate conduct; (4) the DOJ sought harsher punishment for pro-life activists than for pro-abortion activists; and (5) the DOJ inappropriately tried to help a pro-abortion organization with an application for a grant.Reviewing Human Embryonic Stem Cell Research. In January 2026, the NIH announced a pause on submissions to the NIH Human Embryonic Stem Cell Registry and issued a request for information on ways to reduce—and potentially replace—current reliance on research using human embryonic stem cells.[REF]Pro-Life Budget Request for FY 2027. In April 2026, the Office of Management and Budget released its budget request for the upcoming fiscal year. The request includes long-standing provisions in current law, such as Hyde protections across multiple departments (foreign and domestic), conscience protections, and bioethics-related funding restrictions for certain research. Additional requests include protections separating foreign aid funding from organizations that perform or promote abortions, including additional conscience protections for medical trainees, stripping Planned Parenthood of any HHS funding, and ending funding for fetal tissue research.[REF] This proposal is a request and Congress will ultimately decide FY 2027 funding and dollar amounts. As with the FY 2026 request, the Administration demonstrated its strong commitment to pro-life policymaking throughout the government.Redirecting Teen Pregnancy Prevention Funding to Align with Pro-Family Priorities. In June 2026, the HHS canceled most federal Teen Pregnancy Prevention Program grants two years early, some of which had gone to comprehensive sex-education curricula taught by abortion providers like Planned Parenthood. The HHS opened new funding opportunities that will be available to grantees who align programming with the Administration’s priorities of sexual risk avoidance education and not encouraging, normalizing, or promoting sexual activity for minors.[REF]Conscience RightsThe Trump Administration is prioritizing enforcement of federal conscience protection laws. The HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR) is ensuring that no person or organization is discriminated against over their convictions on abortion and gender ideology.In January 2026, the OCR announced a list of enforcement actions and policy changes, including:A notice of violation determining that the Illinois law requiring abortion referrals violates the Weldon and Coats–Snowe Amendments.[REF]A nationwide “Dear Colleague” letter summarizing federal health care conscience protections that the OCR is tasked with enforcing and reaffirming the Administration’s commitment to protect individuals and organizations from being discriminated against due to their sincere moral or religious convictions.[REF]Recission of Biden Administration guidance that wrongly claims that federal law on emergency medical care requires doctors to perform elective abortions.[REF]Recission of Biden Administration guidance that wrongly instructed pharmacies to stock and dispense dangerous abortion pills, even though pharmacies and pharmacists have a right to not violate their conscience by participating in abortion. Under President Biden, the HHS walked back part of this guidance after losing a court case to pharmacies challenging the guidance.[REF] Now the guidance has been rescinded entirely.[REF]Disavowal of[REF] the Biden Administration’s August 2021 decision to withdraw the Trump Administration’s 2020 Notice of Violation that California broke federal conscience rights law over its insurance coverage mandate for elective abortion.Disavowal of[REF] the Biden Administration’s July 2021 decision to withdraw the Trump Administration’s Notice of Violation that the University of Vermont Medical Center broke federal conscience rights law by requiring a health care professional to participate in an abortion procedure despite strong objection.In March 2026, the HHS announced that the OCR is investigating 13 states over possible violations of the Weldon Amendment, which indicates government cannot discriminate against health care entities that do not pay for or provide coverage of abortions.[REF] The states under investigation have abortion coverage requirements for plans sold in their respective jurisdictions.[REF]In May 2026, the HHS announced an additional reorganization within the OCR.[REF] The OCR is tasked with enforcing federal civil rights laws related to conscience, religious freedom, privacy, cybersecurity, and more. In 2018, during President Trump’s first term, the HHS created a Conscience and Religious Freedom Division within the OCR. Under President Biden, this division was shuttered and absorbed, with the Civil Rights Division, into the Policy Division.[REF] Rights of conscience and religious freedom are not “less than.” Restoring the Conscience and Religious Freedom Division will provide the OCR with the tools it needs to best serve all Americans and ensure that their fundamental rights are respected.More to AccomplishBoth Congress and the Administration have successfully advanced important pro-life policies, but there is still more work to do.In CongressDefunding Big Abortion, maintaining long-standing pro-life policy riders, and holding bad actors accountable must continue to be a priority.Planned Parenthood. Preventing Planned Parenthood and other abortion providers from receiving Medicaid reimbursements for one year was a signature accomplishment in the 2025 OBBB budget reconciliation package. Medicaid makes up most of Planned Parenthood’s federal funding sources. However, this defunding provision was the only one in the entire bill subject to a one-year time frame rather than the full 10 years to which the bill can apply. Planned Parenthood and other large abortion providers became eligible to receive Medicaid funds again on July 4, 2026.[REF] If Congress discusses another reconciliation bill, the defunding provision should be incorporated for the full 10-year time frame so that taxpayers do not have to continue funding abortion providers.Appropriations. Congress has continued to include long-standing riders like the Hyde Amendment and similar language in annual appropriations bills, prohibiting taxpayer dollars from paying for most abortions. But many other pro-life policies can be enacted via appropriations riders. From expanding conscience protections to reinstating commonsense safety protections for risky abortion pills, there is more that Congress should do to promote life in must-pass spending legislation.[REF]Oversight. Congress should continue to invoke its oversight and investigatory role to hold bad actors accountable and ensure that that pro-life priorities in the Administration are not sidelined. For example, in 2022, activists obtained the remains of five preemie-size unborn babies who had been aborted at a notorious Washington, DC, late-term abortion mill. According to expert testimony, these babies may have been aborted using the illegal partial-birth abortion technique. One baby was still in the amniotic sac and may have been born alive and left to die.[REF] Local authorities stonewalled questions from Congress and the press about any investigation of this activity. Pro-life activists and Members of Congress feared that the DC Office of the Chief Medical Examiner would destroy the five bodies, but in February 2024 it confirmed that it would not immediately do so.[REF] During a June 2025 hearing, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi indicated that there was an ongoing investigation.[REF]Demand FDA Action on Dangerous Abortion Drugs. Congress should continue demanding transparency from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on its long-promised comprehensive review of the abortion pill. It is abundantly clear that current FDA postmarketing safety policies are not adequately protecting women and children.[REF] In light of the politicized approval process that put this risky drug on the market in the first place, a complete and thorough review is long overdue. Leadership changes at the FDA should not slow down or deprioritize this important work. Individual members and congressional committees should continue emphasizing the dangers these drugs pose to women, girls, and unborn children.In the Trump AdministrationThe Trump Administration should rescind Biden-era regulations and policies that promoted abortion and sought to undermine the 2022 Dobbs decision overturning Roe v. Wade. These include:Abortion Travel for Unaccompanied Illegal Alien Children (UACs). A senior Office of Refugee Resettlement official told The Daily Signal[REF] that the agency is working on reversing a Biden-era regulation allowing taxpayer-funded abortion travel for UACs.[REF] The changes were submitted to the Office of Management and Budget’s Regulatory Information Service Center in January 2026, but the updated regulation has not been formally proposed yet. The HHS should ensure that the rule advances quickly.A Privacy Regulation That Undercut Abuse Reporting. In June 2025, a federal court struck down[REF] most of a Biden Administration regulation that purported to strengthen protections for sensitive private health information, including information related to abortion. In reality, the rule improperly limited state child abuse reporting laws.[REF] The HHS should formally rescind the rule.The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s (EEOC) Wrongful Interpretation of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA). In 2024, the EEOC issued rulemaking interpreting the PWFA’s definition of “medical condition” related to pregnancy to include elective abortion, thus requiring employers to provide accommodations like time off from work to have an abortion or time off to recover from the procedure.[REF] Litigation related to the entire rule is ongoing. In May 2025, a federal court provided nationwide relief for employers who care deeply about the well-being of their employees (and their children, born and unborn) by vacating the elective abortion accommodation provision.[REF] The EEOC should clean up the mess and formally rescind its erroneous interpretation of the PWFA. Pro-life Members of Congress would not have supported this bipartisan bill if it empowered the federal bureaucracy to invent a requirement for abortion accommodations.A Rollback of a Conscience Protection Regulation from President Trump’s First Term. The Biden Administration partially rescinded[REF] President Trump’s 2019 rule about enforcing more than a dozen federal laws that protect conscience rights for individuals or entities that do not want to participate in or facilitate morally fraught procedures such as abortion.[REF] The Biden rule gutted the HHS Office for Civil Rights’ ability to adequately enforce conscience laws that protect Americans’ civil rights. The regulation from President Trump’s first term should be restored.Addressing Title X Family Planning Program Funds Used as a Slush Fund for the Abortion Industry. The Biden Administration rescinded a regulation from President Trump’s first term that required recipients to physically and financially separate all abortion activity from Title X activity and prohibited Title X projects from promoting or referring for abortion.[REF] The Biden regulation also required sites that do not offer a broad range of contraception to provide a prescription or referral. This created a new barrier for sites that offer fertility awareness-based methods (FABMs) but cannot in good conscience provide or refer for other methods. The Title X program should not be used as a slush fund for abortion providers. The Trump Administration should restore the regulation from President Trump’s first term.A Clean Up of Policies Concerning the Affordable Care Act’s (ACA) Nondiscrimination Provision. Among other things, Section 1557 of the ACA prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, color, national origin, age, disability, and sex in covered health programs or activities.[REF] Just weeks after the Dobbs decision overturning Roe v. Wade, the Biden Administration moved to redefine conditions related to “sex” to include abortion, as the Obama Administration had also done in 2016. The Trump Administration should revive the abortion-related provisions of this regulation from President Trump’s first term, issued in 2020.[REF]Ensuring that Issuers Comply with ACA Abortion Rules. Thirteen states require plans sold on their marketplace to include coverage for abortion. Section 1303 of the ACA says that such plans cannot use federal funds (including premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions) for elective abortions. Section 1303 also requires issuers to collect a separate payment from each enrollee for the abortion coverage portion and segregate those funds in separate allocation accounts solely used for abortion coverage. Plans are also required to provide notice to enrollees at the time of enrollment that the plan includes abortion coverage. But under Presidents Obama and Biden, CMS policy was essentially an accounting gimmick that did not enforce the letter or spirit of the ACA. The CMS should re-issue the Section 1303 regulation from President Trump’s first term. That rule[REF] rightly required that separate payments be just that: separate.Stopping Elective Abortions in the Indian Health Service (IHS) Program. The Biden Administration issued a rule that weakens the prohibition on abortion funding within the IHS.[REF] Per the Hyde Amendment, federal funds cannot be used to pay for abortion except in very limited circumstances. Under the Biden rule, if Congress ever fails to include the Hyde Amendment in annual appropriations legislation, then the IHS would be able to fund elective abortions.Robustly Enforcing Federal Conscience Protection Laws. Laws like the Church, Coats–Snowe, and Weldon Amendments are meant to ensure that no one faces discrimination for declining to perform, participate in, or pay for an abortion in HHS-funded programs. Under previous Administrations that prioritized a radical pro-abortion agenda, conscience protection was not a priority. The Trump Administration is reversing that trend. The HHS and the OCR should continue to protect Americans from discrimination in federally funded programs. For example, a February 2026 letter to the HHS from Alliance Defending Freedom identifies 49 HHS-funded family medicine residency programs that, it says, violate federal conscience laws by requiring residents to participate in abortion training.[REF]Prioritizing Health and Safety at the FDA and Department of Justice, Not the Abortion Industry’s Bottom Line. The FDA should expeditiously conduct its long-promised review of the abortion drug mifepristone and revisit the dangerous drug’s approval. At a minimum it must restore commonsense safety protections like in-person evaluation and dispensing. To that end, the DOJ also has a role to play in addressing mail-order abortion pills. For starters, it should rescind the Biden-era memorandum[REF] about interpretation of the Comstock Act, which prohibits mailing any “article or thing designed, adapted, or intended for producing abortion.”[REF] As explained in a Heritage Foundation Legal Memorandum, the Office of Legal Counsel’s interpretation of Comstock is so narrow “that it would be virtually unenforceable…. The plain and ordinary meaning of [Comstock] unambiguously prohibits mailing abortion drugs.”[REF]Pro-Life Progress Is PossibleSlim Republican–Democrat margins in Congress left little room for error when it comes to any legislative priority, including pro-life policies. That is why tools like budget reconciliation and must-pass appropriations legislation are so critical to advancing protections for babies and mothers.The Trump Administration has steadily rolled back much of the damage wrought by the Biden Administration, but key priorities are still unfinished. With the President’s second term in full swing, pro-life Americans expect to see policymakers continue to deliver more meaningful protections for women, girls, and unborn babies.Melanie Israel is a Visiting Fellow in the Richard and Helen DeVos Center for Human Flourishing at The Heritage Foundation.

    Oversight. Congress should continue to invoke its oversight and investigatory role to hold bad actors accountable and ensure that that pro-life priorities in the Administration are not sidelined. For example, in 2022, activists obtained the remains of five preemie-size unborn babies who had been aborted at a notorious Washington, DC, late-term abortion mill. According to expert testimony, these babies may have been aborted using the illegal partial-birth abortion technique. One baby was still in the amniotic sac and may have been born alive and left to die.[REF] Local authorities stonewalled questions from Congress and the press about any investigation of this activity. Pro-life activists and Members of Congress feared that the DC Office of the Chief Medical Examiner would destroy the five bodies, but in February 2024 it confirmed that it would not immediately do so.[REF] During a June 2025 hearing, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi indicated that there was an ongoing investigation.[REF].

    Demand FDA Action on Dangerous Abortion Drugs. Congress should continue demanding transparency from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on its long-promised comprehensive review of the abortion pill. It is abundantly clear that current FDA postmarketing safety policies are not adequately protecting women and children.[REF] In light of the politicized approval process that put this risky drug on the market in the first place, a complete and thorough review is long overdue. Leadership changes at the FDA should not slow down or deprioritize this key work. Individual members and congressional committees should continue emphasizing the dangers these drugs pose to women, girls, and unborn children.

    The Trump Administration should rescind Biden-era regulations and policies that promoted abortion and sought to undermine the 2022 Dobbs decision overturning Roe v. Wade. These include:.

    Slim Republican–Democrat margins in Congress left little room for error when it comes to any legislative priority, including pro-life policies. That is why tools like budget reconciliation and must-pass appropriations legislation are so critical to advancing protections for babies and mothers.

    The Trump Administration has steadily rolled back much of the damage wrought by the Biden Administration, but key priorities are still unfinished. With the President’s second term in full swing, pro-life Americans expect to see policymakers continue to deliver more meaningful protections for women, girls, and unborn babies.

    Melanie Israel is a Visiting Fellow in the Richard and Helen DeVos Center for Human Flourishing at The Heritage Foundation.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Since early November, many rural communities in the Catatumbo region, near the Colombia-Venezuela border, have suffered violent abuses and forced displacement as the 33rd Front, a dissident group of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), has clashed with the National Liberation Army (ELN) over control of the territory.

    During a field visit from November 9 to 12, Human Rights Watch interviewed community members, representatives of civil society organizations, humanitarian workers, and local authorities, who said these groups have continued to kill civilians, recruit children, plant antipersonnel mines, carry out drone attacks, and impose strict social control over communities.

    People told us that on November 8 in Caño Salado, a rural community in Tibú, members of the 33rd Front threatened residents and accused them of collaborating with the ELN. Two community leaders were killed. “They told people to leave, or they would kill anyone who was involved with the ELN,” a civil society member told Human Rights Watch.

    Dozens of families have also been displaced from Bocas de San Miguel and El Diamante, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.

    According to media reports, armed groups have also carried out six attacks using drones armed with explosives in Catatumbo in the first half of November, killing at least five people, including one civilian, and injuring 14 civilians.

    The situation in Catatumbo has been critical since early 2025, when Human Rights Watch documented that armed groups killed, assaulted, kidnapped, disappeared civilians and caused the displacement of more than 100,000 people.

    Sources indicate that according to official announcements, since President De la Espriella took office in August, the government has carried out three airstrikes in Catatumbo, resulting in 10 deaths. The strikes were followed by Colombian army ground operations that resulted in six arrests, and the recovery of two children who had been recruited by armed groups. Community members told us these actions have done little to reduce armed groups’ violence and control over communities.

    The government should urgently protect civilians, by ensuring that its security strategy goes beyond military operations. It should include effective law enforcement and criminal prosecutions, a stronger humanitarian response, support for affected communities, and targeted social and economic policies to reduce the high levels of poverty that fuel the strength of armed groups in the region.

    The Veteran’s Example for America

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that veterans Day is more than a commemoration of military service.
    • According to recent reports, veterans Day is more than a commemoration of military service.
    • Our service members do much more than most of us realize, and our society is the better for it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that veterans Day is more than a commemoration of military service. It is also a reminder that freedom depends on citizens willing to serve something larger than themselves—and not just when they are in uniform.Our service members do much more than most of us realize, and our society is the better for it.Across generations, American veterans have answered the nation’s call in war and peace out of a commitment to duty, sacrifice and country. Their example demonstrates that citizenship carries responsibilities as well as rights, and that self-government endures only when citizens place the common good above personal interest.The freedoms that Americans enjoy today were secured by all veterans who served. They defended not merely our borders but also the principles upon which this nation was founded: liberty, representative government and the rule of law.By defending the constitutional order, veterans helped preserve a nation in which political differences are settled through lawful debate and elections rather than force. Veterans Day is an opportunity to recognize the men and women whose sacrifices have made that peaceful self-government possible.>>> The Three Values That Are the Real Keys to America’s GreatnessVeterans have helped secure liberty against some of the most oppressive ideologies in human history, including communism and national socialism. American veterans were instrumental in defeating the Nazi regime during World War II, helping liberate Europe from a government built on tyranny, aggression and the systematic denial of human freedom.During the Cold War, generations of American servicemen and women stood watch against the expansion of Soviet communism, preserving the security of the free world through deterrence and steadfast resolve. Their service helped create the conditions that led to the collapse of the Soviet Union and the liberation of millions of people in Central and Eastern Europe.The freedom enjoyed today by nations once trapped behind the Iron Curtain is part of the legacy of those veterans who answered their country’s call.Across these conflicts, American veterans served as guardians of the principle that free people have the right to govern themselves. Veterans Day also reminds us that liberty is never self-executing. The constitutional freedoms secured through military sacrifice endure only when citizens practice the discipline, responsibility and respect for law that self-government requires.The veteran’s example therefore reaches beyond the battlefield, offering a model for preserving freedom in civic life.Veterans also participate in freedom’s defense at home at some of the highest rates in American society. According to the 2025 Veterans Civic Health Index, 81% of veterans were registered to vote in the 2024 election, compared with 74% of nonveterans. Seventy-three percent of veterans cast ballots, compared with 66% of nonveterans.The index also reports stronger veteran participation in volunteering, in civic organizations and in engagement with public officials and community institutions. Together, these measures point to a broader pattern: For many veterans, military service becomes a lifelong commitment to citizenship, civic responsibility and the preservation of our constitutional republic.Veterans continue to serve as teachers, business leaders, first responders, elected officials and civic volunteers, bringing military habits of integrity, discipline and teamwork into civilian life. At Military.com, Medal of Honor recipient Clint Romesha captures that enduring impulse, saying, “So many of us veterans just want to continue to serve after service.”Mr. Romesha identifies teamwork as one of the military’s greatest lessons—“It’s not about me; it’s about the team”—and as a principle that continues to guide veterans long after they leave the uniform behind.The veteran profiles of “American Heroes: Stories of Service” and “Pledge to Patriots” show this continuing commitment in action. These stories feature veterans mentoring young people, supporting one another, leading nonprofits, responding to disasters and strengthening communities.>>> Nina and the BikersThousands of veterans serve as poll workers, election officials and observers, helping to administer and safeguard elections. As a former election official and U.S. Navy veteran, I have seen them step forward when communities need poll workers. Through the nonpartisan Vet the Vote initiative, more than 163,000 veterans and military family members served as poll workers during the 2024 election cycle, up from approximately 63,500 during the 2022 midterms.National Guard members have supported election operations, security, coordination and emergency response at the request of state authorities. Their commitment to duty, adherence to procedures and record of public service can strengthen confidence in the electoral process they defended in uniform.On Veterans Day, we honor those who wore the uniform in defense of our nation. We should also follow the example they continue to set—as citizens, poll workers, community leaders and public servants—reminding us that freedoms secured on far-off battlefields must be preserved through faithful participation in self-government at home.Veterans Day recognizes a profound commitment to country, but it also challenges every American to accept the duties of citizenship.

    According to recent reports, veterans Day is more than a commemoration of military service. It is also a reminder that freedom depends on citizens willing to serve something larger than themselves—and not just when they are in uniform.

    Our service members do much more than most of us realize, and our society is the better for it.

    In a recent development, across generations, American veterans have answered the nation’s call in war and peace out of a commitment to duty, sacrifice and country. Their example shows that citizenship carries responsibilities as well as rights, and that self-government endures only when citizens place the common good above personal interest.

    The freedoms that Americans enjoy today were secured by all veterans who served. They defended not merely our borders but also the principles upon which this nation was founded: liberty, representative government and the rule of law.

    Sources indicate that by defending the constitutional order, veterans helped preserve a nation in which political differences are settled through lawful debate and elections rather than force. Veterans Day is an opportunity to recognize the men and women whose sacrifices have made that peaceful self-government possible.

    >>> The Three Values That Are the Real Keys to America’s Greatness.

    In a recent development, veterans have helped secure liberty against some of the most oppressive ideologies in human history, including communism and national socialism. American veterans were instrumental in defeating the Nazi regime during World War II, helping liberate Europe from a government built on tyranny, aggression and the systematic denial of human freedom.

    During the Cold War, generations of American servicemen and women stood watch against the expansion of Soviet communism, preserving the security of the free world through deterrence and steadfast resolve. Their service helped create the conditions that led to the collapse of the Soviet Union and the liberation of millions of people in Central and Eastern Europe.

    The freedom enjoyed today by nations once trapped behind the Iron Curtain is part of the legacy of those veterans who answered their country’s call.

    Industry observers note that across these conflicts, American veterans served as guardians of the principle that free people have the right to govern themselves. Veterans Day also reminds us that liberty is never self-executing. The constitutional freedoms secured through military sacrifice endure only when citizens practice the discipline, responsibility and respect for law that self-government requires.

    The veteran’s example therefore reaches beyond the battlefield, offering a model for preserving freedom in civic life.

    According to recent reports, veterans also participate in freedom’s defense at home at some of the highest rates in American society. According to the 2025 Veterans Civic Health Index, 81% of veterans were registered to vote in the 2024 election, compared with 74% of nonveterans. Seventy-three percent of veterans cast ballots, compared with 66% of nonveterans.

    In a recent development, the index also reports stronger veteran participation in volunteering, in civic organizations and in engagement with public officials and community institutions. Together, these measures point to a broader pattern: For many veterans, military service becomes a lifelong commitment to citizenship, civic responsibility and the preservation of our constitutional republic.

    Veterans continue to serve as teachers, business leaders, first responders, elected officials and civic volunteers, bringing military habits of integrity, discipline and teamwork into civilian life. At Military.com, Medal of Honor recipient Clint Romesha captures that enduring impulse, saying, “So many of us veterans just want to continue to serve after service.”.

    Recent findings suggest that mr. Romesha identifies teamwork as one of the military’s greatest lessons—“It’s not about me; it’s about the team”—and as a principle that continues to guide veterans long after they leave the uniform behind.

    In a recent development, the veteran profiles of “American Heroes: Stories of Service” and “Pledge to Patriots” show this continuing commitment in action. These stories feature veterans mentoring young people, supporting one another, leading nonprofits, responding to disasters and strengthening communities.

    >>> Nina and the Bikers.

    Thousands of veterans serve as poll workers, election officials and observers, helping to administer and safeguard elections. As a former election official and U.S. Navy veteran, I have seen them step forward when communities need poll workers. Through the nonpartisan Vet the Vote initiative, more than 163,000 veterans and military family members served as poll workers during the 2024 election cycle, up from approximately 63,500 during the 2022 midterms.

    National Guard members have supported election operations, security, coordination and emergency response at the request of state authorities. Their commitment to duty, adherence to procedures and record of public service can strengthen confidence in the electoral process they defended in uniform.

    On Veterans Day, we honor those who wore the uniform in defense of our nation. We should also follow the example they continue to set—as citizens, poll workers, community leaders and public servants—reminding us that freedoms secured on far-off battlefields must be preserved through faithful participation in self-government at home.

    Veterans Day recognizes a profound commitment to country, but it also challenges every American to accept the duties of citizenship.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Beirut) – Israeli authorities are detaining activists and community organizers attempting to protect Palestinian farmers during what the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has recorded as the most violent West Bank olive harvest season in its 20 years of records, Human Rights Watch remarked today.
