    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Beirut) – Israeli authorities are detaining activists and community organizers attempting to protect Palestinian farmers during what the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has recorded as the most violent West Bank olive harvest season in its 20 years of records, Human Rights Watch remarked today.

    Between October 1 and 26, 2026, OCHA recorded 397 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage, the highest monthly figure it has recorded since its documentation began in 2006. Israeli soldiers were present in 26.5 percent of such incidents documented by the Israeli human rights organization Yesh Din between September 27 and October 14. The Israeli military has detained hundreds of people trying to protect Palestinian farmers during their harvest, according to local media reports.

    “The olive harvest season should be a period of joy, strengthened community, and income for thousands of Palestinian families, but rising settler violence and harsh restrictions by the Israeli military have turned it into a period of anxiety and fear,” mentioned Sarah Sanbar, acting Israel and Palestine director at Human Rights Watch. “Rather than stopping settler violence, the Israeli military is detaining the people trying to ensure that Palestinian farmers can safely harvest their olives.”.

    It has been revealed that human Rights Watch interviewed four activists organizing groups or volunteers protecting Palestinians harvesting their olives, two of whom had been detained and released since 2025. Human Rights Watch wrote to the Israeli military on November 16; its responses are reflected below.

    Settler violence in the West Bank has been steadily rising since the current Netanyahu government took office in December 2022. Settlers responsible for attacks operate with the financial, material, and legal backing of the Israeli state. Attacks by armed settlers often occur alongside Israeli army units or with soldiers standing by.

    Absent state protection, Palestinian communities and activists have organized to protect themselves using a tactic called protective presence. This is a form of nonviolent activism and human rights monitoring where international, Israeli, and Palestinian volunteers physically accompany vulnerable communities.

    “[Their presence helps] to deter settlers, or have less violent attacks, and speed up the harvest so people do not have to stay for long exposed in the areas,” Rabie Abu Naim, a Palestinian farmer and activist from Al-Mughayyir village, northeast of Ramallah, told Human Rights Watch.

    However, the international presence is no longer able to deter settler attacks, or the military’s obstruction of the harvest. “I have been doing this for more than ten years,” an organizer stated. “What we used to think could protect farmers no longer works. Since 2023, all red lines have been crossed.”.

    Industry observers note that abu Naim described recent attacks by settlers in Al-Mughayyir, including beatings, burning cars, use of tear gas, and stopping cars on the road: “Anyone who takes the road to Abu-Falah on the western side of the village, which is now the only entry to Al-Mughayyir, claims their shahada [the Islamic declaration of faith, said as final words before dying]. They are entering an ambush … they either survive or they don’t.”.

    Sources indicate that “This year’s olive harvest season is one of the worst that Al-Mughayyir ever knew,” Abu Naim noted. “[Settler attacks] are becoming an hourly thing, not daily.”.

    Abu Naim was arrested in October 2025 and administratively detained for nine months. “I suspect it was because of coordinating [protection during] the olive harvest season,” he said.

    It has been revealed that al-Mughayyir’s farmers have been steadily losing access to their olive groves. In August 2025, the head of the Israeli military’s Central Command signed an order for the uprooting of olive trees on 300 dunams (30 hectares) of land in Al-Mughayyir, ostensibly for security reasons after a Palestinian reportedly shot and wounded a settler who had trespassed on the village’s land. According to Israeli human rights group Kerem Navot, settlers from the Shiloh area carried out clearing operations on about 620 dunams (62 hectares), more than twice the area covered by the order, then took over parts of the land.

    Industry observers note that “This year, there are no [protection] campaigns for Al-Mughayyir, because there are no lands we can access,” Abu Naim mentioned. “This year’s season, we can say that there isn’t a harvest.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the Israeli human rights organization Peace Now reported in October that the Israeli military had signed orders barring Palestinians from entering approximately 88,300 dunams (around 21,800 acres) of land in the West Bank, 30 percent more than in 2025, unless they coordinate with the military in advance. The military barred Israeli citizens from only 6,890 dunams of West Bank land, Peace Now reported.

    It has been revealed that the Israeli army routinely designates areas as “closed military zones” to forbid Palestinian farmers and international activists from accessing their lands. Legally, this means the land is entirely closed to Palestinians unless authorized by the military. Those entering their fields without prior coordination are committing a criminal offence under Israeli law and face potential removal or arrest.

    It has been revealed that community organizers said, though, that coordinating with the military does not always guarantee their security. “For Area C [i.e. areas under full Israeli security control and civil administration], it is completely forbidden to go, even if we do the necessary coordination,” Abu Naim said. “If we get there with the coordination then settlers come, they provoke, attack, call the army and tell them they’re being attacked, so the army comes and clears the area.”.

    In a recent development, activists remarked that the military has claimed certain land is a “closed military zone” without providing documentation, to deter farmers and activists from reaching the olive groves. “They came to us and asked us to leave because we are in a closed military zone,” said Matten Kadish-Berner, an Israeli activist and organizer with Protect the Harvest. “When we asked them to show us the order, they refused, and in the end, they left because they did not have any document.”.

    The Israeli military told Human Rights Watch that the designation of closed military zones is intended to “prevent friction and public order disturbances,” noting that this year, “ahead of the harvest, a dedicated harvest situation room was established for the first time in the Civil Administration.”.

    Israeli authorities routinely intimidate and arrest Palestinians and deport international activists engaged in organizing protection for Palestinian farmers during olive harvest season.

    According to recent reports, on October 27, Israeli soldiers raided Burin village, south of Nablus, and detained about 60 people, mentioned the Sumood Network, a Palestinian grassroots organization. All were released except Ghassan Najjar, a farmer and rights defender who co-founded the Sumood Network.

    The Sumood Network remarked that before the season began, security agents from the Shin Bet threatened to detain Najjar if he continued to coordinate protection for the olive harvest in the Nablus area.

    Industry observers note that on November 17, an Israeli judge approved a four-month administrative detention order for Najjar, the Sumood Network mentioned. During the judicial review, the Israeli Military Prosecution acknowledged that the administrative detention of Najjar is related to political activities that are unarmed and nonviolent, the Sumood Network said. The Israeli military said Najjar “is suspected of hurling stones at Israeli civilians,” which the Sumood Network disputed.

    Israeli authorities often detain Palestinians on the basis of secret evidence that neither the detainee nor their lawyer can see. Orders last up to six months and can be renewed repeatedly, with no limit. International law allows detention without trial only as an exceptional measure, for imperative security reasons, with impartial judicial review. When it is used routinely, it becomes a tool of punishment and control and therefore arbitrary and unlawful.

    According to the Israeli organization HaMoked, Israel held 3,101 Palestinians in administrative detention as of October.

    On October 21, the military detained about 80 US, Israeli, and British volunteers helping Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem, including now US Congressman-elect Brad Lander, several rabbis, and Israel’s former deputy attorney general. A few days earlier, Israeli settlers attacked a delegation of French, Belgian, and Polish diplomats, Catholic clergymen, and a French mayor.

    Israeli authorities should release all those held unlawfully under administrative detention, end the systematic use of administrative detention, and ensure Palestinian farmers can safely reach their land.

    Other countries should act to prevent further atrocities across the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including by imposing targeted sanctions on those implicated in ongoing grave abuses, suspending arms transfers to Israel, banning trade with illegal settlements, considering suspending preferential trade agreements with Israel, and supporting the International Criminal Court and its ongoing investigations, including by executing its arrest warrants.

    Recent findings suggest that “Organizing an olive harvest is not a crime,” Sanbar noted. “Israeli authorities should end their repression of activists and instead fulfill their obligations to protect the Palestinian population.”.

    November 23, 2026: This news release has been updated to clarify which activists were released following the October 27 raid in Burin village.

Families know their own children the best. Teachers know their own students as individuals far better than a national government or the United Nations or UNICEF could ever know them.Using international aid to push an ideological agenda is the wrong policy. Education policy choices should emphasize local knowledge rather than national and international one-size-fits-all, top-down impositions.>>> Stablecoins Strengthen the Dollar and Empower the Developing WorldEducators also should teach economic and financial literacy.     Education policymakers around the world often overlook a simple formula: To increase educational opportunity, increase economic development.

    But to improve development, a country needs the institutions that promote it. That’s why nations that want to help more children succeed should pursue economic freedom.

    The latest Economic Freedom of the World report from the Fraser Institute tells the story clearly. The highest-ranked 25% of countries for economic freedom dramatically outperform the lowest-ranked 25%. Incomes are seven times greater, while people work six fewer hours per week. People live 14 years longer. Fewer children die in infancy, and environments are cleaner.

    It has been revealed that economic freedom translates into education and economic opportunity. Fewer students in developing nations will drop out in middle school to go to work. More families will be able to afford transportation to school. There will be more opportunities for graduates to get more productive, higher-paying jobs.

    >>> Latin America Shifts Toward Market-Oriented Conservatism.

    According to recent reports, take, for instance, Kurdistan in Iraq, which is focusing more on education now. Iraq ranks 159 out of 165 countries for its legal system and property rights, 152 for size of government, 141 for sound money, 149 for regulation of the economy, and 129 for freedom to trade internationally.

    Imagine how many more students in Kurdistan could finish school with a great education if incomes were seven times higher. Imagine the hard trade-offs today that would not be necessary if Iraq were richer.

    This point holds worldwide. What would best help a country’s children receive a strong education in the long run? Focus first of all on the country’s economic and legal institutions.

    Education is about making prepares for society’s future. That means a small government with reliable courts, sound money, secure property rights, and free competition.

    It has been revealed that economic development doesn’t automatically mean more government funding for government schools. In many countries, it can mean trusting families with education dollars to choose what is best for their own children.

    Indeed, parents are a great education resource. They are the first line of influence to keep their children on track for success, and you don’t even have to pay them a salary.

    Governments can do more to consider how to empower parents and teachers. Families know their own children the best. Teachers know their own students as individuals far better than a national government or the United Nations or UNICEF could ever know them.

    Using international aid to push an ideological agenda is the wrong policy. Education policy choices should emphasize local knowledge rather than national and international one-size-fits-all, top-down impositions.

    >>> Stablecoins Strengthen the Dollar and Empower the Developing World.

    Educators also should teach economic and financial literacy. The scientific evidence is decisive that socialism fails and market economies succeed. We mark Nov. 7 each year as Victims of Communism Day in the United States by remembering the more than 100 million people who died of starvation or were killed under communist and socialist regimes in the 20th century.

    Industry observers note that on an individual level, each student should be taught the basics of economics and entrepreneurship. These lessons include the fundamentals of human action and incentives, supply and demand, and the invisible hand of Adam Smith. This also includes learning how to be alert to opportunities to create value for others in society while improving one’s own life.

    This education means respecting and admiring entrepreneurs. Students should understand why people should be allowed to keep the fruit of their own labor. Students also should understand the value of building capital rather than consumption if they want to prosper.

    Recent findings suggest that to prepare students for employment and participation in society, teach economics and inspire entrepreneurship and an entrepreneurial mindset. Then the next generation will better understand the institutional reforms needed to help their country thrive.

    Sources indicate that given the results of the latest U.S. election, now that latest policymakers with socialist leanings (and actual socialists) will govern in states such as Michigan, New York, California, and elsewhere starting next year, this advice is not just for other countries. It’s also for us. Will we listen?

    Virginia S. Ct.: Felons Who Served Their Sentences Regain Second Amendment Rights Unless …

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that from today's long decision of the Virginia Supreme Court in Ginevan v.
    • On January 24, 2023, police responded to a possible domestic disturbance where they encountered Ginevan in a dispute with a woman.
    • According to recent reports, A review of Ginevan's prior criminal history revealed various and sundry felony convictions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that from today's long decision of the Virginia Supreme Court in Ginevan v. Commonwealth, written by Justice Wesley Russell:.

    On January 24, 2023, police responded to a possible domestic disturbance where they encountered Ginevan in a dispute with a woman. The woman claimed that Ginevan had grabbed a shotgun and pointed it at her. Although Ginevan admitted to possessing the shotgun, he denied having pointed it at the woman. He told police that he had the shotgun for protection. After Ginevan confirmed that he was a convicted felon, he was arrested and charged with possessing a firearm as a convicted felon in violation of Code § 18.2-308.2.

    According to recent reports, A review of Ginevan's prior criminal history revealed various and sundry felony convictions. In 2011, Ginevan was convicted of possession with intent to distribute a Schedule I/II controlled substance. Over the following four years, he was convicted three times for felony probation violations. Then, in 2018, Ginevan was convicted of obtaining money by false pretenses as well as possession of ammunition by a convicted felon. Notably, pursuant to Code § 17.1-805(C), the General Assembly has classified possession of ammunition by a convicted felon as a violent felony, but none of Ginevan's other felony convictions are so classified.

    The court held that the Virginia statute banning felons from possessing guns was unconstitutional as applied to Ginevan. Some brief excerpts from the long opinion:.

    Beginning with its decision in Heller, the Supreme Court has often included statements in its Second Amendment cases suggesting that bans on previously convicted felons possessing firearms were acceptable or, at the very least, that nothing in its decisions should be read as addressing felon-in-possession bans. For example, in Heller, the majority stated that.

    nothing in our opinion should be taken to cast doubt on longstanding prohibitions on the possession of firearms by felons and the mentally ill, or laws forbidding the carrying of firearms in sensitive places such as schools and government buildings, or laws imposing conditions and qualifications on the commercial sale of arms….

    Industry observers note that critically, however, these statements about dispossessing felons all were made in cases where the question of whether the Second Amendment allowed legislatures to forever bar felons from possessing firearms was not an issue…. As such, the statements about felon-in-possession bans contained in these cases are properly understood as dicta and not holdings of the Supreme Court….

    In Bruen, … the Supreme Court set forth an analytical framework that courts must apply in evaluating Second Amendment challenges to limitations on a person's right to keep and bear arms. In explaining the framework, the Supreme Court wrote that.

    Industry observers note that we hold that when the Second Amendment's plain text covers an individual's conduct, the Constitution presumptively protects that conduct. To justify its regulation, the government may not simply posit that the regulation promotes an important interest. Rather, the government must demonstrate that the regulation is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation. Only if a firearm regulation is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition may a court conclude that the individual's conduct falls outside the Second Amendment's "unqualified command." ….

    In a recent development, our conclusion that the Bruen framework and not the Heller dicta provides the rule of decision does not answer the question of whether or not, as applied to Ginevan, Code § 18.2-308.2 violates the Second Amendment. Rather, it requires that we apply the framework to Ginevan's conviction and circumstances as revealed by the record in this case….

    [T]he first part of the Bruen framework requires that we determine whether Code § 18.2-308.2's prohibition conflicts with the text of the Second Amendment. To answer this question, the Supreme Court counsels asking three "subsidiary questions": (1) "[D]oes the law apply to 'the people?'"; (2) Does the law apply to Second Amendment "[a]rms, i.e., any weapon customarily used for offensive or defensive purposes?"; and (3) Does the law restrict a person's ability to keep or bear an arm that is protected by the Second Amendment?

    Sources indicate that in this case, there has not and cannot be any dispute that the second and third questions must be answered in the affirmative. The weapon Ginevan is charged for possessing is an ordinary shotgun, which clearly falls within the scope of a weapon in common use for lawful purposes. {Although there is evidence in this case that Ginevan may have pointed his shotgun at someone, he was neither charged with nor convicted for any use of the shotgun. He was charged only with mere possession, so our review is focused on whether the Commonwealth may ban his possession of a firearm.} Accordingly, it unquestionably is an arm for the purposes of the Second Amendment.

    Similarly, because Code § 18.2-308.2 is a blanket ban on Ginevan even possessing such a shotgun, there can be no question that it restricts his ability to keep and bear arms. Thus, the only inquiry from Bruen's first step that could even be in dispute is whether Ginevan's prior felony convictions removed him from "the people" protected by the Second Amendment….

    Starting with Heller and continuing in more recent cases, the United States Supreme Court has indicated that "the people" protected by the Second Amendment includes "all members of the political community[.]" … The fact that the phrase "right of the people" means the same thing in the First, Fourth, and Second Amendments is, by our reckoning, sufficient to resolve whether a felony conviction, without more, removes a person from the political community.

    It almost goes without saying that no one would contend that, once convicted of a felony, a non-incarcerated person would fall outside the protections of the First Amendment, and therefore no longer enjoy "the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances." Similarly, no one maintains that a felony conviction forever forfeits "[t]he right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures[.]"Because a felony conviction does not remove a person from "the people" referenced in the First and Fourth Amendments, we conclude that, as a matter of language and logic, it does not remove a person from "the people" referenced in the Second Amendment.

    Of course, our conclusion that Ginevan is not excluded from "the people" referenced in the Second Amendment represents the beginning and not the end of the analysis. As then-Judge Barrett observed, the conclusion that felons do not fall outside the Second Amendment "does not mean that the government cannot prevent them from possessing guns. Instead, it means that the question is whether the government has the power to disable the exercise of a right that they otherwise possess, rather than whether they possess the right at all." Accordingly, we now turn to Bruen's second step and whether the Commonwealth had the power to disable Ginevan's exercise of his rights under the Second Amendment….

    [1.] Lack of an historical twin.

    Although governments are not required to prove the existence of an historical twin from the relevant historical period to justify a modern regulation, the existence or absence of one certainly is something to consider…. Statutes banning convicted felons from possessing firearms as a result of their prior felony convictions are a creature of twentieth century legislatures. When asked at oral argument, the Commonwealth could not identify a single American statute that banned all convicted felons from possessing firearms that predated the federal effort in the 1960s….

    [2.] Felon punishment at the time of the Founding.

    The Commonwealth argues that a total ban on felons possessing firearms is permissible because, at the time of the Founding, felonies routinely warranted "punishments far harsher than disarmament, including execution, estate forfeiture, or life imprisonment. And if the greater punishment of death and estate forfeiture was permissible to punish felons, then the lesser restriction of permanent disarmament is also permissible." … Although this approach provides a reasonably clear rule of decision and has some facial appeal, we, for the reasons detailed below, do not believe it withstands scrutiny….

    Industry observers note that the argument has its genesis in the English common law and how felons were punished. In England prior to the Founding, felonies often were punished by death and estate forfeiture. Before the sentence of death was actually carried out or in the instances in which a sentence of less than death was imposed, the convicted person was subject to attainder. Attainder was the common law process "of extinguishing a person's civil rights when that person is sentenced to death or declared an outlaw for committing a felony or treason." It inflicted what has been called civil death or civiliter mortuus, rendering the person as devoid of rights as if he were actually dead.

    Although the recognized process in England, not all aspects of the process were adopted in the colonies or in the nascent American republic. In his treatise on Blackstone's Commentaries, St. George Tucker noted that "[c]onfiscations, forfeitures, and corruption of blood, do not follow in case of conviction or attainder for any treason or felony either in the commonwealth of Virginia, or under the federal government." … By the late 1800s, multiple courts, including this one, explicitly recognized that, to the extent that civil death existed in America, it was temporary and ended when the convict had completed any period of incarceration….

    Not only do we find that the historical practice does not support the Commonwealth's argument regarding Second Amendment rights, but we reject the logical endpoint of the Commonwealth's argument. If the greater potential punishment of death allowed for all lesser punishments, including the stripping of Second Amendment rights, it also allowed for the stripping of all other constitutional rights. After all, the Supreme Court has made clear that the Second Amendment right is not a lesser right and is of equal dignity as the other rights elucidated in the Bill of Rights.

    Just as a dead man cannot keep and bear arms, he cannot freely exercise religion or speech (First Amendment), be secure in his papers, homes, and effects (Fourth Amendment), remain silent upon criminal questioning (Fifth Amendment), demand a speedy trial or have the assistance of counsel in a criminal case (Sixth Amendment), and so on. The Commonwealth has offered no example of a legislature at the time of the Founding, the ratification of the 14th Amendment, or anytime thereafter asserting that a felony conviction stripped a person of all constitutional protections or that a previously convicted felon only enjoyed those protections as a matter of grace that could be rescinded by the legislature as opposed to as a matter of constitutional law that could not. Because the Commonwealth has identified no such attempt for other protections provided by the Bill of Rights and because the Second Amendment right is a coequal right to those, we simply cannot accept, as a matter of logic, the Commonwealth's greater includes the lesser argument….

    It has been revealed that the Commonwealth next relies on the common law punishment of estate forfeiture as a historical analogue. The Commonwealth asserts that, in many of the colonies and then in some of the states of early America, complete forfeiture of one's estate, often but not always coupled with a sentence of death or life-imprisonment, was a common punishment imposed for conviction for many types of felonies…. [But] the historical evidence of which we are aware suggests that, once released from incarceration, convicted felons could acquire property because their rights were "merely suspended during the term of the sentence." ….

    According to recent reports, another historical analogue offered by the Commonwealth are laws that prohibited those loyal to the British crown from possessing firearms during the Revolution…. As others have noted, English laws from the late 17th century extending well into the 18th century "disarmed Roman Catholics …." Yet others have pointed to laws that … disarmed Native Americans …. [But e]ach of the proffered analogues sought to disarm people not because the groups were perceived to pose a heightened threat of criminal activity or as punishment for prior criminal activity, but because each of the groups were perceived as disloyal to the State and as posing a threat of rebellion against the State as a whole. Disarmament was a function of being an enemy of the State, not because one was a common criminal….

    [4.] Dispossession of dangerous individuals.

    Industry observers note that the Commonwealth next points to surety and "going armed" laws from the relevant time period. The Commonwealth posits that these laws demonstrate that, consistent with the Second Amendment, those who have been determined to pose a danger to others can be disarmed….

    Recent findings suggest that in advancing these analogues, the Commonwealth stands on firmer ground…. Regarding surety laws, the Supreme Court [has] noted that the regime had a significant common law pedigree, that such laws continued in the colonies and early America, and were applied to the carrying of firearms….

    The question before us now is whether Code § 18.2-308.2's permanent ban on Ginevan possessing ammunition is sufficiently similar to the temporary disarmament that accompanied the historical surety and going armed laws that allowed a conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8)(C)(i) to survive a Second Amendment challenge in Rahimi. Although there are many potential points of comparison between those proffered analogues and Code § 18.2-308.2, we believe the best and narrowest comparison that answers the question revolves around whether Ginevan's prior felony convictions represent a finding "by a court" that Ginevan "pose[s] a credible threat to the physical safety of another[.]" In short, do any of Ginevan's prior felony convictions represent a judicial determination that he is dangerous, i.e., he poses a credible physical threat to the safety of another?

    The Commonwealth argues that the General Assembly's classification of the offenses is sufficient to require such a conclusion. Alternatively, it argues that the very nature of Ginevan's prior conviction for possession of ammunition by a previously convicted felon is sufficient to support the conclusion that Ginevan has been found to be dangerous. We address each argument in turn….

    Although … the General Assembly sets the public policy of the Commonwealth and that courts normally must defer to those policy choices, that deference is not unlimited. As noted above, the very purpose of the Bill of Rights was to "take[ ] certain policy choices off the table….

    [And a] review of the elements of Ginevan's previous conviction for possession of ammunition by a felon in violation of Code § 18.2-308.2 reveals that no proof or judicial finding of Ginevan posing a credible threat to the physical safety of another was necessary for the Commonwealth to obtain the conviction….

    The evidentiary record developed in the trial court in this case is understandably sparse given that the matter was resolved by way of a guilty plea. The fact that Ginevan had prior felony convictions—including convictions for possession with intent to distribute, obtaining money by false pretenses, and possession of ammunition by a convicted felon—was established in the trial court. However, the record in the trial court (and properly before us now) reveals nothing about the circumstances surrounding those convictions. We do not know whether the circumstances involved any level of violence or threat, let alone a sufficient level to allow us to conclude that those convictions could represent a finding "by a court" that Ginevan "pose[s] a credible threat to the physical safety of another[.]".

    The lack of such evidence in the record properly before us is fatal to the Commonwealth's position. The Commonwealth bears the burden of establishing that Ginevan's disarmament "is consistent with the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation." To do so in this case, it needed to demonstrate that at least one of his prior convictions represented a finding "by a court" that Ginevan "pose[s] a credible threat to the physical safety of another[.]" ….

    [W]e emphasize that our decision today "is a narrow one." … A case dealing with different offenses, a defendant with a different criminal history, or a different evidentiary record may well lead to a different conclusion….

    Recent findings suggest that the ongoing riots in France have once again brought the world’s attention to large enclaves of Muslim immigrants in and around the country’s overcrowded housing projects. But then another member state—Slovenia—elected a liberal government with lax enforcement policies. And that single breach in the defenses left interior countries like France vulnerable once again.Almost three years have passed since I discovered (and reported) the Slovenia breach in what had been for the previous seven years an effective barrier erected by the European Union. Many of these were fast-tracked into the public housing communities now at the center of France’s continuous street violence.>>> France Is Learning the Hard Way What Happens When the Socialist Bill Comes DueThe flow of migrants began in mid-2022 with a key Slovenian election and spiked in 2023 before declining in 2024. Much of the traffic moved along the same Balkan routes traveled by some 800,000 to 900,000 mostly Muslim immigrants during the 2014-2016 crisis, during which there were an estimated two million illegal E.U. border crossings.The 466,000 migrants who applied for French asylum or refugee status in 2022-23 hailed from places like Afghanistan, Turkey, Syria, and Tunisia, as well as Muslim-majority nations in North Africa. Of those, authorities detected approximately 244,000 who traveled on routes through the Balkans; untold thousands more are believed to have traveled those same routes undetected. Among those who registered were France-bound immigrants like an Afghan I interviewed in a Bosnian migrant camp who was en route to the Slovenia gap.“Taliban good!” he told me in pidgin English when I asked his opinion about the ruling terrorist group in his home country.A Breach in the DefensesThe Balkan routes generally run northwest from Turkey through countries like Greece, Macedonia, Serbia, Bosnia, and Croatia. Migrants know that once they penetrate into the periphery of the E.U., a borderless inter-nation agreement (the Schengen Zone) enables inspection-free travel to rich and desirable interior countries like France.A decade ago, ISIS fed its terrorist operatives into the migrant flows. They went on to kill and wound hundreds of French and Belgian citizens in 2015 and 2016, while dozens of other border-crossing migrants committed small terror attacks throughout Europe. Because of this mayhem, the E.U.’s external countries buttoned up their borders with stout fences and instant-expulsion policies backed by rigorous patrolling.E.U. member Hungary started it off in 2015 with an electrified barbed wire double fence, which immediately choked off the main channel through Croatia and Serbia. And there they were, inside the E.U. with no opposition, free to travel to France.E.U. governments pleaded with Croatia to police the territory. Inshallah!”—if God wills it.Earlier this year, Slovenians elected a conservative government that looks to rebuild the fence. But that’s too late for France.>>> Spain’s Housing Backlash Is a Warning for AmericaAmerican SloveniasOf course, though it was the liberal Slovene government that opened the side door into the E.U., it was government policies in destination countries that lured them through. One France-bound Algerian I encountered in northwest Bosnia answered this way when I asked how vital the low probability of deportation was to him: “It’s 90 percent important,” he immediately responded. “If you do all the trip and they catch you and deport you, it’s very, very difficult. This point is very important.”There’s a lesson for Americans in this practically unknown aspect of French politics: the United States can easily become like France if voters elect liberal politicians who favor lenient immigration policies.Not just that, though. To avoid becoming France, U.S. policies must include making sure that Mexico and the transit countries of Central America never become the Slovenia I saw a few years ago.

    The ongoing riots in France have once again brought the world’s attention to large enclaves of Muslim immigrants in and around the country’s overcrowded housing projects. But foreign observers may be surprised to learn how many of the most recent arrivals came in through the tiny Balkan nation of Slovenia, which enabled a mass migration in 2022-2024. The dynamics of how and why this happened in Europe are well worth our attention in America because, mutatis mutandis, they also obtain along our own southern border. Think of Mexico as our Slovenia.

    Recent findings suggest that in 2023, I spent four weeks visiting eight of the countries involved in the transit routes to learn why they had come back to life. What I learned has profound implications for American policy. Led by pioneering member state Hungary, the E.U. had erected a solid barrier along its eastern frontier. But then another member state—Slovenia—elected a liberal government with lax enforcement policies. And that single breach in the defenses left interior countries like France vulnerable once again.

    Almost three years have passed since I discovered (and reported) the Slovenia breach in what had been for the previous seven years an effective barrier erected by the European Union. The E.U. effectively put an end to Europe’s catastrophic mass migration crisis of 2014-2016, during which both refugees and terrorists were able to travel freely along the so-called “Balkan Route.”.

    The Slovenia gap, as I’ll call it, helped flood France with at least 466,000 first-time foreign national asylum and refugee claimants from mostly Muslim-majority nations in 2022-23 alone. Many of these were fast-tracked into the public housing communities now at the center of France’s continuous street violence.

    >>> France Is Learning the Hard Way What Happens When the Socialist Bill Comes Due.

    It has been revealed that the flow of migrants began in mid-2022 with a key Slovenian election and spiked in 2023 before declining in 2024. Much of the traffic moved along the same Balkan routes traveled by some 800,000 to 900,000 mostly Muslim immigrants during the 2014-2016 crisis, during which there were an estimated two million illegal E.U. border crossings.

    Industry observers note that the 466,000 migrants who applied for French asylum or refugee status in 2022-23 hailed from places like Afghanistan, Turkey, Syria, and Tunisia, as well as Muslim-majority nations in North Africa. Of those, authorities detected approximately 244,000 who traveled on routes through the Balkans; untold thousands more are believed to have traveled those same routes undetected. Among those who registered were France-bound immigrants like an Afghan I interviewed in a Bosnian migrant camp who was en route to the Slovenia gap.

    “Taliban good!” he told me in pidgin English when I asked his opinion about the ruling terrorist group in his home country.

    A Breach in the Defenses.

    In a recent development, the Balkan routes generally run northwest from Turkey through countries like Greece, Macedonia, Serbia, Bosnia, and Croatia. Migrants know that once they penetrate into the periphery of the E.U., a borderless inter-nation agreement (the Schengen Zone) enables inspection-free travel to rich and desirable interior countries like France.

    A decade ago, ISIS fed its terrorist operatives into the migrant flows. They went on to kill and wound hundreds of French and Belgian citizens in 2015 and 2016, while dozens of other border-crossing migrants committed small terror attacks throughout Europe. Because of this mayhem, the E.U.’s external countries buttoned up their borders with stout fences and instant-expulsion policies backed by rigorous patrolling.

    E.U. member Hungary started it off in 2015 with an electrified barbed wire double fence, which immediately choked off the main channel through Croatia and Serbia. When migrants diverted west to avoid it, Austria built another, forcing Slovenia to build a razor-wire fence along the border with Croatia to head off further spillover.

    By 2016, the Balkan routes were considered effectively closed. It also helped that the E.U. paid Turkey and some proxy North African nations (and violent militias) billions of euros to stop and block emigration from their territories.

    So how did another mass migration start in 2022 that would flood France with tens of thousands more?

    In June 2022, Slovenian voters threw out the center-right Slovenian Democratic Party that had built that fence. They elected the center-left Freedom Movement and installed Prime Minister Robert Golob, who had campaigned to tear down Slovenia’s fence and immediately set about doing so.

    News Travels Fast.

    Word spread that a gap in Slovenia’s Balkan route had just opened, so migrants came pouring through it. I toured the forlorn remnants of Slovenia’s fence, observing broken-down sections lying where they had been pushed down. Anyone could walk through at will. I never saw a single police officer as I crossed back and forth repeatedly on foot and by car.

    According to recent reports, smugglers and self-directed immigrants (including many from Latin America) rapidly figured out they could fly without visas into Serbia for a time, or trek on their own up from Greece and into Bosnia for the onward journey through a narrow sliver of Croatian territory to Slovenia. And there they were, inside the E.U. with no opposition, free to travel to France.

    In a recent development, E.U. governments pleaded with Croatia to police the territory. But with no wall and a porous border, Croatia was effectively unable to oblige. Immigrants on the Bosnia side told me they planned to push for the Slovenia gap and go on to France.

    On the U.N.’s Camp Lipa in northwest Bosnia, for instance, nine young men from Morocco and Algeria were hardly worried about Croatian police catching them as they prepared for the short trek across Croatia to the Slovenia border.

    “No problem!!!” almost everyone shouted, laughing as they turned and disappeared into the dark forest, chanting, “Inshallah! Inshallah!”—if God wills it.

    Industry observers note that earlier this year, Slovenians elected a conservative government that looks to rebuild the fence. But that’s too late for France.

    >>> Spain’s Housing Backlash Is a Warning for America.

    American Slovenias.

    Of course, though it was the liberal Slovene government that opened the side door into the E.U., it was government policies in destination countries that lured them through. France, the U.K., and other European countries have clung to policies and processes that prevent quick deportations and, at the same time, provide the arrivals with public welfare. These are powerful lures.

    In 2023, immigrants told me they knew France and other destination countries wouldn’t—or couldn’t—deport them. One France-bound Algerian I encountered in northwest Bosnia answered this way when I asked how important the low probability of deportation was to him: “It’s 90 percent important,” he immediately responded. “If you do all the trip and they catch you and deport you, it’s very, very difficult. This point is very important.”.

    There’s a lesson for Americans in this practically unknown aspect of French politics: the United States can easily become like France if voters elect liberal politicians who favor lenient immigration policies.

    Not just that, though. To avoid becoming France, U.S. policies must include making sure that Mexico and the transit countries of Central America never become the Slovenia I saw a few years ago.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The French Senate on November 20 approved a controversial bill that risks deepening impunity for use of lethal force by police.

    The bill introduces a legal presumption of self-defense for law enforcement officers using firearms during the exercise of their duties, unless victims or their families can establish the use of lethal force was unlawful.

    Sources indicate that because victims’ families lack access to key evidence to assess the legality of police-caused death, placing the burden of proof on them is likely to deepen impunity and seriously jeopardize pathways for accountability where lethal force was unlawful, unnecessary, or disproportionate. This is inconsistent with France’s human rights obligations with respect to protecting the right to life and use of force by law enforcement.

    In a recent development, the use of lethal force by police is a major concern in France. In 2023, a police officer fatally shot 17-year-old Nahel M., a racialized boy, during a traffic stop, triggering widespread scrutiny of police use of firearms.

    France’s national human rights body and the previous mandate holder of the independent ombudsperson as well as a United Nations rights expert raised serious rights concerns about the bill, while rights groups, activists, and legal professionals staged protests and petitioned parliament to stop the bill.

    It has been revealed that the Senate’s vote followed approval of the bill by France’s National Assembly on July 7. Unless government officials or parliamentarians refer the bill for constitutional review, the president has 15 days to sign it into law.

    Since 2017, when lawmakers broadened the scope of permissible use of firearms by police well beyond international human rights standards requiring necessity and proportionality, numbers of fatal police vehicle stops in France have risen fivefold compared to before.

    Recent findings suggest that A state cannot delegate its legal duty to investigate to those affected by lethal police force. This reversed burden of proof contravenes international human rights law, which requires states to thoroughly investigate every circumstance of lethal police force.

    Industry observers note that if the French authorities are serious about avoiding incidents of excessive use of lethal force, and rebuilding public confidence in policing, lawmakers should drop this bill. The government and parliament should instead focus legislative efforts on strengthening accountability and ensuring that police powers are subject to effective procedural safeguards to protect people from police abuse, discrimination, violence, and, increasingly, disproportionate use of firearms.

    In a recent development, consumers are justifiably angry about persistent inflation, interest rates, and a frozen housing market. High fuel prices were one of the most cited motivations in the midterm election’s exit polls. But politicians can’t address all these factors of the affordability crisis, without understanding one of its largest contributors.The Iran war obviously caused serious disruptions to global energy markets, and the resultant shortfall in supply drove up prices. Even with some oil and natural gas moving through the Strait of Hormuz, the cost to move that product is up dramatically as expenses like insurance have exploded.Since energy affects the price of everything we do and buy, more expensive energy pushes up prices throughout the economy. This occurs not only because of things like higher transportation costs, but also because energy is used to make many products too.Virtually all plastic in our lives is synthesized from either oil or natural gas. This includes countless products from automotive parts to polyester clothing, but also cosmetics to pharmaceuticals. Almost all fertilizer is also made from oil and gas.>>> Today’s Inflation Is Really an Energy ShockSince energy is an input for so many products sold to consumers and industry alike, the effects of price changes are far-reaching, though it takes time for consumers to feel the full effect.For example, consumers are only recently experiencing the higher food prices stemming from energy market disruptions that started eight months ago. As farmers paid more for diesel and fertilizer, they began passing those costs on through supply chains via distributors, wholesalers, and grocers.But the cost of the war goes beyond consumer prices, as evidenced by the monthly Treasury statement for October. Spending on national defense last month spiked, hitting $129 billion—up 44.9 percent from September. That was a key contributor to the worst deficit ever for October: $404 billion. And military spending for this fiscal year is projected to exceed $1.1 trillion.All that additional spending and borrowing is adding to the national debt and costing taxpayers, both today and in the future. The cost to service the $41 trillion debt has become genuinely massive. Gross interest on the debt equaled 32.3 percent of all tax receipts in October, a figure projected to worsen.Excessive government spending and borrowing is further fueling inflation, a tax on today’s savers and wage earners that has also robbed more than 30 percent of the dollar’s value since the start of 2020.But the flood of debt issuance has also greatly increased the demand for loanable funds, or savings. That increased demand puts upward pressure on the price for loanable funds, which is the interest rate. The government is borrowing so much money that its crowding out the private sector and increasing interest rates on everything from mortgages to auto loans.>>> Overseas Wars Put Affordability on Hold, but That’s Only TemporaryThat’s a key reason why homeownership affordability, which had improved to a three-year high in February, has fallen each month since the Iran war started as interest rates marched relentlessly higher. Those higher interest rates also stem from inflation expectations rising due to the war’s energy market disruptions.That’s created a deadly combination for the housing market where both home prices and interest rates have risen dramatically in recent years. That one-two punch has made housing unaffordable and cratered home sales.It now takes more than half of the median household’s after-tax income to afford the monthly mortgage payment on a median price home. For families whose budgets are already strapped from high consumer prices, homeownership is simply out of reach.Unfortunately, there’s more pain to come from what’s already working its way through supply chains. According to the producer price index, annual inflation rates hit 16.9 percent for unprocessed products that businesses sold to each other, while processed products hit 14.6 percent. Those price increases will eventually work their way to consumer prices too.To be clear, the affordability crisis started five years ago during the Biden administration, not with the Iran war. But the conflict was fuel on the fire and reversed the good progress made in the first 13 months of the second Trump administration. Solving the problem requires removing its causes, and the war is low-hanging fruit.

    In a recent development, consumers are justifiably angry about persistent inflation, interest rates, and a frozen housing market. High fuel prices were one of the most cited motivations in the midterm election’s exit polls. But politicians can’t address all these factors of the affordability crisis, without understanding one of its largest contributors.

    The Iran war obviously caused serious disruptions to global energy markets, and the resultant shortfall in supply drove up prices. Even with some oil and natural gas moving through the Strait of Hormuz, the cost to move that product is up dramatically as expenses like insurance have exploded.

    It has been revealed that since energy affects the price of everything we do and buy, more expensive energy pushes up prices throughout the economy. This occurs not only because of things like higher transportation costs, but also because energy is used to make many products too.

    According to recent reports, virtually all plastic in our lives is synthesized from either oil or natural gas. This includes countless products from automotive parts to polyester clothing, but also cosmetics to pharmaceuticals. Almost all fertilizer is also made from oil and gas.

    >>> Today’s Inflation Is Really an Energy Shock.

    Since energy is an input for so many products sold to consumers and industry alike, the effects of price changes are far-reaching, though it takes time for consumers to feel the full effect.

    For example, consumers are only recently experiencing the higher food prices stemming from energy market disruptions that started eight months ago. As farmers paid more for diesel and fertilizer, they began passing those costs on through supply chains via distributors, wholesalers, and grocers.

    According to recent reports, but the cost of the war goes beyond consumer prices, as evidenced by the monthly Treasury statement for October. Spending on national defense last month spiked, hitting $129 billion—up 44.9 percent from September. That was a key contributor to the worst deficit ever for October: $404 billion. And military spending for this fiscal year is projected to exceed $1.1 trillion.

    All that additional spending and borrowing is adding to the national debt and costing taxpayers, both today and in the future. The cost to service the $41 trillion debt has become genuinely massive. Gross interest on the debt equaled 32.3 percent of all tax receipts in October, a figure projected to worsen.

    Excessive government spending and borrowing is further fueling inflation, a tax on today’s savers and wage earners that has also robbed more than 30 percent of the dollar’s value since the start of 2020.

    It has been revealed that but the flood of debt issuance has also greatly increased the demand for loanable funds, or savings. That increased demand puts upward pressure on the price for loanable funds, which is the interest rate. The government is borrowing so much money that its crowding out the private sector and increasing interest rates on everything from mortgages to auto loans.

    >>> Overseas Wars Put Affordability on Hold, but That’s Only Temporary.

    That’s a key reason why homeownership affordability, which had improved to a three-year high in February, has fallen each month since the Iran war started as interest rates marched relentlessly higher. Those higher interest rates also stem from inflation expectations rising due to the war’s energy market disruptions.

    Sources indicate that that’s created a deadly combination for the housing market where both home prices and interest rates have risen dramatically in recent years. That one-two punch has made housing unaffordable and cratered home sales.

    It now takes more than half of the median household’s after-tax income to afford the monthly mortgage payment on a median price home. For families whose budgets are already strapped from high consumer prices, homeownership is simply out of reach.

    In a recent development, unfortunately, there’s more pain to come from what’s already working its way through supply chains. According to the producer price index, annual inflation rates hit 16.9 percent for unprocessed products that businesses sold to each other, while processed products hit 14.6 percent. Those price increases will eventually work their way to consumer prices too.

    According to recent reports, to be clear, the affordability crisis started five years ago during the Biden administration, not with the Iran war. But the conflict was fuel on the fire and reversed the good progress made in the first 13 months of the second Trump administration. Solving the problem requires removing its causes, and the war is low-hanging fruit.

    Latest Update: Court Blocks FCC from Early Review of ABC Broadcast Licenses

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, from today's decision by Judge Loren Alikhan (D.D.C.) in ABC, Inc.
    • It has been revealed that plaintiffs assert that Defendants violated their First Amendment rights by designating their broadcast licenses for early renewal as retaliation for Plaintiffs' broadcasting unfavorable speech about President Donald J.
    • In a recent development, because broadcast media requires access to radio spectrum to operate, and because radio spectrum is a finite public resource, the FCC is responsible for granting and renewing broadcast licenses….
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, from today's decision by Judge Loren Alikhan (D.D.C.) in ABC, Inc. v. FCC:.

    It has been revealed that plaintiffs assert that Defendants violated their First Amendment rights by designating their broadcast licenses for early renewal as retaliation for Plaintiffs' broadcasting unfavorable speech about President Donald J. Trump and the Republican Party….

    In a recent development, because broadcast media requires access to radio spectrum to operate, and because radio spectrum is a finite public resource, the FCC is responsible for granting and renewing broadcast licenses…. The FCC may grant an initial license or a license renewal for a term of no more than eight years, and it "ordinarily" grants licenses for eight-year terms, with term dates staggered by the geographic location of each station. "However, if the FCC finds that the public interest, convenience and necessity will be served thereby, it may issue either an initial license or a renewal thereof for a lesser term." ….

    Industry observers note that the FCC argued that the ABC licenses were being designated for early review because the FCC was investigating the possibility that Disney and ABC were discriminating in employment for "DEI" reasons. But Judge Alikhan concluded that this was likely a pretext, and the likely real reason for the FCC's action was unconstitutional Administration retaliation against ABC's speech:.

    "Courts have recognized that [] circumstantial evidence, including proximity in time between the protected speech and government's adverse actions, the defendant's expression of hostility to the protected speech, and the absence of a proffered legitimate alternative explanation for the action[,] can support a finding that protected speech caused the agency's response.".

    Here, robust circumstantial evidence strongly supports Plaintiffs' theory of causation. Although Defendants proffer a legitimate alternative explanation, the court does not find that explanation to be credible on the record before the court. Starting with expressions of hostility, President Trump has set his sights on Plaintiff ABC for several years now. What started in 2020 as questions about how ABC "can keep getting a license" if it "report[s] fake news" has crescendoed into repeated calls for the Commission to strip ABC's broadcast licenses for their editorial decisions.

    The court counts eleven such calls made by President Trump over the past two years—the most recent being in July 2026. See ECF No. 1 ("When you have a network and you have evening highlights, and all they do is hit Trump[,] … I think maybe their license should be taken away. It will be up to [Chairman] Carr."); ECF No. 2-3, at 109-10 ("[T]hey ought to take away [ABC's] license."); id. at 157 ("ABC's license should be TERMINATED."); id. at 166 ("CBS should lose its license, and it should be bid out to the Highest Bidder, as should all other Broadcast Licenses, because they are just as corrupt as CBS—and maybe even WORSE!"); id. at 252 ("I think ABC should lose its license."); id. at 303 ("ABC & NBC FAKE NEWS … SHOULD, ACCORDING TO MANY, HAVE THEIR LICENSES REVOKED BY THE FCC."); id. at 306 ("ABC and NBC FAKE NEWS … should lose their Licenses."); id. at 321 ("[T]he Federal Communications Commission should look into the license of … ABC Fake News."); id. at 340 ("I think the license should be taken away from ABC because your news is so fake and it's so wrong. And we have a great commissioner, the chairman, who should look at that."); ECF No. 2-4, at 13 ("If Network NEWSCASTS, and their Late Night Shows, are almost 100% Negative to President Donald J. Trump, MAGA, and the Republican Party, shouldn't their very valuable Broadcast Licenses be terminated? I say, YES!"); id. at 99 ("ABC fake news ha[s] [] said that [it] would not cover this speech…. Fraud like this should mean a revocation of their licenses.").

    To be sure, President Trump is within his rights "to persuade Americans, including by speaking forcefully or critically, in ways that [he] believes would advance the public interest." Here, however, the President's persistent "rhetoric demonstrates that [he] harbored animosity" toward Plaintiffs because of their protected speech, specifically—to quote the President—their "negative" and "unfair coverage" of him and the Republican Party.

    What is more, Chairman Carr has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders. The same week he was tapped to be President Trump's FCC chair, following months of President Trump's calling for "ABC [to] lose its license" for how it covered the presidential campaign, then-Commissioner Carr lauded "license revocation" as a "remedy" to "deter this kind of conduct." Then, early in his tenure as chairman and after committing himself to President Trump's agenda, Chairman Carr ordered the Enforcement Bureau to investigate Disney's employment practices, and soon ordered another investigation into The View.

    In a recent development, when President Trump first called for Mr. Kimmel to be fired—as well as for ABC's license to be "taken away"—Chairman Carr vowed to intervene if Plaintiffs did not "take action on Kimmel." Months later, when President Trump decried Mr. Kimmel's skit about the First Lady, the Commission, at Chairman Carr's behest, initiated early license renewal proceedings the next day. Chairman Carr said of the move, "If you didn't take us seriously, now you should.".

    Most recently, when President Trump touted that Plaintiffs' not broadcasting his address justifies "revocation of their licenses," Chairman Carr announced that the Commission was "looking into" Plaintiffs' decision, and that he expected it to come up during the early license renewal proceedings. This conduct and rhetoric are "powerful evidence of [Defendants'] retaliatory motive.".

    Industry observers note that in response, Defendants point to Chairman Carr's assurances that the Commission "has not singled out any one company for special treatment," and will remain "open-minded" throughout the early license renewal proceedings. But these assurances fall flat when Chairman Carr is simultaneously making comments that the Commission is "looking into" Plaintiffs' "decision [not] to air" a presidential address as part of the proceedings, especially given that Chairman Carr has mentioned that this specific presidential address is "something that broadcasters should be carrying.".

    Turning to temporal proximity, against the backdrop of President Trump and Chairman Carr's call-and-response, it is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel's skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings. Indeed, in the wake of Mr. Kimmel's September 2025 comments about President Trump and his supporters, Chairman Carr stated, "We can do this the easy way or the hard way. These companies can find ways to take action on Kimmel, or there is going to be additional work for the FCC ahead.".

    Chairman Carr made this promise at the same time that President Trump noted of the situation: "When you have a network and you have evening demonstrates, and all they do is hit Trump[,] … I think maybe their license should be taken away. It will be up to [Chairman] Carr." Chairman Carr's "fast-moving" inquest into Plaintiffs' business operations and editorial decisions from the moment he was appointed as chairman and seemingly at the President's direction further "indicates [Defendants'] retaliatory animus." ….

    The court therefore enjoined the FCC from "from taking any continuing or further action against Plaintiffs in relation to the early license renewal proceedings before the Federal Communications Commission, including issuing a Hearing Designation Order;".

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that azerbaijan’s parliament on November 18 approved sweeping amendments to legislation governing nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) that would expand government powers to suspend and dissolve independent groups, impose newly introduced registration requirements, and further restrict their operations. The following day, a court sentenced prominent rights defender Bashir Suleymanli to seven and a half years in prison, the latest in a series of harsh sentences against civil society activists prosecuted over foreign funding.

    The proposed legislation would allow authorities, rather than courts, to suspend NGOs for up to a year for broadly defined violations, including failure to meet transparency and anti-money laundering requirements. It would also expand grounds for court-ordered dissolution to include activities deemed a threat to the “legally protected interests of the state and society”—vague standards open to abuse.

    Sources indicate that existing NGOs would have just 30 days after the law takes effect to revise their charters and apply for re-registration. The minimum capital to establish a nonprofit foundation, a type of nongovernmental organization, would increase tenfold, from 10,000 to 100,000 manats (approx. US$ 59,000). Together, these requirements would create additional barriers to establishing and maintaining independent civil society organizations in Azerbaijan.

    In a recent development, human Rights Watch has documented how existing restrictions on registration and foreign funding have forced many independent groups to close or severely curtail their activities. The European Court of Human Rights has repeatedly found violations of freedom of association in cases involving Azerbaijani civil society organizations.

    Sources indicate that authorities took another strike at civil society on November 19 when the Baku Grave Crimes Court convicted Suleymanli, director of the Institute for Citizens’ Rights, of apparent politically motivated charges of money laundering and abuse of office. Arrested in March 2025, authorities prosecuted Suleymanli as part of a reopened investigation into foreign-funded NGO work.

    Courts have also handed down lengthy prison sentences to other activists prosecuted in connection with the same investigation, including eight years for Asaf Ahmadov and seven years and three months for Zamin Zaki (Zakiyev). Election monitor Anar Mammadli received a 13-year sentence in September following an unfair trial.

    Recent findings suggest that azerbaijani authorities should withdraw the proposed amendments, release Suleymanli and other civil society activists imprisoned for their legitimate work, and end the misuse of criminal law against independent groups. Azerbaijan’s international partners should press the government to uphold its obligations to protect freedom of association.

    Becoming a teacher is no way to get rich, but becoming the head of a teachers union? That’s a different story.

    Take Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, who received $546,158 in total compensation last year, according to the union’s latest financial disclosure.

    That’s over seven times the $74,495 average salary earned by public-school teachers nationwide.

    And the new documents, recently filed with the federal Labor Department, show that an AFT president’s cronies can profit handsomely, too.

    Outside consultants, a Latest York law firm, a public-relations firm and others appear to have raked in more than $2.2 million from AFT coffers to help Weingarten produce her 2025 book “Why Fascists Fear Teachers”—up from the more than $1.4 million previously estimated by the Freedom Foundation and reported by The Post.

    The payments break down across two filings, covering two separate fiscal years.

    >>> Randi Weingarten’s Dirty Back-to-School War on Target.

    The first, for a one-year period from 2024 to 2025, documented substantial costs connected to the book paid by the AFT—including payments to Weingarten’s literary agent Inkwell Management, to a fact-checker credited in her acknowledgments, and to a photographer for her author’s headshot.

    The latest form adds further amounts apparently related to the same project.

    Industry observers note that on Sept. 25, 2025, nine days after the book’s release, the AFT paid Inkwell Management $28,125 for a “publication expense,” bringing combined payments to the agent across both filings to $92,215.

    Separately, the union paid Feldman Strategies, a publicity firm, $202,500; shortly after the pub date, the PR group posted, “It has been a true honor for our entire team at Feldman Strategies to help promote” Weingarten’s book.

    The latest filing also records an $80,000 “royalty payment” sent on Oct. 23, 2025, to a limited liability manufacturer controlled by Weingarten.

    That sum follows a $125,000 royalty payment to the same entity disclosed in the union’s prior annual report, bringing the combined royalty transfers from AFT to the Weingarten-controlled firm to $205,000.

    And in its 2026 filing, the union paid Patterson Belknap Webb & Tyler LLP — the law firm credited in the book with reviewing Weingarten’s manuscript—another $591,174, bringing cumulative legal fees to the firm across both years to nearly $1.6 million.

    The union says the firm toiled on the book “pro bono,” but the attorneys’ extensive financial ties to the AFT create an obvious incentive to characterize that work as such.

    The royalty payments require additional explanation: Public filings show the AFT itself receiving publisher advances connected to the book, then disbursing a portion of those funds as a “royalty payment” to Teachers Want What Kids Need, LLC—an entity controlled by Weingarten.

    The publisher did not pay royalties to Weingarten or her LLC directly; the money flowed through the union, in an arrangement that remains opaque.

    Weingarten has stated that some of the book’s proceeds would go back to the AFT, the AFT Disaster Relief Fund, and the AFT Educational Foundation.

    Even if that claim holds, dues-paying teachers shouldn’t be required to subsidize a book project that profits their union’s president.

    In July, the GOP-led House Committee on Education and the Workforce opened a formal inquiry into the matter based on The Post’s initial report, requesting documents on the AFT’s book-related expenditures, contracts and royalty flows.

    That inquiry is controlled by the committee majority, however—and once Democrats take control of the House in January, the probe is expected to stall or be closed.

    The minority can still request materials and issue reports, but it cannot compel the same level of investigation.

    Separately, the Department of Labor’s Inspector General has already opened its own review to probe whether union dues were improperly used for Weingarten’s book project.

    That executive-branch inquiry can continue under President Donald Trump’s administration, regardless of which party controls Congress.

    >>> Randi Weingarten’s Convention Exposes the Teachers’ Union as a Political Machine.

    The new 2026 filing supplies further evidence that any ongoing review should examine: The additional royalty payment, the fresh publication expense routed to the literary agent, the large PR contract and the further $591,174 to Patterson Belknap all post-date the period covered by the prior report.

    Payments to the Weingarten-controlled entity, the literary agent, the PR firm and the consultants raise questions about whether dues money collected from teachers was used for the personal benefit of the union’s top officer.

    Federal labor filings exist precisely so that members and the public can review such expenditures.

    When these records show repeated transfers linked to an officer’s private project, the disclosures themselves supply the basis for scrutiny.

    Teachers who don’t want their hard-earned paychecks to underwrite an officer’s vanity project have a practical alternative.

    Organizations such as the Teacher Freedom Alliance offer membership—including free liability insurance—without routing teacher dues to electoral campaigns or left-wing causes.

    If enough fed-up teachers leave the AFT, people like Randi Weingarten might think twice about wasting members’ money on personal and political pet projects.

    • I am still in awe of Francis, a community leader from Solomon Islands who traveled to Antalya to share his story.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Leaving the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, I can’t shake the disconnect between the reality of entire communities losing their homes to rising seas and some governments’ apathy and obstruction of the process. The conference ended without consensus on the proposed Antalya Pact—the overarching political agreement for the COP31 climate summit.

    I am still in awe of Francis, a community leader from Solomon Islands who traveled to Antalya to share his story. “Walande… the birthplace written in my passport, no longer exists,” he told a hushed room. “It is submerged beneath the waves.” His words moved the high-level event’s moderator to tears.

    Sources indicate that COP31’s inability to reach an overarching agreement leaves communities like Walande—and hundreds of other communities that have been forced to relocate—to face consequences of the climate crisis on their own. Despite coordinated calls from civil society, related outcome decisions do not include explicit discussion of displacement and planned relocation, and governments failed to increase funding to help frontline communities adapt. Nor was there recognition of the International Court of Justice’s landmark opinion affirming that governments have human rights obligations to address the climate crisis.

    I leave Antalya holding both heartbreak and hope: the summit remains a vital space for global solidarity. Alongside partners in the Coalition on Dignified Climate Relocation, we brought frontline leaders, policymakers, and funders together to exchange lessons, and push for rights-respecting national policies and increased funding for communities forced to relocate. After watching our immersive documentary Solwata, several government officials and climate fund directors stepped up, committing to support finance and policies for relocating communities.

    Sources indicate that official negotiations fell woefully short, and the UN policy process failed to meet the moment in Antalya. But Marshall Islands, Bangladesh, Fiji, Nepal and other forward-thinking governments are proving that another path is possible. Dignified, rights-respecting solutions already exist—and they can be scaled up.

    Ethiopia, as host of COP32, should learn lessons from Australia and Türkiye’s failures, and center efforts to advance finance for adaptation and loss damage which are vital to protect the rights of climate displaced communities.

    The Persecution of Environmentalists and Indigenous Leaders in Indonesia.

    Climate Change, Planned Relocation, and People with Disabilities in Siargao, Philippines.

    Most immigration to the U.S. after 1965 came from the “developing,” or Third World, so we will see more of them and their children running for office as time goes on. What does that portend? I looked for common threads in the family backgrounds of the present Congress.

    A survey of U.S. congressional representatives and senators who were born abroad or to immigrant parents finds a not-surprising pattern. If you ignore those whose parents were abroad on military service or work, most of those with first- or second-hand experience with communist rule or under dictatorships tend to be conservative.
