    In the Senate, Ted Cruz (R-TX) was born in Canada, but his parents were Cuban. They escaped Castro’s revolution and the subsequent confiscation of property and economic stagnation. To keep the lid on popular discontent as communist rule kept Cuba poor, Castro and his minions like Ernesto “Che” Guevara ruthlessly suppressed political opposition and free speech. Sen. Cruz is a fierce defender of capitalism, free speech, and democracy.

    It has been revealed that sen. Bernie Moreno (R-OH) was born in Bogota, Colombia, and came here in 1971, when he was four. At that time, the left-wing British Guardian admits, “leftist, Marxist-inspired insurgencies” including the ELN and FARC “conducted kidnappings…and carried out a campaign of terror that aimed to unseat the central government…” Moreno’s family wasn’t poor, and his father was a cabinet secretary under a conservative president, but they surely saw how communism threatened Colombia—and all of Latin America.

    In a recent development, the third senator born abroad is Mazie Hirono (D-HI), born in Japan. Her mother was Japanese-American from Hawaii, but her father fought for Emperor Hirohito in WWII. Hirono is one of the most left-wing members of Congress, according to Heritage Action.

    It has been revealed that of the nine senators born in the U.S. with one or more immigrant parents, all are Democrats. Six had parents born in Europe; two in Mexico, one in South Korea.

    In the House of Representatives, of the 16 Members I found who were born abroad to foreign parents, only three are Republican. Carlos Gimenez (R-FL) was born in Cuba, and Victoria Spartz (R-IN) was born in Ukraine—both communist countries at the time. The third Republican, Juan Ciscomani (R-AZ), was born in Mexico.

    The other 13 Members born abroad to foreign parents were Democrats—born in the Dominican Republic, Guatemala, India, Mexico, Peru, Somalia, South Korea, and Ukraine.

    I found 28 Members who were born in the U.S. to two immigrant parents. Of these, 21 are Democrats, and only seven are Republicans. Do the Republicans have anything in common? One had parents from China, three had Cuban parents, one had parents from Hungary and Poland, one had Portuguese parents, and one had Syrian parents.

    >>> Freedom Isn’t Automatic—Each Generation Must Fight To Keep It.

    So, five of the seven Republicans had parents who left communist countries for the U.S. and likely taught their children why. The remaining two had parents who left countries ruled by dictators at the time: Portugal and Syria.

    Of the 21 Democrats whose parents were both immigrants, Mexico (5) and India (3) were the most common countries of origin. Both countries have been at least nominal democracies for generations, albeit with a heavy dose of socialist economics. All six Indian-Americans in Congress appear to be Democrats, which is surprising given that they or their parents experienced India’s “License Raj” socialism that lasted from independence in 1947 until the 1990s. Indian Americans are also a reliable Democrat voter bank.

    In a recent development, ilhan Omar (D-MN) won 83.6% of Democratic [Farmer-Labor] primary votes in 2024 in Ward 6 of Minnesota’s Fifth Congressional District. It has “the largest concentration of Somalis in the state, and possibly is the highest concentration of diaspora Somalis in the world.” Despite credible reports that she lied about her age to become an American citizen and later married her brother to get him a green card, Omar was just re-elected to a fifth term in Congress, with 76% of the vote.

    Congress is changing as the country’s demographics change. If ethnic-bloc voting does not break down quickly with assimilation, we will see an increasingly Balkanized legislature. And if experience does not teach immigrants the failures of socialism and the superiority of the American way of life, we will be doomed to repeat the mistakes of the places they fled.

    India: Modi Rule Has Weakened Democratic Institutions

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, (London) – Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government has systematically weakened institutions established to protect human rights and democratic freedoms, Human Rights Watch mentioned in a report released today.
    • Industry observers note that the 95-page report, “‘So What’s This Democracy We’re Talking About?’: Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India,” finds that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government is undermining parliamentary procedures, suppressing the political opposition, and weaponizing federal investigative agencies for political ends.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, (London) – Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government has systematically weakened institutions established to protect human rights and democratic freedoms, Human Rights Watch mentioned in a report released today. Indians have increasingly taken to the streets to protest government repression, corruption, and a deeply flawed revision of voter lists.

    Industry observers note that the 95-page report, “‘So What’s This Democracy We’re Talking About?’: Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India,” finds that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government is undermining parliamentary procedures, suppressing the political opposition, and weaponizing federal investigative agencies for political ends. Human Rights Watch found that the government is also weakening constitutional and statutory bodies, such as the Election Commission, Central Information Commission, the anti-corruption ombudsman, and human rights commissions, and interfering in the judicial branch.

    Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India.

    Download the full report in English.

    According to recent reports, “Over the past decade, the Modi government has been hollowing out India’s independent institutions that are critical to checking executive power and protecting civil liberties,” noted Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The government has eroded the rule of law and promoted Hindu majoritarianism, rolling back human rights protections, undermining the rights of marginalized communities, and deepening India’s authoritarian slide.”.

    Human Rights Watch interviewed over 40 lawyers, journalists, activists, researchers, academics, current and former judges, and former government officials between January 2025 and September 2026.

    The Modi administration has frequently disregarded parliamentary oversight mechanisms to impose its political agenda. In December 2023, the government adopted a law that entrenched executive control over the appointment of election commissioners and granted them sweeping legal immunity for actions, decisions, or statements made while carrying out their official duties. The law was passed even as opposition members were suspended in unprecedented numbers from both houses for the entire session of the parliament, 100 from Lok Sabha (the House of the People or lower house) and 46 from Rajya Sabha (the Council of States or upper house).

    The BJP did not have a majority in the Rajya Sabha from 2014 to 2024. While all bills must be approved by both houses to become law, some regulating financial matters can be introduced in the Lok Sabha as “money bills,” which do not require Rajya Sabha approval. The Modi administration aggressively used money bills to push through laws with serious consequences for fundamental rights that would not qualify as money bills.

    According to recent reports, in 2019, the government used this approach to amend the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, significantly expanding the authority of the Enforcement Directorate, the federal enforcement agency it has used to improperly target political opponents, activists, and critics. The expansion of Enforcement Directorate powers would not appear to fall within the parameters set out for a money bill.

    According to recent reports, the Election Commission has repeatedly failed to hold Modi and senior BJP leaders to account despite apparent violations of the election code of conduct by use of hate speech. The commission has also failed to credibly investigate allegations by voters, activists, academics, and political parties of manipulation of registered voter lists, suppression of polling data, irregularities in counting votes, or interfering with voting machines.

    The commission is currently facing a massive crisis of credibility amid concerns over its ability to function independent of the executive. A Special Intensive Revision, purportedly to delete dead, duplicate, or ineligible voters, has arbitrarily removed over 130 million names from electoral rolls since June 2025, sparking nationwide protests in October 2026.

    Industry observers note that the administration has used federal agencies to pressure members of rival parties to defect to the BJP. After amending the law against money laundering, official data indicates that the Enforcement Directorate filed cases against 193 politicians between April 2015 and February 2025, most of whom were government opponents. This was more than a 600 percent jump from the 26 politicians investigated in the decade preceding the Modi administration. Such investigations are promptly stalled, or charges are dropped if the accused switches loyalties, leading opposition parties to call the BJP a “washing machine.”.

    The Modi government has since 2014 increasingly used federal investigation agencies to target domestic and international rights groups, human rights lawyers, activists, and media organizations under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act and other laws dealing with financial irregularities. It has used the abusive counterterrorism law, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), to wrongfully jail human rights activists, journalists, students, peaceful protesters, academics, and critics, sometimes for years without trial.

    India’s courts have also failed to uphold fundamental freedoms. In 2022, the Supreme Court endorsed and expanded the authority of enforcement agencies for arrest and search and seizure under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act. Legal scholars criticized the verdict as gutting rights to life and liberty.

    The Supreme Court is currently hearing petitions regarding the legitimacy of the electoral roll revision process. In May 2026, even after millions of names had been eliminated from voter lists, the court ruled that the data did not indicate “systemic disenfranchisement.” In April, after 9 million names—12 percent of the electorate—in West Bengal state had been removed, the court effectively mentioned it was acceptable for them not to vote at that time so long as they would be added back to the rolls. Shortly afterward, the BJP won control of the state for the first time. By November, the Election Commission, after protests, started reversing some of the decisions that had led to the arbitrary removal of names.

    The Modi administration’s actions over the past decade are not isolated institutional failures but mutually reinforcing elements of an authoritarian playbook, Human Rights Watch mentioned. A weakened opposition has fewer means to resist laws that entrench executive control. Institutions led by political appointees, such as the federal and state human rights commissions, have not adequately responded to efforts to prevent the silencing of civil society. When courts fail to provide timely and effective remedies, these abuses go unchecked.

    India’s allies should publicly and privately raise concerns about ongoing abuses and the deterioration of democratic institutions, including during high-level engagements and interactions, at the United Nations Human Rights Council, and in negotiations for bilateral trade and security agreements.

    According to recent reports, “Checking India’s democratic decline means ending the use of state institutions as weapons against government critics and rebuilding them as safeguards for everyone’s rights,” Pearson noted. “India’s allies should press the Modi government to end its assault on independent institutions and restore checks on executive power.”.

    Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India.

    Breaking: Croatia: Border Pushbacks of Adults, Children Violate Rights

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Brussels, November 24, 2026) – Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks at the border, including of unaccompanied children and families with young children, despite European Union efforts to end the practice, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today.
    • Recent findings suggest that the 43-page report, “Doing Europe’s Dirty Work: Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina,” finds that Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks, often violently.
    • Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Brussels, November 24, 2026) – Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks at the border, including of unaccompanied children and families with young children, despite European Union efforts to end the practice, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today.

    Recent findings suggest that the 43-page report, “Doing Europe’s Dirty Work: Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina,” finds that Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks, often violently. An EU-funded Croatian border monitoring program has had little impact on Croatian police pushbacks. Instead, the EU has increased funding to Croatia for border management without addressing the abuse at the border.

    Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

    Download the full report in English.

    Download the Summary & Recommendations in Bosnian.

    Download the Summary & Recommendations in Croatian.

    Annex: Unofficial Translation of the Croatia Ministry of Interior's Response to Human Rights Watch.

    Croatia Ministry of the Interior's Response to Human Rights Watch (Original Email in Croatian).

    In a recent development, “Violent pushbacks by Croatian police are a continuing problem, affecting children as well as adults, and the EU-funded systems set up to curb them aren’t working,” remarked Michael Garcia Bochenek, senior children’s rights counsel at Human Rights Watch. “The EU needs to act to ensure that Croatia respects EU law and protects the rights of those at its borders.”.

    Human Rights Watch interviewed more than 80 people, including seven unaccompanied children, four children travelling with family members, and six parents travelling with their children, and also interviewed 15 aid workers and others who offer information and other support to asylum seekers and migrants.

    Recent findings suggest that people interviewed said that Croatian police beat or kicked them, took all their money, and confiscated or destroyed their phones. In some cases, people said, the border police seized their documents, took their shoes, or even forced them to strip to their underwear before pushing them back across the border.

    “We told them that we are a family, but [the Croatian police] still took my husband away in one van and me and my daughters in another,” said a woman from Ghana. “We were separated for two days from my husband. They pushed me and my daughters to Bosnia through the woods. No phone, no food, no water. We were walking all day. We were lost and scared for many hours.”.

    Industry observers note that croatian authorities demonstrate official tolerance for unlawful police pushbacks through inadequate oversight, ineffective investigations and a lack of meaningful accountability, and repeated minimization—and often outright denial—of these practices, Human Rights Watch found. The government has not prosecuted any police officers for taking part in pushbacks, even in cases in which people suffered serious injuries or extreme forms of humiliation. Seven officers received disciplinary sanctions for mistreatment of migrants between 2020 and 2025, the Croatian Interior Ministry told Human Rights Watch.

    The only accommodation option in Bosnia and Herzegovina for most people pushed back from Croatia, including unaccompanied children and families with children, is the Lipa Migrant Reception Centre, 25 kilometres from Bihać, the nearest city. The center has experienced water shortages and power outages and has no local bus service. Healthcare services are limited, and the center provides no education for children.

    To its credit, the Croatian government strengthened the authority of a border monitoring mechanism established in 2021 with EU funding to prevent and address pushbacks and other abuses at the border.

    But the program has had little impact on Croatian police pushbacks, which remain common, Human Rights Watch said.

    European Union institutions have tools for direct oversight and enforcement of Croatia’s adherence to human rights, refugee, and EU norms, including the prohibition of collective expulsion—removing people without an individualized examination of their circumstances—as well as the best interests of the child, the right to seek asylum, and the prohibition of torture and other ill-treatment. But it has not used its authority to end the pushbacks. Instead, the EU has promoted and funded increased external border control by Croatia at the expense of people’s rights and protection needs.

    According to recent reports, the European Commission can open infringement proceedings against an EU member state that fails to implement EU law. The European Parliament can examine violations of EU law by member states. Neither has taken place in respect of Croatia’s border abuses.

    According to recent reports, the European Rule of Law Mechanism allows an annual dialogue between the European Commission and member states. Recent rule of law reports have not examined the weaknesses of Croatia’s border monitoring mechanism, nor have they addressed pushbacks more directly.

    According to recent reports, croatian authorities should immediately end pushbacks at its borders, provide opportunities to seek asylum, and ensure that the upcoming border monitoring mechanism is a robust and independent safeguard against pushbacks and other official abuse, Human Rights Watch noted. The European Commission should withhold border control funding until Croatia investigates and ends pushbacks and other mistreatment.

    Authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina should move families with children and unaccompanied children to facilities that are appropriate for their needs. The authorities should also ensure that all temporary reception centers, including for adults, are accessible by public transit and to shops, schools, hospitals, and other essential services.

    The EU and its member states should also create pathways for safe, orderly, and regular migration, Human Rights Watch said.

    “The EU needs to act to end the violent and abusive pushbacks at its borders and to hold Croatia to account for persistent and flagrant violations of EU law and international norms,” Bochenek said.

    Landmines: Fresh Use, Production Undermine Ban Treaty

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (913 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Geneva, November 24, 2026) – New use, production, and acquisition of antipersonnel landmines contributed to killing or injuring at least 6,929 people in 2025, which is the highest annual total since 2020, Human Rights Watch remarked today with the release of the “Landmine Monitor 2026” by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines.
    • The 200-page report examines global compliance with the 1997 Mine Ban Treaty and the challenges facing the treaty nearly three decades after its adoption.
    • “At a time when civilian casualties are rising and latest technologies make mines easier to deploy, supporting the Mine Ban Treaty is more important than ever,” said Verity Coyle, deputy crisis, conflict and arms director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Geneva, November 24, 2026) – New use, production, and acquisition of antipersonnel landmines contributed to killing or injuring at least 6,929 people in 2025, which is the highest annual total since 2020, Human Rights Watch remarked today with the release of the “Landmine Monitor 2026” by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines. Human Rights Watch is a founding member of the campaign and contributed to the report.

    The 200-page report examines global compliance with the 1997 Mine Ban Treaty and the challenges facing the treaty nearly three decades after its adoption. The treaty comprehensively bans antipersonnel mines and commits countries to eliminate stockpiled weapons, clear contaminated land, and assist mine victims and affected communities.

    “At a time when civilian casualties are rising and latest technologies make mines easier to deploy, supporting the Mine Ban Treaty is more important than ever,” said Verity Coyle, deputy crisis, conflict and arms director at Human Rights Watch. “All countries should join the treaty, and members should fully uphold its obligations.”.

    Recent findings suggest that antipersonnel mines continue to kill and maim civilians long after fighting moves elsewhere. Whether they are placed by soldiers on the ground or delivered remotely by weapons systems and drones, the mines contaminate land, roads, and communities for years. Their presence can prevent displaced families from returning home, obstruct humanitarian operations, and undermine efforts to rebuild livelihoods and food production.

    It has been revealed that A total of 162 countries are now bound by the Mine Ban Treaty. Three countries joined during the reporting period: Lebanon, Marshall Islands, and Tonga. Five other countries withdrew from the treaty in 2025 and 2026: Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland.

    According to recent reports, ukraine announced on July 18, 2025, that it would “suspend the operation” of the treaty while engaged in armed conflict with Russia, citing Russia’s extensive use of landmines. Suspensions, however, are unlawful under the treaty, notably during armed conflict, and Ukraine remains fully bound by all the treaty’s obligations. During the reporting period, Ukraine has acquired, produced, and used newly assembled antipersonnel mines, including types that are delivered by drone, in violation of the treaty.

    In addition to Ukraine’s use of antipersonnel mines, states not party to the treaty used them, including Iran, Myanmar, North Korea, and Russia.

    Sources indicate that antipersonnel mines were increasingly used in border conflicts, involving Cambodia and Thailand, Bangladesh and Myanmar, and in Thailand along the borders with Myanmar and Malaysia. Non-state armed groups also used antipersonnel mines, in many cases improvised, in Colombia, India, Myanmar, Pakistan, Sudan, and in locations in Western and Central Africa, including in the Chad Basin, Burkina Faso, and Mali.

    Industry observers note that the Landmine Monitor reported that 15 states not party to the treaty either right now produce antipersonnel mines or maintain the option to produce them in the future. Of these, India, Myanmar, Poland, Russia, and South Korea appear to be actively producing or developing antipersonnel mines. Finland, Latvia, and Lithuania—all of which withdrew from the treaty in 2025—have indicated their intent to develop or acquire antipersonnel mines. Non-state armed groups have produced improvised mines that explode due to the presence, proximity, or contact of a person in Colombia, India, Africa’s Sahel region, and sporadically in Thailand.

    In a recent development, in 2025, casualties from antipersonnel landmines and explosive remnants of war occurred in at least 54 countries and areas. Of these, 39 are party to the Mine Ban Treaty. Myanmar, which is not a party, recorded the highest number of annual casualties (1,891) for the third consecutive year, and Syria recorded 1,602 casualties. Civilians made up at least 84 percent (5,078) of all recorded casualties, while children accounted for 50 percent (1,690) of civilian casualties where the age group was known.

    According to recent reports, even as renewed mine use is contaminating new territory, progress remains possible. Croatia declared completion of its mine clearance obligations in March 2026, following Oman in 2025. Since the Mine Ban Treaty entered into force in 1999, 32 states parties have successfully cleared all known antipersonnel mine contamination from their territory.

    Recent findings suggest that the near elimination of government stockpiles remains one of the treaty’s greatest achievements. Of the 162 states parties, 157 report that they do not possess stockpiled antipersonnel mines. Ninety-four countries have finished destroying their stocks, a total of more than 55 million mines. As during previous reporting periods, Greece and Ukraine continue to possess stockpiles of antipersonnel mines, in violation of article 4 of the treaty.

    Industry observers note that “The world should be moving closer to ending the suffering caused by antipersonnel mines, not witnessing a resurgence in their use,” Coyle said. “Governments should be seeking global adoption of the ban treaty and reinforcing compliance, not stepping away from one of the world’s most successful humanitarian disarmament treaties.”.

    The “Landmine Monitor 2026” is the 28th annual publication by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, the global coalition of nongovernmental organizations that received the 1997 Nobel Peace Prize. Human Rights Watch co-founded the campaign in 1992 and contributes to its Landmine Monitor reporting initiative.

    Principles for Implementing the Declaration on Explosive Weapons in Populated Areas.

    • Industry observers note that I previously  wrote about Trump's latest executive order seeking to deny birthright citizenship to various classes of children born on US soil, and noted the first legal challenges to it.
    • Judge Cooper rightly concludes that nearly all the various classes of children barred from birthright citizenship by the newly introduced order are in fact protected by the reasoning of Barbara and other Supreme Court precedents, because they and their parents are clearly subject to US law, and required to obey it:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that yesterday, in the case of Nathan v. Trump, federal district Judge Christopher Cooper of the District of DC issued a ruling against Trump's fresh executive order restricting birthright citizenship. The ruling is very similar to an earlier September decision by Judge Boardman of the District of Maryland. The one difference is that the class action injunction in Nathan covers a class that literally consists of all children illegally deprived of birthright citizenship under the new order, whereas the class in the Maryland case is slightly narrower.

    Industry observers note that I previously  wrote about Trump's latest executive order seeking to deny birthright citizenship to various classes of children born on US soil, and noted the first legal challenges to it. As I pointed out then, almost every part of the new order is at odds with the Supreme Court's recent ruling in Trump v. Barbara, which struck down Trump's executive order denying birthright citizenship to children of undocumented immigrants born in the United States, and those born to non-citizen parents here on temporary visas. The Fourteenth Amendment guarantees citizenship to all children "born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof." In Barbara, the Supreme Court majority made clear that "subject to the jurisdiction thereof" includes children of all persons who are subject to and required to obey US law.

    Judge Cooper rightly concludes that nearly all the various classes of children barred from birthright citizenship by the newly introduced order are in fact protected by the reasoning of Barbara and other Supreme Court precedents, because they and their parents are clearly subject to US law, and required to obey it:.

    It has been revealed that earlier this year, the Supreme Court struck down President Trump's Executive Order 14160, which purported to deny citizenship to children born to parents temporarily or unlawfully present in the country. Those children, like "nearly all children born in the United States," the Court explained, are "citizens at birth" because they are born "subject to American law." Trump v. Barbara, 609 U.S. 719, 734–37, 740–41 (2026). Barbara reaffirmed that birthright citizenship extends to all but three narrow categories of children, each long understood to be beyond the Nation's governing authority at birth: children of foreign officials enjoying full diplomatic immunity, children of enemy forces in hostile occupation of U.S. territory, and children born aboard foreign public ships.

    According to recent reports, yet Barbara's ink had scarcely dried when the President issued a second executive order—Executive Order 14418, at glitch here—directing federal agencies to withhold recognition of citizenship from additional categories of U.S.-born children with noncitizen parents. Among those now targeted are children whose parents work for foreign governments or international organizations but lack diplomatic immunity, children born through commercial surrogacy arrangements, and children with a parent suspected of membership in certain gangs or terrorist organizations. As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out upcoming exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws. The Court will therefore certify a class consisting of children who are or will be unlawfully denied citizenship under the Order. And it will preliminarily enjoin the Government from enforcing the Order against members of that class.

    As explained in my original August post on the new executive order, that order covers four groups almost all of whose members are clearly subject to US law:.

    Sources indicate that children of "alien enemies," defined as those where at least one of two non-citizen parents is a "designated Foreign Terrorist Organization under 8 U.S.C. 1189 or Specially Designated Global Terrorist, consistent with the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, 50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq., and Executive Order 13224 of September 23, 2001 (Blocking Property and Prohibiting Transactions With Persons Who Commit, Threaten to Commit, or Support Terrorism).".

    Children born to at least one non-citizen parent who is a "foreign government employee" or employed by an "international organization that possess[es] international-organization immunity.".

    Children where "either parent" has engaged in "birth tourist" transactions of various kinds (deliberately seeking to give birth in the US so the child would get birthright citizenship).

    Children "born in a territory or territorial waters of the United States where citizenship is not conferred by Federal statute." …[T]his only applies to children born in American Samoa, the one populated overseas US territory to whose residents Congress has not conferred citizenship by statute….

    Industry observers note that as I explained more fully in my August post, all of the children in these four categories are obviously subject to US law, with the exception of those born to foreign diplomats who have diplomatic immunity. This latter group is already excluded from birthright citizenship. In that post, I also explained why the analogy between "alien enemies" (as defined in the order) and children of members of an invading army occupying US territory fails.

    It has been revealed that judge Cooper's opinion analyzes all four categories thoroughly and effectively. He's particularly strong on the case of children of "alien enemies," a category which - he explains - the Trump order defines far more broadly than is justified by legal precedent, and which in any case does not include anyone not "subject to the jurisdiction" of the United States, because all such people are under US control and required to obey US law when on American soil. That differentiates them from the historically recognized exception for children of enemy troops in "hostile occupation" of US territory during a war. The US does not have effective jurisdiction over territory occupied by a hostile enemy army. But the last time any such thing occurred was during World War II, when the Japanese occupied a number of US island possessions in the Pacific.

    I noted some additional problems with Trump's "alien enemies" carveout in my August post about the second birthright citizenship order:.

    Finally, the [order is wrong about] children of "alien enemies," defined…. as members of various designated "terrorist" entities. If they enter the United States, they are subject to US law. That's why they can be prosecuted for any crimes they commit on US soil - including acts of terrorism!

    Recent findings suggest that members of these groups may be bad people. Some have committed horrendous crimes. But that is no reason to visit the sins of the parents upon the children. If a murderer or a rapist has a child born on US soil, the child is entitled to birthright citizenship, notwithstanding the reprehensible behavior of the parents. The same logic applies here.

    It is also worth noting that the "foreign terrorist organization" (FTO) designation has been slapped onto various groups that are not actually terrorists in the ordinary meaning of the word, most notably groups engaged in smuggling illegal drugs.

    Sources indicate that trump may be trying to use the "alien enemy" designation here to analogize these children to children of members of an invading army, born  at a time and place where the invaders have seized control of US territory, thereby preventing the exercise of US "jurisdiction." Trump v. Barbara reaffirms the longstanding view that such children are excluded from birthright citizenship, because born in an area where US jurisdiction does not (at the time) meaningfully apply.

    Sources indicate that but FTOs have not, in fact, "invaded" or occupied any part of the United States. Thus, US jurisdiction still applies. Therefore, children of members these organizations are not analogous to children born to members of an occupying foreign army. No part of the United States has actually been invaded and occupied since the Japanese seized various US territories in the Pacific during World War II.

    In my article, "Immigration is Not Invasion….," I explain in much more detail why the activities of drug dealers do not qualify as an "invasion," why an FTO designation cannot change that reality, and why courts should not defer to the president's claims that an "invasion" has occurred.

    EU: Forced Labor Remedies Should Center on Workers

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Brussels) – Companies that receive complaints of forced labor in their operations or supply chains should make sure affected workers have access to full and effective remedies, Human Rights Watch and a group of civil society organizations and trade unions mentioned in a report released today.
    • In the White Paper on Remediation of Forced Labour in the Private Economy, the organizations set out what appropriate and effective remedies look like for workers, and the concrete steps companies should take to deliver it.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Brussels) – Companies that receive complaints of forced labor in their operations or supply chains should make sure affected workers have access to full and effective remedies, Human Rights Watch and a group of civil society organizations and trade unions mentioned in a report released today.

    In the White Paper on Remediation of Forced Labour in the Private Economy, the organizations set out what appropriate and effective remedies look like for workers, and the concrete steps companies should take to deliver it.

    “Forced labor does not end when a product is pulled from the shelves but only when workers who were trapped by debt, deceived, or threatened get their wages, documents, and dignity back,” said Hélène de Rengervé, senior advocate at Human Rights Watch. “Companies should remedy labor abuses in their supply chains and engage with workers from the start to define appropriate solutions.”.

    In a recent development, the groups propose concrete steps for companies to prepare, deliver and assess their remediation obligations. The report comes as the European Union prepares to enforce its Forced Labour Regulation, which will ban products made with forced labor from the EU market across all sectors and stages of production beginning on December 14, 2027. Under the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, companies in its scope will also have a legal duty to remedy harm they cause, completely or in part.

    It has been revealed that an estimated 17.3 million people were in situations of forced labor in the private economy in 2022, according to global estimates by the International Labour Organization (ILO), Walk Free, and the International Organization for Migration. The number of victims increased by 8 percent between 2016 and 2021. The ILO estimates that forced labor in the private economy generates US$63.9 billion in illegal profits every year.

    Academics and experts found that forced labor is rarely only the result of a few bad actors, but is rooted in poverty, discrimination, weak labor protections, and restrictive migration regimes. Migrant workers face heightened risks, including recruitment fees that lead to debt bondage, deceptive recruitment practices, and visas tied to a single employer. Fear of deportation and retaliation often keeps victims from seeking redress.

    The civil society groups mentioned that companies should put in place remediation measures that restore as much as possible the situation for workers if the abuse had not occurred. This would require the cessation of the abuse, restitution, rehabilitation, compensation, apologies, and guarantees of non-repetition. Companies should also ensure that workers and their representatives can identify abuses through grievance mechanisms they trust, define remedies, and assess whether they have been delivered to their satisfaction, the groups said. At all times, affected workers should be protected from retaliation.

    In a recent development, companies should treat remediation as part of their human rights due diligence, not as a one-off response to a scandal, the groups said. Their responsibility should reflect their involvement in failing to prevent or meaningfully address the harm. Companies should not “cut and run” from suppliers when and where labor abuses, including forced labor, is found, as this can leave workers worse off. Instead, the groups said, companies should fairly agree on how to address and share remediation costs.

    To prevent forced labor from occurring and recurring, companies should examine structural causes such as poverty, discrimination and impairments to freedom of association but also how their own purchasing practices may drive it. They should pay to cover the cost of decent working conditions and living wages. The groups point to worker-driven models, such as the Fair Food Program in US agriculture and the Dindigul Agreement in India’s textile sector, as evidence of good practices.

    Recent findings suggest that the EU and its member states should ensure that the competent authorities empowered to enforce the Forced Labour Regulation assess whether effective remediation has actually delivered for workers, including through workers’ own accounts and evidence of compensation paid. They should also ensure that, regardless of their migration status, workers can at least access support, file complaints, and recover unpaid wages.

    Recent findings suggest that “Workers know best what they have lost and what it will take to rebuild their lives,” de Rengervé said. “Companies and EU authorities should listen to affected workers and measure the efficiency of remediation by what workers receive and whether they completely remediate the harm suffered.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When Pakistani senators visited the prototype Islamabad Model Jail on November 19 and inspected the healthcare facilities that would be available to prisoners, they called them “adequate.” But the conditions they observed on their curated tour are a far cry from the reality most prisoners experience in Pakistan’s justice system.
    • Industry observers note that human Rights Watch has documented structural and systemic problems in Pakistan’s jails and prisons that leave most inmates with little access to health care.
    • After two prisoners died in Peshawar Central Prison following alleged delays in medical treatment, a lawyer petitioned the Peshawar High Court asking that prisons across the province be required to record when prisoners request medical help and establish clear procedures for emergency hospital transfers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When Pakistani senators visited the prototype Islamabad Model Jail on November 19 and inspected the healthcare facilities that would be available to prisoners, they called them “adequate.” But the conditions they observed on their curated tour are a far cry from the reality most prisoners experience in Pakistan’s justice system.

    Industry observers note that human Rights Watch has documented structural and systemic problems in Pakistan’s jails and prisons that leave most inmates with little access to health care. Many inmates who fall ill in custody fail to receive prompt or decent care at all.

    After two prisoners died in Peshawar Central Prison following alleged delays in medical treatment, a lawyer petitioned the Peshawar High Court asking that prisons across the province be required to record when prisoners request medical help and establish clear procedures for emergency hospital transfers.

    Colonial-era laws have long-enabled Pakistani officials and powerful people to interfere in prison operations, sometimes making use of poor conditions to harass jailed political opponents. In a November 16 letter released by his lawyer, former Prime Minister Imran Khan appealed for urgent medical care for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi, citing his high blood pressure and her need for eye surgery. Khan’s appeal echoes complaints about medical care in custody from former President Asif Ali Zardari and former Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif. All have alleged that prison services denied access to medical care as a form of punishment.

    Federal and provincial governments in Pakistan should bring health care in jails and prisons in line with international standards, notably the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Mandela Rules), which require that prisoners receive necessary free medical care to the same standard available in the community, with prompt attention in emergencies. In October, Justice Project Pakistan called for common standards across provinces so prisoners can see medical specialists when needed and continue treatment after release.

    Pakistan’s federal and provincial governments should provide prescribed medicines free of charge and require prisons to record how long patients wait for care. When care requires an urgent hospital transfer, prison authorities should promptly facilitate transport. Authorities should ensure all prisoners, regardless of political affiliation or status, receive timely and adequate medical care, with continuity of treatment.

    #171567. Philippines: As ICC Tries Duterte, Stalled Justice at Home

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3188 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hrw ↗ Open Full Page

    Philippines: As ICC Tries Duterte, Stalled Justice at Home

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that (Manila) – Philippine authorities have failed to investigate extrajudicial killings in the “war on drugs” since former President Rodrigo Duterte was transferred to the International Criminal Court for prosecution, Human Rights Watch noted today.
    • Recent findings suggest that president Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who took office in June 2022, pledged to pursue prosecutions of Duterte-era “drug war” killings and established a Justice Department task force for the purpose, but only four cases have reached the courts.
    • Industry observers note that “President Marcos’ pledge to hold police accountable for past and ongoing abuses in its anti-drug campaign has been a failure,” said Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that (Manila) – Philippine authorities have failed to investigate extrajudicial killings in the “war on drugs” since former President Rodrigo Duterte was transferred to the International Criminal Court for prosecution, Human Rights Watch noted today. The ICC trial in The Hague against Duterte for crimes against humanity is scheduled to begin on November 30, 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that president Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who took office in June 2022, pledged to pursue prosecutions of Duterte-era “drug war” killings and established a Justice Department task force for the purpose, but only four cases have reached the courts. Families of victims seeking to file new cases face significant barriers. Meanwhile, government records and human rights group reports show that drug-war abuses continue, with police harassing, arbitrarily arresting, and at times killing suspected drug dealers and customers.

    Industry observers note that “President Marcos’ pledge to hold police accountable for past and ongoing abuses in its anti-drug campaign has been a failure,” said Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Philippine government needs to prioritize justice for all drug-war victims and provide their families’ adequate redress.”.

    In a recent development, between September and November 2026, Human Rights Watch interviewed 13 people, including 7 drug-war victims and their families both under Duterte and Marcos, 4 human rights defenders, and 2 government officials; reviewed recent data and reporting on drug-related killings; and analyzed a database of local government Peace and Order and Public Safety Plans. Human Rights Watch also requested and received information from the Philippine Justice Department and Commission on Human Rights on drug-war cases before the courts.

    Relatives of drug-war victims described a justice system in which the burden of uncovering evidence of an unlawful killing fell mostly on them instead of government prosecutors. “It’s so hard to prove that you’re telling the truth,” said a woman whose husband was killed in 2016 in a police “buy-bust” drug sting operation. “It’s tiring pursuing a case here—it’s as if we can never pass the tests.”.

    Industry observers note that some facing obstacles to justice have pinned their hopes on the ICC. “In the Philippines, what was our chance, given how the government works,” stated another woman whose husband was killed by unidentified assailants in 2016. “In the ICC they are impartial, that’s where our hope is.”.

    During the Duterte presidency from 2016 to 2022, the Philippine National Police reported 6,200 deaths during anti-drug operations, although United Nations agencies, the Philippine Commission on Human Rights, the Supreme Court, and domestic human rights groups put the number of killings by police and unidentified assailants at between 20,000 and 30,000.

    Sources indicate that only five cases of Duterte-era “drug war” killings, involving nine police officers, have resulted in convictions. Government prosecutors initiated the first three cases, following the successive murders of three teenage boys in Caloocan in August 2017, which sparked public outrage. The fourth and fifth cases—for killings in 2016—were filed through the efforts of nongovernmental legal groups and led to convictions in 2024 and 2025.

    In November 2024, the Justice Department created a task force to investigate and prosecute extrajudicial killings during Duterte’s “war on drugs” but only four cases it identified have advanced to trial, with three others under preliminary investigation, based on Justice Department data.

    The Marcos administration, after arresting and surrendering Duterte to the ICC in March 2025, announced renewed efforts to advance domestic accountability for the “drug war.” But families and human rights groups who met with Justice Department officials said that they were concerned the government’s witness protection program would not keep their families safe if they pursued charges against police officers. Meetings between victims’ groups and the Justice Department tapered off.

    Duterte will stand trial at the ICC for three counts of crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder allegedly committed when he was mayor of Davao City, and then president between November 2011 and March 2019. The prosecution’s case focuses on a non-exhaustive list of 56 specific incidents and 87 victims, while noting that “[its] evidence demonstrates that the attack [against a civilian population] was broader than this representative sample of incidents.”.

    Industry observers note that the ICC is a court of last resort, only stepping in when domestic authorities are unwilling or unable to investigate and prosecute crimes under its jurisdiction. In November 2021, the Duterte government asked the ICC prosecutor to defer his investigation, opened in September 2021, claiming that national authorities had begun their own drug-war investigations of extrajudicial killings.

    In January 2023, ICC judges ruled that the Philippine government had failed to demonstrate that it took sufficient action to investigate and prosecute Duterte-era killings and authorized the resumption of the ICC prosecutor’s investigation. The decision was upheld on appeal.

    The ICC trial against Duterte begins as the court is under growing pressure from the US government, which has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick.” On October 9, the Trump administration sanctioned the ICC, escalating its attack on the court and adding to existing sanctions on ICC judges and prosecutors, three Palestinian groups, and a UN human rights expert. The Trump administration sanctions reaffirm the ICC’s critical role as a court of last resort, Human Rights Watch mentioned.

    It has been revealed that marcos has never repudiated the “war on drugs” as a government policy and has yet to rescind the orders and other policy statements Duterte issued that underpinned the anti-drug campaign. In its review of a database of 2023-2025 local government budgets, Human Rights Watch found that 77 municipalities had allocated funds for anti-drug campaign awards and rewards, or for financial support to informants, police officials, and other local officials. Two of those municipalities, and another eight municipalities specifically referred to “neutralization” or “negation” of suspects; terms used as euphemisms for “killing” in 2016 police circular that set out the “war on drugs.” While such incentives are not necessarily unlawful, those linked to enforcement goals or operational results can create pressure to meet targets and encourage abusive practices, including extrajudicial killings.

    Despite a significant decline in drug-related extrajudicial killings during the Marcos administration, such killings and other abuses continue, particularly in low-income urban areas where they remain routine. As of November 7, there have been at least 1,342 public reports of drug-related killings under Marcos, according to the independent monitoring of the Dahas project. These reports identified uniformed officers as responsible for 486 of those deaths.

    Sources indicate that the Philippine government’s failure to hold those responsible to account perpetuates a climate of impunity. Families of drug-war victims under the Marcos administration encounter many of the same past obstacles when seeking justice, but the Justice Department has no task force or special mechanism to investigate post-Duterte cases, Human Rights Watch said.

    “Even if killings are down from the ghastly Duterte years, President Marcos’ pledged ‘bloodless campaign’ against drugs has been anything but bloodless,” Buan remarked. “To end these abuses, Marcos needs to stop the brutal ‘drug war’ and put in place a robust and impartial law enforcement and judicial system.”Elusive Justice for Killings during Duterte and Marcos Administrations.

    Under the Duterte administration in 2020, the Justice Department opened an inter-agency panel to “reinvestigate” drug-war killings by the police. The panel identified 52 cases in which the Philippine National Police carried out internalinvestigations. However, by 2024, when Marcos was in office, the panel had only filed six cases in court. In November 2024, the Justice Department created a new task force on Duterte-era drug war killings. It began investigations anew and worked mainly with the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI)—the Justice Department’s investigative arm—instead of with the police to avoid conflicts of interest when developing cases implicating police officers.

    Despite renewed Justice Department efforts, victims’ families still struggled to file charges. Many victims’ families who wanted to pursue charges could not do so because their relative’s death certificate declared an illness as the cause of death, even though they were found with gunshot wounds to their heads and bodies. During the height of Duterte’s “drug war,” police pressured families to sign waivers stating that they did not want to conduct autopsies or pursue charges, in exchange for faster retrievals of the bodies from funeral homes. Many families could not afford the autopsy fees, and without accurate government death records, they could not pursue charges.

    Industry observers note that the woman whose husband was killed in a police operation in 2016 decided in 2022 to retrieve documents about his killing from the police because she believed the climate of fear had lifted under Marcos. “They were not really helping us,” she said. “They just left us there to search their logbooks.” Police officials had named the woman’s husband as a drug suspect killed in an “armed encounter” in a news report that featured her children wailing for their dead father. Yet she never found a police report of the operation, only a record of bystanders injured. She was unable to prove he was shot dead, because his death certificate lists the cause of death as pneumonia and his body was cremated. Government investigators have not pursued a case. The woman recalled the one conversation with the Justice Department: “They said, ‘If you have no document like police report or autopsy, it’s hard to file a case.’ So, what about me? I had no documents.”.

    Industry observers note that the woman whose husband was killed by unidentified assailants did not know for years the circumstances under which her husband was killed. She found his body with gunshot wounds at a funeral home in 2016 and signed a waiver not to conduct an autopsy. His death certificate listed pneumonia as cause of death. After Marcos became president, the woman sought help from a nonprofit law group. In 2023, she had her husband’s body exhumed and examined by a forensic pathologist, Raquel Fortun. The autopsy showed that he died from gunshot wounds to the head.

    Recent findings suggest that that year, she finally found the police report from the night her husband died. It stated that police responding to reports of gunshots found him dead with three sachets of crystal meth, and a piece of cardboard that read “I’m a drug pusher, don’t be like me.” She had an interview with the NBI, who told her they had also summoned local officials and the funeral home. But nothing further happened in the investigation. “No one has followed up with me, I still wonder what happened to that NBI case,” she noted.

    Sources indicate that fortun became a commissioner of the Philippine Truth Commission, a civil society initiative working closely with the Catholic Church to investigate Duterte-era drug war crimes. She has recorded 13 cases in which people were shot and killed but whose death certificates cite illnesses such as heart attack, pneumonia, and high blood pressure as causes of death. Fortun stated during a Truth Commission briefing that government prosecutors have pushed back when presented with evidence of falsified death certificates in court. In one case, the government prosecutor acted on behalf of the defendant, instead of the victim: “I was grilled in cross-examination, and I was surprised that it was the prosecutor. I don’t understand it. So if you’re a poor family with a similar case, would you still have it corrected. It’s so hard.”.

    According to recent reports, the Commission on Human Rights told Human Rights Watch that its investigations of Duterte-era drug-war killings have resulted in cases moving through the justice system. Between 2016 and 2023, 25 cases were filed in court, 37 cases at the Office of the Ombudsman, and 42 with the Justice Department. No further progress was reported by the commission on the cases filed. The commission has no prosecutorial power and can only file cases in a manner similar to private complainants.

    Despite the Commission on Human Right’s limited powers, families seek confirmation from the commission that they have been victims of rights violations, which entitles them to limited financial assistance under the commission’s internal rules of procedure. Yet the commission denied assistance for lack of evidence to two women whose husbands were fatally shot in 2016.

    Industry observers note that only the woman who exhumed her husband’s body was able to challenge the decision; after she submitted the postmortem examination report in August 2026, the commission told her to file a petition for reinvestigation. “I just want to prove that what I’m saying is the truth,” she stated.

    The commission told Human Rights Watch that it created its own task force, which is currently reinvestigating 493 cases of Duterte-era drug-war killings, with the goal of resolving 140 before the end of 2026.

    Duterte-Era Drug-War Policy Persists.

    Sources indicate that the mother of a man killed by police in Central Luzon in 2022—after Marcos became president—said that she tried to pursue murder charges. She cited a witness who told her that her son was lured to the location the night of the killing, and an autopsy report that indicated he had been shot execution-style and not during an armed encounter as police had claimed. The witness has since gone missing. Prosecutors dismissed her case twice, most recently in 2025, because a medical expert’s testimony was required. The mother said that she was working on finding a medical expert to testify, but even just the cost of reproducing copies of documents was weighing on her.

    Recent findings suggest that no special task force has been created to investigate alleged drug-war crimes under the Marcos government. The government has claimed that its anti-drug campaign is “bloodless” and that “rather than resorting to violence, it focuses on strengthening prevention and rehabilitation efforts.” But Human Rights Watch found that disturbing Duterte-era language, such as “neutralization,” remains in looks for current anti-drugs campaigns.

    There is no legal definition of “neutralization,” but on July 1, 2016, Duterte’s police chief, Ronald Dela Rosa, issued Command Memorandum Circular 16-2016, the operational document for the anti-drug campaign, instructing police officers to “neutralize” suspected criminals.

    It has been revealed that in 2017, two human rights groups, the Center for International Law (CenterLaw) and the Free Legal Assistance Group (FLAG), filed petitions before the Supreme Court seeking to declare the anti-drug campaign unconstitutional, citing the use of the word “neutralization” in the circular. The Supreme Court has yet to rule on the case. ICC prosecutors have accused Duterte of developing “a State policy to ‘neutralize’ through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines who were perceived or alleged to be involved in drug-related and other crimes,” noting the language in the circular.

    In November 2025, the ICC issued a sealed arrest warrant for Dela Rosa. He is alleged to be responsible for the crime against humanity of murder as part of a common plan together with other co-perpetrators—including Duterte—with the aim of killing drug suspects between 2011 and 2019. This included issuing the Command Memorandum Circular 16-2016, instructing police officers to “neutralize” suspected criminals. The ICC unsealed the warrant in May 2026; Dela Rosa has since gone into hiding.

    The Marcos government has not rescinded that circular, but in 2024 the Philippine National Police told lawmakers that they were actually following a new circular without the word “neutralize.” The Marcos government also committed todrug policy reform as part of a US$4 million joint human rights program with the United Nations.

    A 2026 study by two organizations, No Box Philippines and Harm Reduction International, found that the Philippine government was still allocating millions of US dollars for local anti-drug campaigns whose policy documents retained similar language to the original circular, such as “neutralization” and “negation.” Their findings were based on an analysis of 2023-2025 local government “Peace and Order and Public Safety” budgets. Local governments are supervised by the Department of Interior and Local Government, the executive department that also supervises the police.

    Human Rights Watch analyzed local government aims obtained by the two groups, and found that 85 towns, municipalities, and cities allocated funds for rewards, awards, and incentives for successful anti-drug operations, including 10 municipalities where the funds were specifically for “conducting negation operations” or “neutralizing drug personalities.”.

    During the Duterte presidency, for an area to declare itself “drug-free,” local councils had to monitor, surveil, and compile a drug “watch list.” Human rights groups frequently alleged the lists determined who would be killed, whether the assailants were police officers or masked police agents.

    Under public safety intends in effect under Marcos, local governments still offer financial rewards for making their areas “drug-free,” by giving “incentives to assets,” or “awards/rewards for significant illegal drugs accomplishment” or “neutralization of drug personalities.” ICC prosecutors alleged in their case against Duterte that “law enforcement personnel knew that extrajudicial killings would result in them being financially rewarded.” There have been fewer drug-related killings under Marcos, but human rights defenders who live in drug-war hotspots in Metro Manila and neighboring provinces said abuses continued.

    Sources indicate that “Their raids are not as brazen, but they still plant evidence,” one rights defender noted. The quota system—the number of arrests and kills under Duterte to qualify for rewards—“was still alive.”.

    Under Marcos, human rights defenders monitoring drug-war abuses in their communities have observed that the police are more likely to extort victims than to kill them, targeting many of the same people who were on drug “watch lists.” They said police still arbitrarily arrest people, threaten them with drug charges, and then detain them on criminal anti-street-gambling charges with lighter penalties. The Philippine organization PhilRights has documented that “police officers offer to cover the victims’ release costs in exchange for repayment with interest, effectively profiting from the arrest.”.

    In 2025, a man came home one night to find police officers in the vicinity, his sister mentioned. “They patted him down and found nothing,” she said. “But a police informant handed sachets of crystal meth and forced him to admit it was his.” The police arrested the man and took his bicycle. She said she made several visits to the police station where her brother had been detained. The police officials told her he had been charged with gambling. “I told them, ‘You said you found drugs, now the charge is gambling. How long are you detaining him?’” she said. “They told us we can ‘just pay P10,000 [$160].’ But we had no money at all at the time.”.

    According to recent reports, the sister took a month processing documents in several police stations before her brother was released. He was detained for a month without being brought before a judge in violation of his rights. “We can still see them surveilling our area from time to time,” the sister said.

    This publication has been updated to attribute the source of the data for drug-related killings under the Marcos administration.

    #171566. Slow Horses has been renewed well into the future

    Slow Horses has been renewed well into the future

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (515 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Featured image credit:  Jack English/Apple TV+ via Rolling Stone.
    • Slow Horses, the wonderful television series based on Mick Herron’s wonderful Slough House books series has been renewed.
    • Recent findings suggest that but the series has been renewed even further than that.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Featured image credit:  Jack English/Apple TV+ via Rolling Stone.

    Yes. Slow Horses, the wonderful television series based on Mick Herron’s wonderful Slough House books series has been renewed. Season 6 just aired this fall, on its home network of Apple TV+, and work on the 7th season has begun.

    Recent findings suggest that but the series has been renewed even further than that. When Season 6 aired, we learned that the show had been renewed for an 8th season. This was great news.

    And now, Apple has confirmed that the series will continue through Season 10! Yes, Seasons 9 and 10 have been announced! This means we have four more seasons to look forward to. That’s four more years of Jackson Lamb and his crew of misfits. That’s a whole American presidential term’s worth of Slow Horses.

    Until Season 6, each season of the show has adapted a single one of Heron’s novels, all in chronological order. Season 6 broke the mold by adapting two: the sequential volumes Joe Country and Slough House. This means there are two extant novels left to adapt, Bad Actors and Clown Town, and early reports have confirmed that seasons 7 and 8 will undertake each of those novels, respectively. This means that Heron’s next novel will also be guaranteed a season, as will the next.

    Industry observers note that will he indeed write more? Yes, it certainly seems so, though there have been no announcements about a latest installment. The most recent novel, Clown Town, was released in 2025, and Heron’s novels typically have a 1-3 year gap in between them. But there’s still plenty of relevant Slough House material rife for adaptation; Heron has also published five Slough House novellas, none of which have been adapted yet. (Interested readers should note that all the novellas thus far have been collected in a volume called Standing By the Wall.).

    Sources indicate that the series Slow Horses stars Gary Oldman as the irascible, perpetually-disheveled, foul-mouthed, flatulent and yet thoroughly lovable MI5 agent Jackson Lamb, who oversees a notorious departmental backwater of the Secret Service called Slough House, an institutional repository for agents who have badly messed up (or pissed off somebody crucial). Time and time again Lamb and his team of oddballs, including Jack Lowden’s put-in-Slough-House-by-sabotage River Cartwright, wind up using their special skills, disregard for the rules, and occasional desire to prove themselves/not be messed with to save the day, often. It’s the best.

    16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Every year during the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence women’s rights defenders come together to remember women facing violence—including those we have lost—and to renew the struggle for gender equality.
    • Industry observers note that this year we face growing gender inequality, as the rights of women and girls are rolled back and threatened by authoritarianism and conflict in many countries.
    • Industry observers note that in the United States and Russia, authorities are dismantling reproductive rights.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every year during the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence women’s rights defenders come together to remember women facing violence—including those we have lost—and to renew the struggle for gender equality.

    Industry observers note that this year we face growing gender inequality, as the rights of women and girls are rolled back and threatened by authoritarianism and conflict in many countries. Across all regions, governments and powerful anti-rights movements seek to dismantle hard-won rights for women and girls. Technology is adding new dimensions to abuse, from online harassment and surveillance to digitally enabled threats, violence, and sexualized deepfake images;  women politicians are often targeted.

    Industry observers note that in the United States and Russia, authorities are dismantling reproductive rights. In Africa, lawmakers, with support from foreign conservative groups, are promoting a charter aiming to roll back women’s rights across the continent. In Argentina, funding for preventing GBV has been scrapped.

    As armed conflict increases across the globe, more women and girls are living in proximity to fighting. During conflict, women and girls face heightened risks of sexual and gender-based violence, displacement, and economic insecurity, often with little access to protection or justice. In Sudan and Democratic Republic of Congo, sexual violence is a common feature of ongoing conflict with survivors facing significant barriers to obtaining protection, services, and justice. In Myanmar, women political prisoners are tortured. Reproductive rights are a casualty of Israel’s closures in the West Bank, its ongoing blockade of the Gaza Strip, and its continued attacks on Palestinian health facilities.

    But activists refuse to accept erosion of women’s rights.

    In March, the Commission on the Status of Women called for strengthening access to justice for all women and girls. In April, the European Parliament passed a resolution calling for consent to be the determining factor in rape legislation across the EU. In November, Hungary confirmed it would ratify the Istanbul Convention, strengthening women’s rights protections. Activists from Afghanistan are fighting to have gender apartheid recognized as an international crime.

    Industry observers note that activists are also pushing back against technology-facilitated abuse, demanding that companies protect, rather than endanger, women and girls. In different countries young women are leading protest movements to challenge corruption and authoritarianism.

    Rights defenders will not lose hope.

    Violence Against Lesbian, Bisexual, and Queer Women and Non-Binary People.

    Accelerating Supply Chain Transparency in the Apparel and Footwear Industry.

    Tech Report: Hong Kong: Fire Anniversary Underscores Growing Repression

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (London) – The Hong Kong government should ensure meaningful accountability for the devastating fire that killed 168 people one year ago and end its suppression of peaceful criticism, Human Rights Watch mentioned today.
    • Sources indicate that on November 26, 2025, Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades engulfed seven residential high-rise buildings at Wang Fuk Court, Tai Po.
    • “The Hong Kong government responded to the horrific Wang Fuk Court fire by using Beijing’s tactics of shutting out the voices of the victims and promising an elusive accountability,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (London) – The Hong Kong government should ensure meaningful accountability for the devastating fire that killed 168 people one year ago and end its suppression of peaceful criticism, Human Rights Watch mentioned today.

    Sources indicate that on November 26, 2025, Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades engulfed seven residential high-rise buildings at Wang Fuk Court, Tai Po. The authorities initiated an independent investigation and arrested three dozen people implicated in crimes. The Housing Minister resigned. But the authorities have also threatened and arbitrarily arrested those engaging in criticism and activism concerning the fire.

    “The Hong Kong government responded to the horrific Wang Fuk Court fire by using Beijing’s tactics of shutting out the voices of the victims and promising an elusive accountability,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities need to recognize that the only way to prevent similar tragedies in the future is to allow people to speak out safely and hold those responsible fully accountable.”.

    The authorities have engaged in apparent acts of repression of free expression in the weeks ahead of the anniversary:.

    Police Commissioner Joe Chow noted police routinely asked organizers about upcoming public events, while decisions on whether to proceed “rested with the organizers themselves.”.

    Amid continued restrictions on freedom of expression and peaceful assembly in Hong Kong, Hong Kong communities around the world have planned commemorations of the fire.

    Sources indicate that deep concerns surrounding the 2026 anniversary follow a year-long government crackdown on criticism, reporting, and civil society-organizing related to the fire. Immediately following the fire, hundreds of people gathered near Wang Fuk Court to donate and distribute supplies to victims, but as the volunteer effort grew, police told them to leave and government workers took over the site.

    Authorities targeted people calling for accountability. Just four days after the fire, national security police reportedly arrested a university student, Miles Kwan, for “seditious intent” after he initiated an online petition calling for an independent investigation into the fire, and two others on suspicion of “inciting hatred against the government.”.

    Hong Kong and Beijing authorities subsequently accused “foreign forces” and “anti-China destabilizing forces” of using the fire to “incite hatred against the government.” Within hours of these announcements, two prominent online commentators, Ellie Yuen and Hailey Cheng, who had been frequently quoted in foreign media, said they would stop reporting on the fire.

    National security police also arrested the online commentator Wong On-yin in December after he planned to hold a news conference about the Wang Fuk Court fire and discussed on YouTube his subsequent questioning by police. The authorities prosecuted him for allegedly obstructing a national security investigation and publishing “seditious material.” He remains in custody awaiting a verdict in January 2027.

    Between April and May 2026, the authorities barred Wang Fuk Court residents from displaying banners from their homes or being accompanied by journalists as they were briefly permitted to return to their apartments to retrieve belongings.

    Also in May, the authorities arrested the former Wang Fuk Court owners’ committee member Kong Cheung-fat and his wife on allegations of fraud and money laundering. Kong had joined other owners in seeking a meeting to discuss insurance and other post-fire concerns. While out on bail, he remarked he would no longer give interviews or comment publicly. Some residents said his arrest made them more cautious about speaking publicly.

    An independent committee, set up by Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee, published a report on October 29 that found wide-ranging regulatory failures across four government bodies, including inadequate oversight of renovation work and fire safety, weaknesses in building maintenance regulation, and supervisory failures by contractors and other professionals. That day, Lee and senior officials formally apologized to the victims of the fire and their families while promising to implement “systemic reforms.” Housing Secretary Winnie Ho later stepped down from office while the authorities arrested 35 people in connection with the fire and possible corruption in the renovation project.

    Recent findings suggest that “An apology and promises of reform are no substitute for ensuring that people can freely question and criticize the authorities,” Pearson said. “The Hong Kong government should act on the independent committee’s recommendations and provide adequate compensation and other support for victims and their families.”.

    Academic Freedom in Hong Kong Under the National Security Law.

    #171561. A Study In Red, White and Blue: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle in the USA

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1429 w)
